questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A procurement company stores its supplier contracts in Amazon S3. A knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases indexes them. Each contract has a metadata file with three attributes: contract_type, year and region. These values do not appear in the contract text.
Staff type questions such as "What is the notice period in our 2023 logistics contracts in Europe?" The application calls the Retrieve API with each question, and many chunks come from other years and contract types. The team does not want to write or maintain any code that turns a question into a filter.
Which change makes each search return chunks from the right contracts?
questions.promptText:
A procurement company stores its supplier contracts in Amazon S3. A knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases indexes them. Each contract has a metadata file with three attributes: contract_type, year and region. These values do not appear in the contract text.
Staff type questions such as "What is the notice period in our 2023 logistics contracts in Europe?" The application calls the Retrieve API with each question, and many chunks come from other years and contract types. The team does not want to write or maintain any code that turns a question into a filter.
Which change makes each search return chunks from the right contracts?

options.text: Add an implicit filter configuration to each Retrieve call that lists contract_type, year and region with a description of each, and the ARN of the model that builds the filter.
Add a Lambda function that asks a model to find the contract_type, year and region in each question, and add these values to each Retrieve call as an equals filter.
Set the search type of each Retrieve call to hybrid, so that the search also matches the contract type, year and region words that each question contains.
Add a reranker model to the reranking configuration of each Retrieve call, so that the chunks that fit the contract type, year and region of each question rank first.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an implicit filter configuration to each Retrieve call that lists contract_type, year and region with a description of each, and the ARN of the model that builds the filter.
This is implicit metadata filtering, which AWS announced as auto-generated query filters for knowledge bases. The Retrieve call lists the metadata attributes that a filter may use, each with its type and a short description, and names the model that builds the filter. The knowledge base then reads each question against this schema, builds a metadata filter from values such as 2023 or logistics, and applies it to the search. So the search returns only chunks from contracts whose metadata files match. The contract type, year and region are exactly the values that the metadata files hold, and the team writes no code that reads the questions.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.2: "Develop comprehensive metadata frameworks to improve search precision and context awareness for FM interactions"

Sources:

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation
  • ImplicitFilterConfiguration
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases now provides auto-generated query filters for improved retrieval

INCORRECT: Add a Lambda function that asks a model to find the contract_type, year and region in each question, and add these values to each Retrieve call as an equals filter.
This design builds the filter in the application. A model finds the values in the question, and the function turns them into a manual metadata filter. It works, and it fits a team that wants full control, for example to check each value against a list before the search. But the team must write this code, test it, and change it each time an attribute is added. The scenario says the team does not want to write or maintain any code that turns a question into a filter.

INCORRECT: Set the search type of each Retrieve call to hybrid, so that the search also matches the contract type, year and region words that each question contains.
Hybrid search combines a search on vector embeddings with a search through the raw text of the chunks. It helps when a question contains exact words, such as a product code, that also appear in the documents. Here the contract type, year and region are only in the metadata files and not in the contract text. A text search for "2023" or "logistics" has nothing to match in these contracts, so chunks from other years and contract types stay in the results.

INCORRECT: Add a reranker model to the reranking configuration of each Retrieve call, so that the chunks that fit the contract type, year and region of each question rank first.
A reranker model calculates how relevant each returned chunk is to the question and puts the chunks in a new order. It helps when the right chunks are in the results but rank too low. The reranking configuration can also let the reranker consider the metadata of each chunk. But a reranker only scores and reorders the chunks that the search found. It applies no filter, so it cannot make sure that only chunks from 2023 logistics contracts in Europe come back. A chunk from another year can still rank high when its text fits the question well.

questions.promptHtml:
A financial services company runs a production RAG application on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. An AWS Lambda function calls RetrieveAndGenerate for every user question about investment products.
Users report that some answers are vague or off topic. The team cannot tell whether the knowledge base returned poor chunks, or the model reasoned badly over good chunks. For every production question, the team must capture which chunks the knowledge base selected and how strongly each chunk matched the question, then analyze that history in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to find failing query patterns.
Which design captures the data that the team needs?
questions.promptText:
A financial services company runs a production RAG application on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. An AWS Lambda function calls RetrieveAndGenerate for every user question about investment products.
Users report that some answers are vague or off topic. The team cannot tell whether the knowledge base returned poor chunks, or the model reasoned badly over good chunks. For every production question, the team must capture which chunks the knowledge base selected and how strongly each chunk matched the question, then analyze that history in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to find failing query patterns.
Which design captures the data that the team needs?

options.text: Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with a Retrieve call and a Converse call, and write each retrieval result with its content, location and score to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with a Retrieve call and a Converse call, and write the stopReason and token usage of each Converse response to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Keep RetrieveAndGenerate, and write the retrieved references in the citations of each response, with their cited text and metadata, to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job each night with the context relevance metric on a dataset of sample questions, and store the job results in Amazon S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with a Retrieve call and a Converse call, and write each retrieval result with its content, location and score to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Retrieve returns the chunks that the knowledge base found, and each result holds the chunk content, its source location, its metadata and a score. The score is the level of relevance of the result to the query, so it shows how strongly each chunk matched the question. When the function calls Retrieve first, it can log every result before it sends the chunks to the model with Converse. With these log entries, CloudWatch Logs Insights can group low scores by type of question, and the team can see whether a vague answer came from poor chunks or from the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.6: "Implement retrieval quality testing to evaluate and optimize information retrieval components for FM augmentation"
Example: "relevance scoring"

Sources:

  • KnowledgeBaseRetrievalResult
  • RetrievedReference
  • Creating a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job

INCORRECT: Replace RetrieveAndGenerate with a Retrieve call and a Converse call, and write the stopReason and token usage of each Converse response to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
The Converse response holds a stopReason, such as end_turn or max_tokens, and the token usage of the call. These values help a team that sees answers cut off or wants to track cost. The split into Retrieve and Converse is the right first step here. But this function logs only details of the model call, so the logs say nothing about which chunks the knowledge base selected or how strongly each one matched the question.

INCORRECT: Keep RetrieveAndGenerate, and write the retrieved references in the citations of each response, with their cited text and metadata, to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Each citation in a RetrieveAndGenerate response links a part of the generated answer to the sources that it is based on. Each retrieved reference in a citation holds the cited text, the location of its source and the metadata of the source file. Logging these references fits a team that must show users where each answer came from. Here the team must also know how strongly each chunk matched the question, and a retrieved reference has no score field. With these logs, the team sees which text each answer cited, but it cannot tell a weak match from a strong one.

INCORRECT: Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job each night with the context relevance metric on a dataset of sample questions, and store the job results in Amazon S3.
A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job tests the retrieval part of a RAG application. An evaluator model scores the retrieved chunks with metrics such as context relevance. It fits a team that compares retrieval settings on a fixed set of test questions. The job runs on the questions in a prompt dataset in Amazon S3, not on each question that a user asks in production. It does not record which chunks the knowledge base returned for each production question, and its results are not in CloudWatch Logs for Logs Insights.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare technology company runs a patient support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Doctors reach it through a third-party medical records application that already authenticates them against the corporate identity provider.
Compliance requires that every call to Bedrock is made with credentials that expire on their own, and that no engineer can route around this by issuing a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key. Audit records must tie each invocation back to a session that started with a doctor signing in.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A healthcare technology company runs a patient support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Doctors reach it through a third-party medical records application that already authenticates them against the corporate identity provider.
Compliance requires that every call to Bedrock is made with credentials that expire on their own, and that no engineer can route around this by issuing a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key. Audit records must tie each invocation back to a session that started with a doctor signing in.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Exchange the identity provider OIDC tokens through an Amazon Cognito identity pool for temporary credentials scoped by an IAM role.
Deny the bearer token actions of both Amazon Bedrock endpoints in a policy whenever the bearerTokenType condition shows a long-term key.
Generate a long-term Bedrock API key for each doctor and rotate the keys on a schedule using AWS Secrets Manager.
Cap the lifetime of long-term Bedrock keys by setting iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialAgeDays to ninety days in the key creation policy.
Attach the AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess managed policy to every principal so that access is restricted to core Amazon Bedrock operations.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Exchange the identity provider OIDC tokens through an Amazon Cognito identity pool for temporary credentials scoped by an IAM role.
An Amazon Cognito identity pool accepts a token from an OIDC identity provider and turns it into an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity request for temporary AWS credentials. The IAM role of the pool sets what those credentials may do. The doctors already sign in to the corporate identity provider, so the medical records application can exchange their tokens and call Bedrock with credentials that expire on their own, and no one stores a long-term secret. CloudTrail logs each AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity request with the information that the identity provider sends. The team can use this information to map each call made with the role session back to the doctor who signed in.

CORRECT: Deny the bearer token actions of both Amazon Bedrock endpoints in a policy whenever the bearerTokenType condition shows a long-term key.
A long-term Amazon Bedrock API key is a bearer token. An API key works with two endpoints, and each one has its own action: bedrock:CallWithBearerToken for the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and bedrock-mantle:CallWithBearerToken for the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint. The bearerTokenType condition key of each action tells a long-term key from a short-term key. A policy that denies both actions when the value is LONG_TERM stops all calls with long-term keys, even when an engineer creates such a key. Calls signed with the federated temporary credentials do not use an API key, so the approved path through the identity pool keeps working.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.3: "Create secure access frameworks to ensure appropriate security controls"
Example: "identity federation between FM services and enterprise systems"

Sources:

  • Control permissions for generating and using Amazon Bedrock API keys

  • Amazon Cognito identity pools

  • API keys for Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Generate a long-term Bedrock API key for each doctor and rotate the keys on a schedule using AWS Secrets Manager.
A long-term Amazon Bedrock API key is an IAM service-specific credential that belongs to an IAM user. It works as a bearer token, so anyone who holds the key can call Amazon Bedrock with it. Regular rotation fits a team that must use long-term keys, because each key is replaced after a set time. But this option creates a long-term key for every doctor, and the compliance rule does not allow long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys. A call made with such a key also leads back to an IAM user, not to a session that started with a doctor signing in.

INCORRECT: Cap the lifetime of long-term Bedrock keys by setting iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialAgeDays to ninety days in the key creation policy.
The iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialAgeDays condition key sets how many days a new long-term API key may stay valid. For example, a policy can allow only keys that expire within ninety days. This fits a team that allows long-term keys but wants each one to expire. Here the compliance rule does not allow long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys at all, so a shorter key life does not meet it. A key that lasts ninety days is still a long-term key, and calls made with it do not lead back to a doctor's sign-in.

INCORRECT: Attach the AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess managed policy to every principal so that access is restricted to core Amazon Bedrock operations.
AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess is an AWS managed policy that grants access to core Amazon Bedrock API operations. It fits a team that wants to give principals a standard set of Bedrock permissions. A permissions policy like this decides which actions a principal may call. It does not decide which kind of credential the principal uses, so a call made with a long-term API key still passes when the key's IAM user has this policy. The compliance rule is about the credential type, and this option does not control it.

questions.promptHtml:
At a software company, an AWS Lambda function asks a large FM in Amazon Bedrock to choose one of 12 product teams for each support ticket. In a test on CPU, a small pre-trained text classification model from the Hugging Face Hub chose the same teams at a lower cost.

Compute charges must stop during the many hours each night when no tickets arrive. In the largest burst, up to 30 tickets arrive at the same time. The function needs the team name in the reply from the model. If compute is still starting, the function waits and calls again. The company accepts this short wait, but no ticket may fail.

How should the company host the small model?
questions.promptText:
At a software company, an AWS Lambda function asks a large FM in Amazon Bedrock to choose one of 12 product teams for each support ticket. In a test on CPU, a small pre-trained text classification model from the Hugging Face Hub chose the same teams at a lower cost.
Compute charges must stop during the many hours each night when no tickets arrive. In the largest burst, up to 30 tickets arrive at the same time. The function needs the team name in the reply from the model. If compute is still starting, the function waits and calls again. The company accepts this short wait, but no ticket may fail.
How should the company host the small model?

options.text: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint with enough memory for the model and a maximum concurrency that fits the largest burst, and call it for each ticket.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on CPU instances, with target tracking auto scaling that adds instances for the largest burst and keeps at least one instance running.
Deploy the model as an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, with scaling policies that scale to zero instances when idle, and call it for each ticket.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances when idle, and send each ticket to the endpoint as a request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint with enough memory for the model and a maximum concurrency that fits the largest burst, and call it for each ticket.
Serverless Inference starts compute when requests arrive and scales the endpoint down to zero when no requests come, so the quiet nights cost nothing for compute. Serverless Inference does not support GPUs, but this small model works on CPU. The maximum concurrency sets how many calls the endpoint processes at the same time, and SageMaker AI throttles every call above that number. With a maximum concurrency of at least 30, no ticket in the largest burst receives a throttling error. A cold start can come after a quiet night or when a burst grows. While SageMaker AI provisions compute, a call can return ModelNotReadyException. The function then waits and calls again, which is the short wait that the company accepts.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.3: "Develop optimized FM deployment approaches to balance performance and resource requirements for GenAI workloads"
Example: "smaller pre-trained models for specific tasks"

Sources:

  • Deploy models with Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference

  • Scale an endpoint to zero instances

  • InvokeEndpoint (Amazon SageMaker API Reference)

INCORRECT: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on CPU instances, with target tracking auto scaling that adds instances for the largest burst and keeps at least one instance running.
A real-time endpoint answers each call quickly, and target tracking adds instances when a burst comes. This design fits steady traffic, where an instance is busy for most of the day. Here the endpoint keeps at least one instance running, so the company pays for that instance during the long nights when no tickets arrive. Compute charges must stop at those times.

INCORRECT: Deploy the model as an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, with scaling policies that scale to zero instances when idle, and call it for each ticket.
An endpoint that hosts inference components can scale to zero instances, so compute charges stop while the endpoint is idle. This fits callers that can wait several minutes for the first answer after a quiet period. With no instance, the endpoint cannot answer, and a new instance takes several minutes to start. During that time, every call to the endpoint returns an error. After each quiet night, the function would wait and call again for minutes, which is not the short wait that the company accepts.

INCORRECT: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances when idle, and send each ticket to the endpoint as a request.
Asynchronous Inference puts each request in a queue and processes it later. It fits large inputs and long processing times, and it can scale to zero instances when there are no requests. But the call returns only an identifier and an Amazon S3 output location, and SageMaker AI writes the result to that location after it processes the request. The function needs the team name in the reply, so the function cannot use a result that arrives in Amazon S3 later.

questions.promptHtml:
A financial services company built a loan application assistant using Amazon Bedrock with multiple guardrails enabled. The guardrails include jailbreak detection, personally identifiable information (PII) filtering, and restricted topic blocking for investment advice. In production, valid questions from applicants about loan terms are occasionally blocked. The development team needs granular visibility into exactly which guardrail rule triggered each block and the specific content that caused the violation to distinguish false positives from actual security threats.
Which configuration provides the MOST comprehensive analysis of guardrail blocking decisions?
questions.promptText:
A financial services company built a loan application assistant using Amazon Bedrock with multiple guardrails enabled. The guardrails include jailbreak detection, personally identifiable information (PII) filtering, and restricted topic blocking for investment advice. In production, valid questions from applicants about loan terms are occasionally blocked. The development team needs granular visibility into exactly which guardrail rule triggered each block and the specific content that caused the violation to distinguish false positives from actual security threats.
Which configuration provides the MOST comprehensive analysis of guardrail blocking decisions?

options.text: Turn on the guardrail trace in each model request and log the trace, and chart the InvocationsIntervened metric by its GuardrailPolicyType dimension in Amazon CloudWatch.
Chart the InvocationsIntervened metric by its GuardrailPolicyType dimension in Amazon CloudWatch, and add an alarm for each policy type that intervenes more often than usual.
Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and count the logged responses whose stopReason is guardrail_intervened with CloudWatch Logs Insights queries.
Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter and an alarm on the logged responses whose stopReason is guardrail_intervened.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on the guardrail trace in each model request and log the trace, and chart the InvocationsIntervened metric by its GuardrailPolicyType dimension in Amazon CloudWatch.
The guardrail trace adds the guardrail's assessment to each response. For each block, it names the policy that acted and what it found: a denied topic by its name, a content filter by its type, such as PROMPT_ATTACK for a jailbreak, with its confidence, or a piece of personal data by its type and the matched text. When the application logs the trace with each question, the team can see which rule stopped a loan question and why, and decide whether it was a false positive. The InvocationsIntervened metric with the GuardrailPolicyType dimension adds the trend: how often each policy type, such as TopicPolicy or SensitiveInformationPolicy, intervenes over time.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "automated detection for misuse, drift, and policy violations"

Sources:

  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock Guardrails using CloudWatch metrics
  • Include a guardrail with the Converse API
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

INCORRECT: Chart the InvocationsIntervened metric by its GuardrailPolicyType dimension in Amazon CloudWatch, and add an alarm for each policy type that intervenes more often than usual.
InvocationsIntervened counts the invocations where a guardrail intervened, and the GuardrailPolicyType dimension splits that count by policy type. Alarms on it fit a team that wants a warning when blocks rise. But a metric holds only counts. It cannot show which denied topic or which filter stopped one applicant's question, or which words caused it, so the team cannot tell a false positive from a real threat.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and count the logged responses whose stopReason is guardrail_intervened with CloudWatch Logs Insights queries.
Model invocation logging records the full request and response data of each model call. When a guardrail blocks content, the stopReason of the response is guardrail_intervened, so a count of this value fits a team that needs the number of blocked calls. The stopReason says only that a guardrail intervened. Without the trace, the logged response does not name the policy or the rule that acted, so the team cannot see which rule needs tuning.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter and an alarm on the logged responses whose stopReason is guardrail_intervened.
A metric filter turns matching log events into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm on that metric warns the on-call team when blocks rise. The metric still counts only that a guardrail intervened. It names no policy and no matched content, so it gives no detail about why each loan question was blocked.

questions.promptHtml:
A bank runs a support chatbot on Amazon Bedrock. When a chat ends, the chat application sends the transcript as a message to an Amazon SQS queue. An archiving function, which the platform team owns, reads each message and writes it to an Amazon S3 bucket. The queue and the bucket already use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys.
The security team requires that no one on the platform team can read any transcript, in the queue, in the function or in the bucket. Support agents must later read each full transcript in the chat application, which runs with its own IAM role.
Which change meets the security team's requirement?
questions.promptText:
A bank runs a support chatbot on Amazon Bedrock. When a chat ends, the chat application sends the transcript as a message to an Amazon SQS queue. An archiving function, which the platform team owns, reads each message and writes it to an Amazon S3 bucket. The queue and the bucket already use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys.
The security team requires that no one on the platform team can read any transcript, in the queue, in the function or in the bucket. Support agents must later read each full transcript in the chat application, which runs with its own IAM role.
Which change meets the security team's requirement?

options.text: In the chat application, encrypt each transcript with the AWS Encryption SDK and a KMS keyring, on a KMS key that only the application role can use to decrypt.
Change the key policy of the bucket's KMS key so that only the chat application role can decrypt, and keep the server-side encryption on the queue and the bucket.
Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject to every principal except the chat application role, and keep the server-side encryption on the queue and the bucket.
In the chat application, mask the names, account numbers and addresses in each transcript with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail before it sends the transcript to the queue.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the chat application, encrypt each transcript with the AWS Encryption SDK and a KMS keyring, on a KMS key that only the application role can use to decrypt.
This is client-side encryption. The AWS Encryption SDK encrypts each transcript inside the chat application, before the transcript is sent anywhere. The KMS keyring generates a data key under the KMS key, and the SDK stores the encrypted transcript and the encrypted data key together in one encrypted message. The queue, the archiving function and the bucket only ever hold this encrypted message, so the platform team sees no text anywhere. To decrypt, a caller needs kms:Decrypt on the KMS key. Only the application role has it, so support agents still read each full transcript in the chat application.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"

Sources:

  • What is the AWS Encryption SDK?

  • Encryption at rest in Amazon SQS

  • AWS KMS keyrings

INCORRECT: Change the key policy of the bucket's KMS key so that only the chat application role can decrypt, and keep the server-side encryption on the queue and the bucket.
A key policy controls who can use a KMS key, and a download of an object encrypted with SSE-KMS needs kms:Decrypt on that key. So this change stops other people from reading the stored objects, which fits a team whose only risk is reads from the bucket. But the queue keeps its own server-side encryption, and Amazon SQS decrypts each message when it sends it to an authorized consumer. The archiving function is that consumer, so the platform team still gets each full transcript in its own function.

INCORRECT: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject to every principal except the chat application role, and keep the server-side encryption on the queue and the bucket.
A bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject to other principals stops direct downloads from the bucket. It fits a team that must block reads of stored files by other roles. It does nothing for the queue or the function. Amazon SQS decrypts each message for the archiving function, which reads the whole transcript before it writes the object, and the platform team owns that function.

INCORRECT: In the chat application, mask the names, account numbers and addresses in each transcript with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail before it sends the transcript to the queue.
A guardrail sensitive information filter can mask personal data, and the ApplyGuardrail API checks any text without a call to a model. Masking replaces each value with its type, such as {NAME}. This fits a team that keeps transcripts for analytics and never needs the original values. Here support agents must later read each full transcript, and masked values cannot be restored. The rest of each conversation also stays readable to the platform team.

questions.promptHtml:
A marketing agency deploys a video generation model from Hugging Face on Amazon SageMaker AI. The model needs GPU instances for inference and takes several minutes to create one video. Marketing teams upload ZIP files of up to 75 MB to Amazon S3 through a web portal. Each ZIP file contains a short campaign brief and product photos, and the system creates one promotional video from each file. The marketing teams accept a wait of up to 20 minutes.

Uploads come at irregular times. GPU instances must stop when no file is waiting. The system must also process a file that arrives when no instance is running.

Which deployment approach meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A marketing agency deploys a video generation model from Hugging Face on Amazon SageMaker AI. The model needs GPU instances for inference and takes several minutes to create one video. Marketing teams upload ZIP files of up to 75 MB to Amazon S3 through a web portal. Each ZIP file contains a short campaign brief and product photos, and the system creates one promotional video from each file. The marketing teams accept a wait of up to 20 minutes.
Uploads come at irregular times. GPU instances must stop when no file is waiting. The system must also process a file that arrives when no instance is running.
Which deployment approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a SageMaker AI asynchronous endpoint that scales to zero GPU instances and scales out on the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.

Use an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that scales to zero GPU instances and scales out on the NoCapacityInvocationFailures metric, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.
Use an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that keeps one GPU instance running at all times, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.
Run a SageMaker AI batch transform job on GPU instances once each night, over all of the ZIP files that the marketing teams uploaded to Amazon S3 that day.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a SageMaker AI asynchronous endpoint that scales to zero GPU instances and scales out on the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.
An asynchronous endpoint puts each request in a queue and processes it in the background. It accepts inputs of up to 1 GB and processing times of up to one hour, so a 75 MB file and a video that takes several minutes both fit. An S3 event notification starts the Lambda function for each new file, and the function passes the location of the file to InvokeEndpointAsync. The endpoint writes the video to Amazon S3. With a minimum of zero instances, no GPU instance runs while no file is waiting. A target tracking policy alone starts an instance only when the queue grows past its target, so a single file could wait for a long time. A CloudWatch alarm on HasBacklogWithoutCapacity starts a step scaling policy as soon as the queue has a request and the endpoint has no instance.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.1: "Deploy FMs based on specific application needs and performance requirements"

Sources:

  • Asynchronous inference

  • Autoscale an asynchronous endpoint

  • Scale an endpoint to zero instances

INCORRECT: Use an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that scales to zero GPU instances and scales out on the NoCapacityInvocationFailures metric, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.
An endpoint that hosts inference components can also scale to zero instances, and a step scaling policy on NoCapacityInvocationFailures starts an instance when a call finds no instance. This saves money for an interactive model with quiet hours and callers that can try again. But a real-time endpoint cannot take a 75 MB file in one call, and a regular call must return within 60 seconds, while each video takes several minutes. The endpoint also keeps no queue, so every call returns an error until a new instance is ready. Amazon S3 invokes the Lambda function asynchronously, and Lambda tries a failed run only two more times, within about three minutes, and then discards the event. So a file can stay unprocessed.

INCORRECT: Use an inference component on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that keeps one GPU instance running at all times, and call it from a Lambda function for each new file.
A real-time endpoint with an instance that always runs suits steady traffic that needs fast answers, such as a chat assistant. It never starts from zero, so no call fails for lack of an instance. Here the uploads come at irregular times, and this GPU instance keeps running and costing money while no file is waiting. GPU instances must stop at those times. A real-time call also cannot take a 75 MB file or wait several minutes for a video.

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker AI batch transform job on GPU instances once each night, over all of the ZIP files that the marketing teams uploaded to Amazon S3 that day.
Batch transform runs inference over a dataset that is ready in advance, with no persistent endpoint. It suits large jobs where the results can wait, for example a nightly run over all of the records of one day. Here a file that arrives in the morning would receive its video only after the next nightly run. The marketing teams accept a wait of up to 20 minutes, not most of a day.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a patent search tool for its legal team. The tool keeps tens of millions of 1,024-dimension embeddings in a k-NN index on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain that runs the latest OpenSearch version. The index uses the HNSW method and stores each vector dimension as a 32-bit float, so the index needs large memory-optimized data nodes.
The company wants to move the domain to data nodes with about one tenth of today's memory. Search results must stay about as accurate as they are today. The lawyers accept a short wait for each list of results.
Which index change meets these goals?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a patent search tool for its legal team. The tool keeps tens of millions of 1,024-dimension embeddings in a k-NN index on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain that runs the latest OpenSearch version. The index uses the HNSW method and stores each vector dimension as a 32-bit float, so the index needs large memory-optimized data nodes.
The company wants to move the domain to data nodes with about one tenth of today's memory. Search results must stay about as accurate as they are today. The lawyers accept a short wait for each list of results.
Which index change meets these goals?

options.text: Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses on_disk mode, so binary vectors stay in memory and full-precision vectors on disk rescore the best matches.
Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses FP16 scalar quantization, so each vector dimension takes 16 bits in memory instead of 32 bits.
Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses byte quantization, so each vector dimension takes 8 bits in memory instead of 32 bits.
Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index with a lower m value for the HNSW graph, so the graph keeps fewer links for each vector in memory.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses on_disk mode, so binary vectors stay in memory and full-precision vectors on disk rescore the best matches.
In on_disk mode, the k-NN index keeps only compressed vectors in memory, and the full-precision vectors stay on disk. With binary compression, each vector dimension takes one bit instead of 32 bits, so the memory that the index needs falls well below one tenth of today's. A search runs in two phases. First, it finds candidate matches with the compressed vectors in memory. Then it reads the full-precision vectors of those candidates from disk and scores them again, so the results keep high quality. Reading from disk makes each search slower than a search in memory, and the lawyers accept a short wait. The mode needs OpenSearch 2.17 or later, and the domain runs the latest version.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.3: "Deploy and configure vector search solutions to enable semantic search capabilities for FM augmentation"
Example: "OpenSearch Service with vector search capabilities"

Sources:

  • Disk-optimized vector engine now available on the Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • OpenSearch Vector Engine is now disk-optimized for low cost, accurate vector search
  • Cost Optimized Vector Database: Introduction to Amazon OpenSearch Service quantization techniques

INCORRECT: Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses FP16 scalar quantization, so each vector dimension takes 16 bits in memory instead of 32 bits.
FP16 scalar quantization stores each vector dimension as a 16-bit float. It halves the memory of the vectors, keeps recall high, and keeps every search in memory and fast. It is a good choice when half of today's memory is enough. Here the company needs about one tenth of today's memory, and half is much more than that.

INCORRECT: Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index that uses byte quantization, so each vector dimension takes 8 bits in memory instead of 32 bits.
Byte quantization stores each vector dimension in one byte, which cuts the memory of the vectors by about three quarters. Searches stay in memory, so this suits an index that must keep very fast answers. But one quarter of today's memory is still more than twice the one tenth that the company wants.

INCORRECT: Reindex the embeddings into a new k-NN index with a lower m value for the HNSW graph, so the graph keeps fewer links for each vector in memory.
The m value sets how many links each vector has in the HNSW graph, and each link takes memory. A lower m helps when vectors have few dimensions, because then the links are a large part of the memory. Here each vector has 1,024 dimensions. The vector data takes most of the memory, so fewer links save only a small part of it. The index would still need far more than one tenth of today's memory.
