For example, an answer about parental leave gives its length but not its pay rules. Spot checks show that the retrieved passages are about the right policy, and that the answers state nothing that the passages do not support.
HR experts wrote a reference answer for each of 300 test questions. Before the team changes the prompt or the model, it must learn whether the missing facts never reached the model, or whether the model left them out.
Which evaluation should the team run?
questions.promptText:
A human resources company runs a policy assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The assistant calls the RetrieveAndGenerate API. Employees say that answers leave out facts. For example, an answer about parental leave gives its length but not its pay rules. Spot checks show that the retrieved passages are about the right policy, and that the answers state nothing that the passages do not support.
HR experts wrote a reference answer for each of 300 test questions. Before the team changes the prompt or the model, it must learn whether the missing facts never reached the model, or whether the model left them out.
Which evaluation should the team run?

options.text: Create a retrieve-only evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question and its reference answer, and score the retrieved texts with Context coverage.
Create a retrieve-only evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question, and score the retrieved texts with the Context relevance metric.
Create a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question, and score the generated answers with the Faithfulness metric.
Create a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question and its reference answer, and score all the generated answers with Completeness.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a retrieve-only evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question and its reference answer, and score the retrieved texts with Context coverage.
A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job tests only the retrieval step of the knowledge base, with no generated answer. Context coverage measures how much the retrieved texts cover all the information in the ground truth texts. For this reason it needs a reference answer for each question in the prompt dataset, and the HR experts already wrote them. A low score on a question shows that facts such as the pay rules were never retrieved, so the fix belongs in retrieval. A high score shows that the facts reached the model, so the problem sits in the generation step. This is what the team must learn before it changes the prompt or the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.6: "Implement retrieval quality testing to evaluate and optimize information retrieval components for FM augmentation"
Example: "context matching verification"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand RAG system performance
  • Create a prompt dataset for retrieve-only RAG evaluation jobs
  • Amazon Bedrock now supports RAG Evaluation (generally available)

INCORRECT: Create a retrieve-only evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question, and score the retrieved texts with the Context relevance metric.
Context relevance measures how relevant the retrieved texts are to each question, and it needs no reference answers. It fits a team that suspects the knowledge base returns text that does not fit the question. Here spot checks show that the passages are about the right policy, so they would score as relevant. A passage that gives the length of parental leave but not its pay rules is still relevant, so this score cannot show which facts are missing.

INCORRECT: Create a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question, and score the generated answers with the Faithfulness metric.
Faithfulness measures how well the generated answers avoid hallucination with respect to the retrieved texts. It fits answers that add facts that the passages do not hold. The spot checks show that the answers state nothing that the passages do not support. The problem here is facts that are left out, and an answer that leaves out the pay rules can still be fully faithful.

INCORRECT: Create a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job with a prompt dataset that holds each test question and its reference answer, and score all the generated answers with Completeness.
Completeness measures how well the generated answers resolve all aspects of the questions, so it would confirm that answers leave out facts. It fits a team that tracks the quality of the final answers. But it grades each answer after both retrieval and generation. A low score cannot show whether the pay rules were missing from the retrieved passages or whether the model left them out, and the team must know this before it changes the prompt or the model.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare organization has strict AI governance requirements mandating that all interactions with foundation models must include content filtering guardrails for HIPAA compliance. The security team configured Amazon Bedrock guardrails to detect and block protected health information (PHI) in both prompts and responses. Every call that developers make with the InvokeModel or Converse API must name the approved guardrail, so that it always checks model responses. The security team will not run a service between developers and Amazon Bedrock. The solution needs to prevent any FM invocations that don't include the required guardrail configuration.
Which solution enforces mandatory guardrail usage MOST operationally efficiently?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare organization has strict AI governance requirements mandating that all interactions with foundation models must include content filtering guardrails for HIPAA compliance. The security team configured Amazon Bedrock guardrails to detect and block protected health information (PHI) in both prompts and responses. Every call that developers make with the InvokeModel or Converse API must name the approved guardrail, so that it always checks model responses. The security team will not run a service between developers and Amazon Bedrock. The solution needs to prevent any FM invocations that don't include the required guardrail configuration.
Which solution enforces mandatory guardrail usage MOST operationally efficiently?

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that denies bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream unless the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier value in the request matches the approved guardrail ARN.
Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that allows bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the approved guardrail ARN and denies bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on every other guardrail.
Send every developer call through an AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway that adds the approved guardrail to each request before it calls Amazon Bedrock.
Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon S3, and have an AWS Lambda function check each new log for the guardrail and alert the security team.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that denies bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream unless the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier value in the request matches the approved guardrail ARN.
The bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key holds the guardrail that a request names. A Deny statement with a condition that the key does not match the approved guardrail ARN blocks every call that names another guardrail. It also blocks every call that names no guardrail, because a "not equal" condition is true when the key is missing from the request. An explicit deny overrides any allow in the role's other policies. The Converse API needs the bedrock:InvokeModel permission, and ConverseStream needs bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so one policy covers all four APIs. IAM checks the policy before the model runs, and no new service sits between the developers and Amazon Bedrock. One limit remains: a developer can use guardrail input tags to keep parts of a prompt out of the check, but the guardrail always checks the response.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.3: "Create organizational governance systems to ensure consistent oversight of FM implementations"

Sources:

  • Enforce the use of specific guardrails in model inference requests
  • Inference using Converse API
  • IAM JSON policy elements: Condition operators

INCORRECT: Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that allows bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the approved guardrail ARN and denies bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on every other guardrail.
A policy on bedrock:ApplyGuardrail controls which guardrails a role may use. It fits, for example, an application that checks text with the ApplyGuardrail API and must use only the approved guardrail. But it does not change the bedrock:InvokeModel permission. A guardrail is optional in an inference call, so a developer can still call InvokeModel or Converse with no guardrail at all, and the model runs without the PHI checks.

INCORRECT: Send every developer call through an AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway that adds the approved guardrail to each request before it calls Amazon Bedrock.
A Lambda function behind API Gateway can act as a central gateway. It can add the guardrail, log each call and apply other company rules, which suits a company that wants one controlled entry point for all model calls. Here the security team will not run a service between developers and Amazon Bedrock. A proxy also prevents nothing on its own: developers whose roles can call Amazon Bedrock directly can still skip the proxy.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon S3, and have an AWS Lambda function check each new log for the guardrail and alert the security team.
Model invocation logs hold the full request data of each call, so a function can find the calls that did not use the guardrail and alert the security team. This is a good detective control for audits. But it acts after the call, when the model has already received the prompt and returned its response. The question asks for a control that prevents any call without the guardrail.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A travel company runs a chat assistant behind an Amazon API Gateway REST API. For each message, an AWS Lambda function written in Python reads the traveler's booking from Amazon DynamoDB, calls the company's pricing service over HTTPS, and then calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API.
Since last week, some replies take far longer than others. During slow requests, the function's memory and CPU use stay low. Several other applications call the same Bedrock model all day.
The team must see, for each slow request, how long each of the three calls took.
Which approach gives the team this view?
questions.promptText:
A travel company runs a chat assistant behind an Amazon API Gateway REST API. For each message, an AWS Lambda function written in Python reads the traveler's booking from Amazon DynamoDB, calls the company's pricing service over HTTPS, and then calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API.
Since last week, some replies take far longer than others. During slow requests, the function's memory and CPU use stay low. Several other applications call the same Bedrock model all day.
The team must see, for each slow request, how long each of the three calls took.
Which approach gives the team this view?

options.text: Add the ADOT Lambda layer with its wrapper setting, turn on active tracing, and compare the time of each subsegment in the X-Ray traces of slow requests.
Turn on active tracing for the function and for the API Gateway stage, and compare the time of each segment in the X-Ray traces of slow requests.
Turn on CloudWatch Lambda Insights for the function, and compare the duration, memory use and CPU time of slow invocations with those of fast invocations.
Graph the InvocationLatency metric of the model ID in CloudWatch next to the Duration metric of the function, and match the peaks of the two lines.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the ADOT Lambda layer with its wrapper setting, turn on active tracing, and compare the time of each subsegment in the X-Ray traces of slow requests.
AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) offers a Lambda layer that instruments a function with no change to its code. With the AWS_LAMBDA_EXEC_WRAPPER setting, the layer creates spans for the function invocation and for each downstream request: here the DynamoDB read, the HTTPS call to the pricing service and the Converse call. Active tracing makes Lambda record its own segments, and X-Ray shows the downstream calls as subsegments. In the trace of a slow request, the team sees how long each of the three calls took and finds the one that adds the time.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.6: "Improve troubleshooting efficiency for FM applications"
Example: "X-Ray to trace FM API calls"

Sources:

  • Send application telemetry from AWS Lambda
  • Migrate to OpenTelemetry Python
  • Visualize Lambda function invocations using AWS X-Ray

INCORRECT: Turn on active tracing for the function and for the API Gateway stage, and compare the time of each segment in the X-Ray traces of slow requests.
Active tracing on its own records two segments for a sampled request. One covers the work that the Lambda service does to prepare the execution environment, and the other covers the work of the function. Tracing on the API Gateway stage adds the time of the API itself. This view helps when the team must find out whether the time goes to the API, to a cold start or to the function. Because the function code is not instrumented, it does not split the function's time into the three calls, and the team must see each call.

INCORRECT: Turn on CloudWatch Lambda Insights for the function, and compare the duration, memory use and CPU time of slow invocations with those of fast invocations.
Lambda Insights collects system-level metrics, such as CPU time, memory, disk and network use, and writes one performance log event for each invocation. It finds functions that run short of memory or CPU. Here the function's memory and CPU use stay low during the slow requests, so these numbers do not explain the delay. Each event also describes the whole invocation, so it cannot show which of the three calls took the time.

INCORRECT: Graph the InvocationLatency metric of the model ID in CloudWatch next to the Duration metric of the function, and match the peaks of the two lines.
InvocationLatency measures the time from when a request is sent to Amazon Bedrock until the last token comes back. Graphed for one model ID, it shows whether that model became slower over time. But the metric has no dimension for the calling application, so it mixes in the calls of the other applications that use the same model all day. It also shows statistics over periods of time, not the three calls of one slow request.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare organization is deploying a clinical decision support assistant on Amazon Bedrock across cardiology, oncology, and emergency medicine.
Compliance sets two rules. Every prompt template must be signed off by a medical reviewer before any department can call it in production. Separately, the full text of every prompt sent and every response returned must be retained for ten years in a form that no employee, administrator, or account owner can alter or delete, because the records may be produced in litigation.
The reviewers have no AWS access and sign off in the hospital's review portal.
Developers do not change a template while a reviewer checks it.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A healthcare organization is deploying a clinical decision support assistant on Amazon Bedrock across cardiology, oncology, and emergency medicine.
Compliance sets two rules. Every prompt template must be signed off by a medical reviewer before any department can call it in production. Separately, the full text of every prompt sent and every response returned must be retained for ten years in a form that no employee, administrator, or account owner can alter or delete, because the records may be produced in litigation.
The reviewers have no AWS access and sign off in the hospital's review portal.
Developers do not change a template while a reviewer checks it.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and replicate the log objects to a second bucket that uses S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a ten-year default retention.
Keep the templates in Prompt Management, and have a Step Functions workflow create a new prompt version only after a callback task receives the approval of the medical reviewer.
Keep the templates in Prompt Management, and let only an IAM role for the medical reviewers create a prompt version after they test each draft in the console.
Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and replicate the log objects to a second bucket that uses S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a ten-year default retention.
Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule that archives the log objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and expires them after ten years.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and replicate the log objects to a second bucket that uses S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a ten-year default retention.
Model invocation logging writes the full request and response data of each call to an S3 bucket. Large bodies go into separate objects in the same bucket. S3 Replication then copies each log object to the second bucket. The log objects carry no retention of their own, so the default retention of the destination bucket applies to each copy. In compliance mode, no user, not even the root user of the account, can overwrite or delete a locked object version, and nobody can shorten its retention period. So no employee, administrator or account owner can change the copied records during the ten years.

CORRECT: Keep the templates in Prompt Management, and have a Step Functions workflow create a new prompt version only after a callback task receives the approval of the medical reviewer.
Prompt Management stores each template as a draft. A prompt version is a fixed snapshot of that draft at the moment the version is created, and the departments call the version in production. The approval runs in Step Functions, outside Prompt Management. A callback task passes a task token to the review portal and pauses until the portal sends the token back with SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. Only after an approval does the next step create the version. Developers do not change a template while a reviewer checks it, so the new version holds exactly the text that the reviewer signed off. The reviewers work in their own portal and never need AWS access.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.3: "Implement comprehensive prompt management and governance systems to ensure consistency and oversight of FM operations"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create parameterized templates and approval workflows"

Sources:

  • What does Amazon S3 replicate?
  • Locking objects with Object Lock
  • AGENTOPS02-BP01 Evolve agent prompts, tool calls, and configurations to reflect evolving business needs

INCORRECT: Keep the templates in Prompt Management, and let only an IAM role for the medical reviewers create a prompt version after they test each draft in the console.
Giving only the reviewers' IAM role the bedrock:CreatePromptVersion permission separates duties. Developers edit the draft, and only the reviewers can create the versions that departments call. This fits a team whose reviewers work in the AWS console. Here the reviewers have no AWS access and sign off only in the hospital's review portal, so they cannot use this role.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and replicate the log objects to a second bucket that uses S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a ten-year default retention.
Governance mode also stops most users from deleting a locked object version or changing its lock settings. But a user with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can override the retention by adding the bypass header to the request. Governance mode fits records that most staff must not delete while a few administrators still can. Here no administrator or account owner may alter or delete the records, so only compliance mode meets the rule.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule that archives the log objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and expires them after ten years.
An S3 Lifecycle rule moves objects to another storage class and expires them after a set time. This is a low-cost way to carry out a retention policy. But a lifecycle rule only schedules transitions and expiration, and it does not lock the objects. A user with delete permission can still remove a record before the ten years end, which breaks the rule for litigation records.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each insurance claim. One state calls a model in Amazon Bedrock for a summary. The next state invokes an AWS Lambda function that calls a partner's fraud scoring API. The function runs in many execution environments at the same time.

Last month, the partner API was down for six hours. The Lambda task already had a Retry field with exponential backoff, so thousands of executions kept calling the API and waiting. Now, after repeated failures, new executions must stop calling the API and send their claims straight to an Amazon SQS review queue. After a set wait, the workflow must try the API again.

Which workflow design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company runs an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each insurance claim. One state calls a model in Amazon Bedrock for a summary. The next state invokes an AWS Lambda function that calls a partner's fraud scoring API. The function runs in many execution environments at the same time.
Last month, the partner API was down for six hours. The Lambda task already had a Retry field with exponential backoff, so thousands of executions kept calling the API and waiting. Now, after repeated failures, new executions must stop calling the API and send their claims straight to an Amazon SQS review queue. After a set wait, the workflow must try the API again.
Which workflow design meets these requirements?

options.text: Store an OPEN status record with an expiry time in an Amazon DynamoDB table when retries fail, and send new claims to the review queue while that record has not expired.
Keep a failure count in a global variable in the Lambda function code, return a fallback result once the count passes a limit, and reset the count after a set wait.
Change the Retry field on the Lambda task to more attempts and a higher backoff rate, so each execution waits longer between its own calls to the partner API.
Add a Catch field on the Lambda task that sends the claim to the review queue after the retries fail, so each execution moves on after its own calls to the partner API fail.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Store an OPEN status record with an expiry time in an Amazon DynamoDB table when retries fail, and send new claims to the review queue while that record has not expired.
This option builds a circuit breaker with Step Functions. A DynamoDB table stores one status record for the partner API, and every execution reads that record in its first state. When the retries of an execution fail, the workflow writes an OPEN record with an expiry time. While that record has not expired, a Choice state sends each new claim straight to the review queue, so new executions do not call the partner API or wait for it. When the expiry time passes, the next execution calls the API again. The record is in one table, so all executions share it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.3: "Design resilient AI systems to ensure continuous operation during service disruptions"
Example: "AWS Step Functions circuit breaker patterns"

Sources:

  • Circuit breaker pattern

  • Using the circuit breaker pattern with AWS Step Functions and Amazon DynamoDB

  • Understanding Lambda function scaling

INCORRECT: Keep a failure count in a global variable in the Lambda function code, return a fallback result once the count passes a limit, and reset the count after a set wait.
Some services keep a failure count in memory. That works when one long-running process handles every request. Lambda is different. The function runs in many execution environments at the same time, and each environment has its own memory. A count in one environment never reaches the others, so most environments keep calling the partner API. The count is also lost when Lambda removes an environment. This option also returns a fallback result instead of sending the claim to the review queue.

INCORRECT: Change the Retry field on the Lambda task to more attempts and a higher backoff rate, so each execution waits longer between its own calls to the partner API.
The Retry field with exponential backoff fits temporary errors that stop after a few tries. Here the Lambda task already had backoff, and the outage lasted six hours. More attempts and longer waits make each execution call the partner API more times and delay its claim longer. Thousands of executions still call the failing API.

INCORRECT: Add a Catch field on the Lambda task that sends the claim to the review queue after the retries fail, so each execution moves on after its own calls to the partner API fail.
A Catch field sends an execution to another state after its retries fail. It fits a single request that fails, because that one claim moves on. But each execution decides on its own. During an outage, every new claim still calls the partner API, retries, and waits before the Catch field sends the claim to the queue. Nothing tells a new execution that the API is already down, so new executions keep calling the failing API.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs RAG search on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. A k-NN index that uses the Faiss engine holds product manual chunks, each with a product_line field. An AWS Lambda function sends a bool query that asks the knn clause for 10 chunks, with a term filter on product_line beside it, and passes the chunks to a model in Amazon Bedrock.
Searches for small product lines often return two or three chunks, or none. In a test, raising k returned more chunks but made each search much slower. Searches must stay fast, and large product lines hold millions of chunks. Other applications read this index, so its layout and settings must not change.
Which change fixes these searches?
questions.promptText:
A company runs RAG search on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. A k-NN index that uses the Faiss engine holds product manual chunks, each with a product_line field. An AWS Lambda function sends a bool query that asks the knn clause for 10 chunks, with a term filter on product_line beside it, and passes the chunks to a model in Amazon Bedrock.
Searches for small product lines often return two or three chunks, or none. In a test, raising k returned more chunks but made each search much slower. Searches must stay fast, and large product lines hold millions of chunks. Other applications read this index, so its layout and settings must not change.
Which change fixes these searches?

options.text: Replace the knn clause with a script_score query that computes exact k-NN scores only for chunks that pass the product_line filter, and return the 10 highest scoring chunks.
Move the product_line term filter into the filter parameter of the knn clause, so the engine applies it while it searches the vectors and returns 10 matching chunks.
Keep the term filter beside the knn clause, raise k on the knn clause to several hundred, and return the 10 highest scoring chunks that pass the product_line filter.
Create a separate k-NN index for each product line, and send each search only to the index of the product line that the user picked in the app.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Move the product_line term filter into the filter parameter of the knn clause, so the engine applies it while it searches the vectors and returns 10 matching chunks.
A filter beside the knn clause runs after the vector search. The search first finds the 10 nearest chunks in the whole index, and then the filter removes every chunk from other product lines. For a small product line, few or none of those 10 chunks are left. A filter inside the knn clause works in a different way. With the Faiss engine, OpenSearch chooses how to apply it for each search: it can filter first and then run the approximate search, or it can run an exact search on the matching chunks. Either way, the search looks only at chunks of the chosen product line, so it can return the 10 chunks that the function asks for. Only the query changes, so the index layout and settings stay the same.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.6: "Optimize FM system performance for GenAI workflows"
Example: "vector database query optimization for retrieval augmentation"

Sources:

  • Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports efficient vector query filters for FAISS
  • k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) search in Amazon OpenSearch Service

INCORRECT: Replace the knn clause with a script_score query that computes exact k-NN scores only for chunks that pass the product_line filter, and return the 10 highest scoring chunks.
A script_score query runs an exact k-NN search on only the documents that match a filter. It always finds the true nearest chunks, and it works well when the filter leaves a small set of documents. Here, large product lines hold millions of chunks. An exact search scores every one of them, so searches on those lines become slow, and the searches must stay fast.

INCORRECT: Keep the term filter beside the knn clause, raise k on the knn clause to several hundred, and return the 10 highest scoring chunks that pass the product_line filter.
Raising k helps when a filter runs after the search: the search finds more neighbors, so more of them pass the filter. The team already tested this, and each search became much slower. Small product lines also need a very large k, because their chunks are rare among millions of others. The filter still runs after the search, so a search can still return fewer than 10 chunks.

INCORRECT: Create a separate k-NN index for each product line, and send each search only to the index of the product line that the user picked in the app.
One index for each product line is a common design when each group of documents has its own searches. Each search then looks only at the right chunks, and it needs no filter. But other applications read this index, and its layout must not change. Moving the chunks into new indexes changes the layout, so the team cannot use this design.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A media company runs a content recommendation system on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon S3 data source. Editors add new articles and delete outdated ones all day. They delete only articles that are more than a month old.

During breaking news, the editors can create or delete up to 500 articles in a few minutes. Every change must still reach the knowledge base within minutes.

The development team will use S3 event notifications, an Amazon SQS queue, and an AWS Lambda function that calls the document operations of the knowledge base.

Which design should the development team build?
questions.promptText:
A media company runs a content recommendation system on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with an Amazon S3 data source. Editors add new articles and delete outdated ones all day. They delete only articles that are more than a month old.
During breaking news, the editors can create or delete up to 500 articles in a few minutes. Every change must still reach the knowledge base within minutes.
The development team will use S3 event notifications, an Amazon SQS queue, and an AWS Lambda function that calls the document operations of the knowledge base.
Which design should the development team build?

options.text: Use a standard queue, and set a maximum concurrency on the SQS event source mapping, so the function sends a limited number of ingest and delete requests at the same time.
Use a standard queue, and let the function scale freely with the number of messages, so it sends one ingest or delete request for every message that it receives from the queue.
Use a FIFO queue instead of a standard queue, so the function processes the create and delete events of each article in the order in which Amazon S3 recorded them.
Use a standard queue, and have the function call StartIngestionJob on the S3 data source once for every message that it receives from the queue.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a standard queue, and set a maximum concurrency on the SQS event source mapping, so the function sends a limited number of ingest and delete requests at the same time.
Amazon SQS keeps every S3 event in the standard queue, so a burst of 500 changes waits in the queue. Amazon Bedrock allows only a limited number of IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments requests at the same time in one account, and this quota cannot be raised. The maximum concurrency limits how many copies of the function the queue can invoke at the same time. At that number, Lambda stops reading more messages, and the other events wait in the queue. The team sets the maximum concurrency within the quota of concurrent requests, so the function sends only a limited number of requests at the same time. If Amazon Bedrock still throttles a request, the request fails, and the function returns an error. After the visibility timeout of the queue, the message appears in the queue again, and Lambda processes the message again. If the function also has reserved concurrency, the reserved concurrency must be at least as high as the maximum concurrency.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.5: "Design and deploy data maintenance systems to ensure that vector stores contain current and accurate information for FM augmentation"
Example: "real-time change detection systems"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas

  • Configuring scaling behavior for SQS event source mappings

  • Amazon S3 Event Notifications

INCORRECT: Use a standard queue, and let the function scale freely with the number of messages, so it sends one ingest or delete request for every message that it receives from the queue.
The standard queue keeps every event during the burst, so this part of the design is correct. The problem is the function. With no limit, Lambda starts more copies of the function as the messages grow, and during breaking news hundreds of copies can run at the same time. Each copy sends its own ingest or delete request. Amazon Bedrock limits how many of these requests can run at the same time in one account, so the extra requests fail. Their messages go back to the queue and can fail again and again while the burst lasts. Many changes then reach the knowledge base too late, or not at all.

INCORRECT: Use a FIFO queue instead of a standard queue, so the function processes the create and delete events of each article in the order in which Amazon S3 recorded them.
A first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue delivers the messages of one message group in a strict order. Order would matter if editors added and deleted the same article within a few minutes. Here editors delete only articles that are more than a month old, so the create and the delete of one article never arrive close together. The main problem is the source of the events. Amazon S3 event notifications cannot send events to a FIFO queue. To reach a FIFO queue, the events must go through Amazon EventBridge, and this design has no such step.

INCORRECT: Use a standard queue, and have the function call StartIngestionJob on the S3 data source once for every message that it receives from the queue.
StartIngestionJob starts a sync of the whole data source. During a sync, the knowledge base scans each document in the data source and checks whether the document is already indexed. A sync does not process one article at a time. Only one ingestion job can run at a time for a data source, so the burst would send hundreds of sync requests while one job is still running, and each job scans the whole source again. The document operations that the team planned to use process one change at a time.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a human resources (HR) assistant as a web app. The web app calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway, and an AWS Lambda function behind the API calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. The function stores each answer with an answer ID in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Each chat session contains many answers.

Users will now rate each answer from one to five stars. Each rating must be stored with the answer it rates, for monthly prompt tuning. HR specialists review only answers rated one or two stars. These answers must not go to every specialist. The specialists share one work list, and each specialist takes the next answer from it.

Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a human resources (HR) assistant as a web app. The web app calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway, and an AWS Lambda function behind the API calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. The function stores each answer with an answer ID in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Each chat session contains many answers.
Users will now rate each answer from one to five stars. Each rating must be stored with the answer it rates, for monthly prompt tuning. HR specialists review only answers rated one or two stars. These answers must not go to every specialist. The specialists share one work list, and each specialist takes the next answer from it.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the answer ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SNS topic that emails the specialists.
Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the session ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SNS topic that emails the specialists.
Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the session ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SQS queue that the specialists work from.
Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the answer ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SQS queue that the specialists work from.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the answer ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SQS queue that the specialists work from.
A new method on the existing REST API gives the web app one place to send each rating. The Lambda function stores the rating under the answer ID that the chat function created, so each rating is stored with the exact answer it rates. The function then sends ratings of one or two stars to an SQS queue, which is the shared work list. When a specialist receives a message, the message stays in the queue but becomes invisible to the other specialists for the visibility timeout. No email goes to every specialist.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.5: "Develop collaborative AI systems to enhance FM capabilities with human expertise"
Example: "API Gateway to implement feedback collection mechanisms"

Sources:

  • API reference (Generative AI Application Builder on AWS)

  • Accessing and analyzing user collected feedback

  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout

INCORRECT: Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the answer ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SNS topic that emails the specialists.
Storing the feedback under the answer ID is correct, because it ties each rating to its answer. The problem is the alert. An SNS topic delivers each message to every subscriber, so every specialist receives an email about each low-rated answer. These answers must not go to every specialist. An email also gives the specialists no shared work list from which each specialist takes the next answer.

INCORRECT: Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the session ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SNS topic that emails the specialists.
A session ID and an email alert can fit a small team that rates whole conversations. Here the design fails twice. Each chat session contains many answers, so a rating stored under the session ID does not point to one answer. The SNS topic also emails every specialist about each low-rated answer, while the specialists want to take these answers one by one from a shared list.

INCORRECT: Add a REST API feedback method whose Lambda function stores the feedback under the session ID, and sends ratings of one or two stars to an Amazon SQS queue that the specialists work from.
The SQS queue suits the specialists, because each specialist takes the next message from one shared queue. The problem is the ID. One chat session contains many answers, so a rating stored under the session ID cannot show which answer it rates. The monthly prompt tuning needs each rating next to its own answer. A session ID fits when users rate a whole conversation, not one answer.

questions.promptHtml:
A company has 30 teams that deploy Amazon Bedrock applications with AWS CloudFormation templates through AWS CodePipeline. Each team writes the IAM policies for its own application roles. Company policy allows model invocation only on a list of approved models. An audit found a deployed role that allowed bedrock:InvokeModel on every resource.
The security team wants a control that stops such a policy before any deployment and shows the team the statement that breaks the rule. Auditors read the deployed policy documents, so no deployed policy may grant an unapproved model, even when another control blocks the call.
Which control meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company has 30 teams that deploy Amazon Bedrock applications with AWS CloudFormation templates through AWS CodePipeline. Each team writes the IAM policies for its own application roles. Company policy allows model invocation only on a list of approved models. An audit found a deployed role that allowed bedrock:InvokeModel on every resource.
The security team wants a control that stops such a policy before any deployment and shows the team the statement that breaks the rule. Auditors read the deployed policy documents, so no deployed policy may grant an unapproved model, even when another control blocks the call.
Which control meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer for the team accounts, and have the security team remove the model permissions that its findings report as unused at the end of each week.
Require a permissions boundary on every application role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel only on the approved models, and attach that boundary to each application role in the templates.
Add an AWS CodeBuild step that runs IAM Access Analyzer policy validation on each policy in the templates, and fails the build on any security warning or error finding.
Add an AWS CodeBuild step that runs an IAM Access Analyzer custom policy check on each policy in the templates against a reference policy, and fails the build on FAIL.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an AWS CodeBuild step that runs an IAM Access Analyzer custom policy check on each policy in the templates against a reference policy, and fails the build on FAIL.
IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks test a policy against your own security standards before you deploy it. The check for new access compares each policy with a reference policy. Here the security team writes a reference policy with two statements. The first allows all actions, and the second denies bedrock:InvokeModel on every model outside the approved list. A CodeBuild step runs the check on each policy in the templates. When a policy grants access that the reference policy does not, the result is FAIL, the reasons name the statement, and the build stops. No policy with an unapproved model reaches an account, and the team sees which statement to fix.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.3: "Create organizational governance systems to ensure consistent oversight of FM implementations"

Sources:

  • Validate policies with IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

  • IAM Access Analyzer introduces custom policy checks powered by automated reasoning

  • CheckNoNewAccess

INCORRECT: Create an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer for the team accounts, and have the security team remove the model permissions that its findings report as unused at the end of each week.
An unused access analyzer watches the roles and users that already exist. It reports permissions that a role has not used for a set time, which helps a team remove access it does not need. Here it comes too late, because the role is already deployed when a finding appears. A permission for an unapproved model that the application does use is never reported as unused at all.

INCORRECT: Require a permissions boundary on every application role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel only on the approved models, and attach that boundary to each application role in the templates.
A permissions boundary sets the most permissions that a role can have. A boundary that allows only the approved models blocks every call to other models, so it is a strong control when the application runs. But the boundary does not change the role's own policy. The deployed policy can still grant bedrock:InvokeModel on every resource, and the auditors read that policy. The company does not allow such a policy, even when another control blocks the call.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS CodeBuild step that runs IAM Access Analyzer policy validation on each policy in the templates, and fails the build on any security warning or error finding.
Policy validation checks a policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. It returns errors, security warnings, warnings and suggestions, and it is a good check in any pipeline. But it does not know the company's own list of approved models. It cannot tell an approved model from an unapproved one, so a policy that grants an unapproved model can pass the build.

questions.promptHtml:
A utility company runs its phone support on Amazon Connect. An existing contact flow stores each caller's stated problem as a contact attribute. The account status of each caller is in a legacy billing system that offers only a REST API. Account status changes during the day, for example after a payment.
The company wants each call to reach the billing, outage or moving queue based on both the stated problem and the account status. A model in Amazon Bedrock must choose the queue. The team must keep the existing flow and only add blocks to it. The choice must be ready within a few seconds, before the call enters a queue.
Which integration routes each call as required?
questions.promptText:
A utility company runs its phone support on Amazon Connect. An existing contact flow stores each caller's stated problem as a contact attribute. The account status of each caller is in a legacy billing system that offers only a REST API. Account status changes during the day, for example after a payment.
The company wants each call to reach the billing, outage or moving queue based on both the stated problem and the account status. A model in Amazon Bedrock must choose the queue. The team must keep the existing flow and only add blocks to it. The choice must be ready within a few seconds, before the call enters a queue.
Which integration routes each call as required?

options.text: Add an AWS Lambda function block in synchronous mode whose function reads the account status from a nightly Amazon DynamoDB copy, sends it and the problem to Amazon Bedrock, and returns a queue name.

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for DISCONNECTED contact events that invokes a Lambda function, which reads the billing API and saves a queue name from Amazon Bedrock on the contact.
Add an AWS Lambda function block in synchronous mode whose function reads the account status from the billing API, sends it and the problem to Amazon Bedrock, and returns a queue name.
Run a nightly job that asks Amazon Bedrock for a queue name for each account status, and add a Lambda function block that reads the caller's queue name from Amazon DynamoDB.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function block in synchronous mode whose function reads the account status from the billing API, sends it and the problem to Amazon Bedrock, and returns a queue name.
In synchronous mode, the AWS Lambda function block moves the call to the next block only after the function finishes. The function reads the caller's account status from the billing system's REST API during the call. The question says that account status changes during the day, so a payment made an hour ago already shows in what the function reads. The function sends that status with the stated problem to a model in Amazon Bedrock and returns the queue name as a key and value. A Check contact attributes block compares that value and takes one branch for each queue. Each branch sets the billing, outage or moving queue with a Set working queue block before the flow transfers the call. The team only adds blocks to the existing flow, and the choice is ready before the call enters a queue. The block waits only a short time, so the function must answer quickly, for example with a small, fast model and a short prompt.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"
Example: "API-based integrations with legacy systems"

Sources:

  • Flow block in Connect Customer: AWS Lambda function

  • Grant Connect Customer access to your AWS Lambda functions

  • Connect Customer contact events

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function block in synchronous mode whose function reads the account status from a nightly Amazon DynamoDB copy, sends it and the problem to Amazon Bedrock, and returns a queue name.
This design uses the same block in synchronous mode, so its timing is right. The difference is where the account status comes from. A nightly copy in Amazon DynamoDB fits when the data changes rarely, or when a legacy API cannot answer fast enough during a call. Here the account status changes during the day, for example after a payment. A caller who paid an hour ago still has the old status in the copy, so the model can choose the wrong queue.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for DISCONNECTED contact events that invokes a Lambda function, which reads the billing API and saves a queue name from Amazon Bedrock on the contact.
Amazon Connect sends contact events to the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge in near real time, and a rule on that bus can start a Lambda function for each event. This works well when a team labels calls for reports after they end. But the DISCONNECTED event comes after the call ends, and the flow does not wait for this function. The queue name arrives too late to route the call.

INCORRECT: Run a nightly job that asks Amazon Bedrock for a queue name for each account status, and add a Lambda function block that reads the caller's queue name from Amazon DynamoDB.
Computing results ahead of time saves time when all the input is known early. Here the nightly job gives each account status a queue name. But the caller states the problem only during the call, and the nightly job never sees it. A caller with an outage and a caller with a billing question on the same account go to the same queue.

questions.promptHtml:
An insurance company deployed a claims processing assistant using Amazon Bedrock that answers policyholder questions about coverage details. Policyholders use it as a chatbot and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. The assistant retrieves information from policy documents using RAG, but quality audits reveal that the model occasionally generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information not present in the source documents. The company needs to automatically detect when responses contain hallucinated content before delivering answers to policyholders. The solution must evaluate factual consistency between retrieved documents and generated responses at scale without manual review.
Which approach detects hallucinations MOST effectively?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company deployed a claims processing assistant using Amazon Bedrock that answers policyholder questions about coverage details. Policyholders use it as a chatbot and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. The assistant retrieves information from policy documents using RAG, but quality audits reveal that the model occasionally generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information not present in the source documents. The company needs to automatically detect when responses contain hallucinated content before delivering answers to policyholders. The solution must evaluate factual consistency between retrieved documents and generated responses at scale without manual review.
Which approach detects hallucinations MOST effectively?

options.text: Before each answer goes out, send the retrieved passages and the draft answer to a second Amazon Bedrock model that judges whether the passages support every claim, and hold back unsupported answers.
Before each answer goes out, check the draft answer with a contextual grounding check in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, with the retrieved passages as the source, and block answers below the threshold.
Every night, run an Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation job with a judge model and the Faithfulness metric on the day's logged answers and passages, and report the low scores each morning.
Before each answer goes out, send the retrieved passages and the draft answer to a queue where claims specialists check every claim, and hold back answers that they reject.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Before each answer goes out, send the retrieved passages and the draft answer to a second Amazon Bedrock model that judges whether the passages support every claim, and hold back unsupported answers.
This design uses a second model as a judge. Before an answer reaches the policyholder, the application calls another model in Amazon Bedrock. The call holds the passages that the assistant retrieved, the draft answer and an evaluation prompt that asks whether the passages support each claim in the answer. The judge checks the answer for factual consistency with the passages and returns its assessment. The application holds back every answer that the judge marks as unsupported. This check runs on every answer with no person involved. The application builds the judge call itself, so it can send the passages and the answer of each turn in a chat with follow-up questions, which is how policyholders use this assistant.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"

Sources:

  • AGENTSEC01-BP03 Monitor for hallucination propagation

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses

  • Use metrics to understand RAG system performance

INCORRECT: Before each answer goes out, check the draft answer with a contextual grounding check in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, with the retrieved passages as the source, and block answers below the threshold.
A contextual grounding check in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails scores each model response against a reference source and the user's query. When the grounding score is below the threshold that the team sets, the guardrail blocks the response. The check fits summarization, paraphrasing and question answering over a source. Here policyholders use the assistant as a chatbot and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. The grounding check does not support chatbot or conversational question answering use cases, so the company cannot use it for this assistant.

INCORRECT: Every night, run an Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation job with a judge model and the Faithfulness metric on the day's logged answers and passages, and report the low scores each morning.
A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job can score answers and passages that the team brings from its own application. A judge model scores each answer, and the Faithfulness metric measures how well an answer avoids hallucination with respect to the retrieved texts. A nightly job fits a team that tracks answer quality over time. Here each answer must be checked before it reaches the policyholder. The nightly job scores answers after policyholders have already read them, so it cannot stop a wrong answer.

INCORRECT: Before each answer goes out, send the retrieved passages and the draft answer to a queue where claims specialists check every claim, and hold back answers that they reject.
A review queue lets claims specialists read each answer and its passages before the assistant sends it. People who know the policies find errors well, and a queue fits a small number of answers with high risk, such as the reason for a claim denial. Here the company must check every answer at scale and without manual review. This queue puts a person on every answer, which breaks both rules.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
An online learning company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write a personalized study guide for each student. Requests arrive steadily during school hours, and each student waits in the app for the guide.

Today each prompt starts with the student's level, recent quiz results, and the text of the requested chapter. The full course syllabus of 8,000 tokens comes at the end. The syllabus is the same for all students on a course and does not change during a term.

The development team wants to use prompt caching to cut the cost of input tokens. Each guide must stay as personalized and as good as it is today.

How should the team arrange each prompt?
questions.promptText:
An online learning company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write a personalized study guide for each student. Requests arrive steadily during school hours, and each student waits in the app for the guide.
Today each prompt starts with the student's level, recent quiz results, and the text of the requested chapter. The full course syllabus of 8,000 tokens comes at the end. The syllabus is the same for all students on a course and does not change during a term.
The development team wants to use prompt caching to cut the cost of input tokens. Each guide must stay as personalized and as good as it is today.
How should the team arrange each prompt?

options.text: Put the syllabus first, set the cache checkpoint right after it, and send the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text after the checkpoint.
Keep the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text first, put the full syllabus after them, and set one cache checkpoint at the end of the prompt.
Keep the current order, and set a cache checkpoint right after the chapter text, so that the cache keeps each chapter text for later requests.
Move the study guide requests to the batch inference API, and set a cache checkpoint after the syllabus to reuse it across the queued requests.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put the syllabus first, set the cache checkpoint right after it, and send the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text after the checkpoint.
A cache checkpoint marks the end of the cached prefix, the part of the prompt that the model can cache. With the syllabus at the front, the prefix is the same on every request for a course. A request that reads the syllabus from the cache pays a lower rate for those tokens than for normal input tokens. Steady requests during school hours keep the cache active, so many requests can read the syllabus from the cache, although prompt caching does not promise a cache hit on every request. The student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text come after the checkpoint, so they can change on every request. The model still receives the same information as today, so each guide stays personalized.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.4: "Create intelligent caching systems to reduce costs and improve response times by avoiding unnecessary FM invocations"
Example: "prompt caching"

Sources:

  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

  • Amazon Bedrock prompt caching

INCORRECT: Keep the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text first, put the full syllabus after them, and set one cache checkpoint at the end of the prompt.
This layout keeps the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text in front of the syllabus. Everything before the checkpoint is the cached prefix, so the prefix contains these values too. They change from one request to the next, and a change in the prefix causes a cache miss. So no request can read the syllabus from the cache. Every request processes the full syllabus again and pays the normal input rate for it, or for some models a higher cache write rate.

INCORRECT: Keep the current order, and set a cache checkpoint right after the chapter text, so that the cache keeps each chapter text for later requests.
Everything before a checkpoint is the cached prefix. In the current order, the student's level, the quiz results, and the chapter text sit in front of this checkpoint, and these values change from one student to the next. A change in the prefix causes a cache miss, so requests for other students or other chapters cannot read what an earlier request cached. The syllabus of 8,000 tokens comes after the checkpoint, so the syllabus is never cached, and every request pays for it as normal input tokens.

INCORRECT: Move the study guide requests to the batch inference API, and set a cache checkpoint after the syllabus to reuse it across the queued requests.
Batch inference sends a large set of prompts as one request and writes the responses to an Amazon S3 bucket after the job is complete. For some models, batch inference also costs less per token than on-demand inference, so it looks like a way to cut the cost of input tokens. But each student waits in the app for the guide, and a batch job returns its results only when the whole job is complete. Prompt caching also works only for on-demand inference, and the batch inference API does not support it, so the checkpoint would have no effect.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A manufacturer's support assistant answers from an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses a vector store the team set up. Its data source is an Amazon S3 bucket, and a schedule already starts a sync every night.
A partner company writes the service manuals in its own document management system. That system can send files only over SFTP, signed in with an SSH key, and it cannot call AWS APIs. The partner allows no software from other companies inside its network.
New manuals must appear in answers after the next sync. The manufacturer will run no servers of its own and will write no file transfer code.
Which design brings the partner's manuals into the knowledge base?
questions.promptText:
A manufacturer's support assistant answers from an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses a vector store the team set up. Its data source is an Amazon S3 bucket, and a schedule already starts a sync every night.
A partner company writes the service manuals in its own document management system. That system can send files only over SFTP, signed in with an SSH key, and it cannot call AWS APIs. The partner allows no software from other companies inside its network.
New manuals must appear in answers after the next sync. The manufacturer will run no servers of its own and will write no file transfer code.
Which design brings the partner's manuals into the knowledge base?

options.text: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server, and add a service-managed user for the partner with its SSH public key and the knowledge base's S3 bucket as its home directory.
Launch an SFTP server on an Amazon EC2 instance for the partner's SSH key, and run a script on the instance that copies each new file to the knowledge base's S3 bucket.
Deploy an AWS DataSync agent as a virtual machine in the partner's network, and create a nightly task from the partner's file server to the knowledge base's S3 bucket.
Create an IAM role that the partner's AWS account can assume, and have the partner's system upload each new manual to the knowledge base's S3 bucket through the S3 API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server, and add a service-managed user for the partner with its SSH public key and the knowledge base's S3 bucket as its home directory.
AWS Transfer Family is a fully managed service that gives a company an SFTP server in AWS with no server infrastructure to run, and it stores the files that clients send in Amazon S3. A service-managed user signs in with the SSH public key that the partner provides. The user's home directory is the knowledge base's bucket, and an IAM role gives the user access to that bucket. The partner's system sends each manual over SFTP, as it already can, so it needs no AWS API calls and no new software. The manufacturer runs no server and writes no transfer code. A sync of the S3 data source processes the documents that were added, changed or deleted since the last sync, so the nightly sync adds each new manual to the knowledge base.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.4: "Use AWS services to create integration components to connect with resources"
Example: "document management systems"

Sources:

  • What is AWS Transfer Family?

  • Working with service-managed users

  • Do I need an AWS DataSync agent?

INCORRECT: Launch an SFTP server on an Amazon EC2 instance for the partner's SSH key, and run a script on the instance that copies each new file to the knowledge base's S3 bucket.
An SFTP server on an Amazon EC2 instance gives a team full control of the server software and its settings. It fits a team that needs a setup that a managed service does not offer. The partner's system could send files to it over SFTP. Here the manufacturer will run no servers of its own and will write no file transfer code. This design needs an instance that the team patches and runs, and a script that the team writes to copy each file to Amazon S3.

INCORRECT: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent as a virtual machine in the partner's network, and create a nightly task from the partner's file server to the knowledge base's S3 bucket.
AWS DataSync copies files from storage that a company manages to AWS storage, and a nightly task fits files that change every day. For storage outside AWS, DataSync needs an agent. The agent is a virtual machine that runs in the environment where the storage sits. Here the partner allows no software from other companies inside its network, so the agent cannot run there.

INCORRECT: Create an IAM role that the partner's AWS account can assume, and have the partner's system upload each new manual to the knowledge base's S3 bucket through the S3 API.
A role that a third party's AWS account can assume gives that party access to the company's resources without shared security credentials. It fits a partner whose software uploads files to Amazon S3 through the AWS APIs. Here the partner's system can send files only over SFTP and cannot call AWS APIs, so it cannot assume the role or upload through the S3 API.

An insurance company receives multi-page claim forms as PDF files in an Amazon S3 bucket. It trained an Amazon Textract adapter on its own forms, and its audit team approved field extraction only through that adapter.
For each form, the process must extract the fields with the adapter, have an Amazon Bedrock model summarize the incident description, and store the fields and the summary in Amazon DynamoDB. The operations team must see in one console where each form is in this process and which step failed.
Which design should the company build?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow starts asynchronous Textract analysis with the adapter in a task that waits for a callback when Textract finishes, then calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.
An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow runs synchronous Textract analysis with the adapter on each PDF file in a task, then calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.

An S3 event starts a Lambda function that runs asynchronous Textract analysis with the adapter, and the Textract completion notice in Amazon SNS starts a second function that calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.
An S3 event starts a Lambda function that sends each form to an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project whose custom blueprint returns the claim fields and the incident summary.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow starts asynchronous Textract analysis with the adapter in a task that waits for a callback when Textract finishes, then calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.
Amazon Textract reads multi-page documents only with its asynchronous operations. StartDocumentAnalysis accepts the adapter ID and version, so the extraction uses the trained adapter that the audit team approved. When the job finishes, Textract publishes its completion status to an Amazon SNS topic. In a Standard workflow, a task can wait for a callback. Step Functions passes a task token, for example to a Lambda function that starts the job and stores the token with the job ID in a table, and the task pauses. A second function receives the SNS notice and returns the token with SendTaskSuccess, so the workflow moves on to the Amazon Bedrock call and the DynamoDB write. The Step Functions console shows each execution as a graph with the status of each step, and it highlights the step that caused an error, so the operations team sees every form in one place.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.3: "Create business system enhancements"
Example: "Step Functions to orchestrate document processing systems"

Sources:

  • Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions

  • Calling Amazon Textract Asynchronous Operations

  • Using Adapters during Inference

INCORRECT: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow runs synchronous Textract analysis with the adapter on each PDF file in a task, then calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.
The synchronous AnalyzeDocument operation also accepts an adapter, and it returns results in near real time. It fits single-page documents, such as a one-page form or a photo of a receipt. Here the claim forms have many pages. Textract analyzes multi-page documents only with its asynchronous operations, so this task cannot read the whole form.

INCORRECT: An S3 event starts a Lambda function that runs asynchronous Textract analysis with the adapter, and the Textract completion notice in Amazon SNS starts a second function that calls Amazon Bedrock and writes to DynamoDB.
This design uses events. One Lambda function starts the asynchronous job with the adapter. When the job finishes, Textract sends its completion notice to an Amazon SNS topic, and the notice starts a second function. This fits a short process that no one needs to follow step by step. Here the operations team must see in one console where each form is and which step failed. The two functions pass work only through events, so no single view shows the state of each form, and the team would have to build one.

INCORRECT: An S3 event starts a Lambda function that sends each form to an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project whose custom blueprint returns the claim fields and the incident summary.
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation extracts data from documents. A custom blueprint lists the fields to extract, the format of each field and instructions in plain words. This design fits a company that has no trained extraction model and wants one managed service to extract the fields. Here the audit team approved field extraction only through the company's trained Textract adapter. This design extracts the fields with a blueprint instead of that adapter, so it breaks the audit rule.

The developer must design a solution that meets the following requirements:
Ensure a standardized, open-protocol interaction pattern for tool discovery, schemas, and execution without writing custom API-wrapping translation code.

The developer must design a solution that meets the following requirements:
Ensure a standardized, open-protocol interaction pattern for tool discovery, schemas, and execution without writing custom API-wrapping translation code.
Isolate the execution environments for the tools based on their runtime complexity and resource demands.
Use native AWS compute paradigms that optimize for both on-demand execution and persistent long-running workloads.
Which deployment design meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure the lightweight, stateless utility tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. Deploy the complex, compute-intensive tools as containerized MCP servers running as long-lived services on Amazon ECS.

Configure all tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. To handle the resource demands of the compute-intensive tools, configure the Lambda functions with maximum memory allocation and reserved concurrency.

Deploy all tools as containerized MCP servers running as long-lived services on Amazon ECS. To optimize costs for the lightweight utility tools, configure ECS task auto-scaling with a minimum task count of zero and a scale-in cooldown of 60 seconds.

Configure the lightweight, stateless utility tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. Deploy the complex, compute-intensive tools as containerized MCP servers on Amazon ECS. To manage tool discovery across both backends, deploy a separate AWS Lambda function that maintains a centralized tool registry and dynamically routes incoming MCP tool discovery requests to either backend based on a configuration file stored in Amazon S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Configure the lightweight, stateless utility tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. Deploy the complex, compute-intensive tools as containerized MCP servers running as long-lived services on Amazon ECS.
This design splits the tools by the work they do. The utility tools are small and keep no state, so they run as MCP servers on AWS Lambda. Lambda runs the code when a request comes in, scales on its own, and charges only for the resources used. The compute-intensive tools run as MCP servers in containers on Amazon ECS. ECS keeps these services running, so they can serve long-running work with the resources they need. Each group runs in its own environment, which meets the isolation requirement. Both groups use MCP, so the agents discover and call every tool through the same open protocol, with no custom translation code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.7: "Develop model extension frameworks to enhance FM capabilities"
Example: "Lambda functions to implement stateless MCP servers that provide lightweight tool access"

Sources:

  • Deployment Pattern 2, AWS Lambda + Amazon API Gateway
  • Deployment Pattern 3, Amazon ECS (Containerized)
  • Configure Lambda function timeout

INCORRECT: Configure all tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. To handle the resource demands of the compute-intensive tools, configure the Lambda functions with maximum memory allocation and reserved concurrency.
This option runs every tool as an MCP server on Lambda. More memory and reserved concurrency are real Lambda settings, and they fit tools that run quickly and keep no state, such as the utility tools. They do not change how Lambda runs code. A synchronous request to a function has a maximum run time. Lambda keeps an execution environment only for a while between requests, and the code must not assume that the environment stays. So a function cannot hold long-lived state or serve as a persistent workload. The requirements ask for persistent, long-running workloads for the compute-intensive tools, and containers on Amazon ECS give them that.

INCORRECT: Deploy all tools as containerized MCP servers running as long-lived services on Amazon ECS. To optimize costs for the lightweight utility tools, configure ECS task auto-scaling with a minimum task count of zero and a scale-in cooldown of 60 seconds.
This option runs every tool as a container on Amazon ECS. ECS fits the compute-intensive tools. A minimum task count of zero is a real setting, and it stops all tasks when there is no work. But when the count is zero and requests arrive, Service Auto Scaling first waits for a metric data point and then starts a task, so the first requests wait. The team also has to manage scaling settings for tools that do small, quick jobs. Lambda runs these lightweight, stateless tools on demand and scales them with no scaling settings. The requirements ask for an on-demand compute choice for the lightweight tools, and Lambda gives them that.

INCORRECT: Configure the lightweight, stateless utility tools as MCP servers hosted on AWS Lambda functions using streamable HTTP transport. Deploy the complex, compute-intensive tools as containerized MCP servers on Amazon ECS. To manage tool discovery across both backends, deploy a separate AWS Lambda function that maintains a centralized tool registry and dynamically routes incoming MCP tool discovery requests to either backend based on a configuration file stored in Amazon S3.
This option splits the tools between Lambda and Amazon ECS in the right way, and then adds a custom Lambda function that keeps a tool registry and routes discovery requests with a file in Amazon S3. That layer is not needed. With MCP, the agent's client lists the tools of each MCP server that it connects to and registers them with the agent, so tool discovery comes from the protocol itself. A team that wants one endpoint for many MCP servers can use a managed gateway, such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which combines the tools of its MCP targets into one tool list. The registry is custom routing code that the team must write and maintain, and the requirements ask for a standard protocol with no custom translation code.
