questions.promptHtml:
A company's HR assistant answers employee questions from an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The team wrote the documents for the questions that employees asked in the first month, and the application stores every question in Amazon S3. Company policy forbids storing the model's answers.
Over several months, answers became vague, because employees began to ask about topics that the documents do not cover. No one noticed for weeks. The number of questions per day and their length stayed the same.
The team wants an automatic alarm when the topics of the questions move away from that first month, so it can add documents.
Which monitoring design meets this need?
questions.promptText:
A company's HR assistant answers employee questions from an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The team wrote the documents for the questions that employees asked in the first month, and the application stores every question in Amazon S3. Company policy forbids storing the model's answers.
Over several months, answers became vague, because employees began to ask about topics that the documents do not cover. No one noticed for weeks. The number of questions per day and their length stayed the same.
The team wants an automatic alarm when the topics of the questions move away from that first month, so it can add documents.
Which monitoring design meets this need?

options.text: Each night, a Lambda function embeds the day's questions, measures their distance from stored embeddings of first-month questions, and publishes it as a CloudWatch metric with an alarm on a threshold.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric of the assistant's model that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Invocations metric of the assistant's model that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
Each week, a Lambda function sends a sample of the week's logged questions and answers to an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and alarms when scores fall below first-month scores.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Each night, a Lambda function embeds the day's questions, measures their distance from stored embeddings of first-month questions, and publishes it as a CloudWatch metric with an alarm on a threshold.
This design watches for drift in the inputs. An embedding model turns each question into a vector, and questions about similar topics get vectors that sit close together. The team keeps the embeddings of the first-month questions as the baseline. Each night, the function embeds the day's questions with the same model and measures how far the new set of vectors sits from the baseline, for example with the Wasserstein distance. It publishes that distance as a CloudWatch custom metric, and an alarm fires when the distance goes above a threshold that the team sets. New topics move the vectors even when the number and the length of the questions stay the same. The design needs only the stored questions, not the answers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.4: "Troubleshoot retrieval system issues to identify and resolve problems that affect information retrieval effectiveness for FM augmentation"
Example: "drift monitoring"

Sources:

  • Detecting drift in production applications

  • Using CloudWatch anomaly detection

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InputTokenCount metric of the assistant's model that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
InputTokenCount counts the tokens in the input of each model call. An anomaly detection alarm learns the trend and the hourly, daily and weekly patterns of a metric, and it fires when a value goes above the band of expected values. This fits a sudden change in prompt size, such as users who paste long documents. Here the number of questions and their length stayed the same, so the token count stays inside its band while the topics change.

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Invocations metric of the assistant's model that uses anomaly detection and fires when the value goes above the band of expected values.
Invocations counts the requests to the model that Amazon Bedrock accepted for processing. An anomaly detection alarm on this metric finds a change in traffic that breaks the normal daily pattern, such as a sudden rise in requests. Here the number of questions per day stayed the same. Only the topics changed, and a count of requests does not show what the questions are about.

INCORRECT: Each week, a Lambda function sends a sample of the week's logged questions and answers to an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, and alarms when scores fall below first-month scores.
An Amazon Bedrock evaluation job can score answers that the team brings from its own application, and a judge model scores each answer. A weekly score on a sample of real traffic, compared with the scores of the first month, shows a drop in answer quality. This fits a team that keeps its logged answers. Here company policy forbids storing the model's answers. The job has no answers to score this week, and the team has no first-month scores to compare them with.

A developer is building a public-facing generative AI chatbot using an Amazon Bedrock foundation model. The chatbot helps users troubleshoot their billing accounts. Users type card numbers so the chatbot can find charges.
The developer must design a solution that meets the following requirements:
Protect the foundation model from adversarial prompt injection attacks (for example, users instructing the model to ignore previous instructions and leak system prompts).
Automatically mask any Personally Identifiable Information (PII), such as credit card numbers or social security numbers, in the model's response before it is returned to the user.
Minimize API latency and the development of custom code.
Which guardrail setup meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A developer is building a public-facing generative AI chatbot using an Amazon Bedrock foundation model. The chatbot helps users troubleshoot their billing accounts. Users type card numbers so the chatbot can find charges.
The developer must design a solution that meets the following requirements:
Protect the foundation model from adversarial prompt injection attacks (for example, users instructing the model to ignore previous instructions and leak system prompts).
Automatically mask any Personally Identifiable Information (PII), such as credit card numbers or social security numbers, in the model's response before it is returned to the user.
Minimize API latency and the development of custom code.
Which guardrail setup meets these requirements?

options.text: In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in outputs only, and call InvokeModel with the guardrail and input tags around the user's message.

In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in inputs and outputs, and call InvokeModel with the guardrail and input tags around the user's message.

In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in outputs only, and check the user's message and the model's reply in separate ApplyGuardrail calls.

In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in inputs and outputs, and check the user's message and the model's reply in separate ApplyGuardrail calls.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in outputs only, and call InvokeModel with the guardrail and input tags around the user's message.
The prompt attack filter in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails detects prompt injection, such as a message that tells the model to ignore earlier instructions. In the Standard tier, it also detects prompt leakage, such as a request to reveal the system prompt. With InvokeModel, the filter checks only user input that sits inside the guardrail's input tags, so the application puts the user's message inside those tags. A sensitive information filter has separate actions for inputs and outputs. Here the mask action applies to outputs only, so the model still reads the card number that the user types, and the guardrail replaces each PII value in the reply with its type, such as {CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_NUMBER}. In one InvokeModel call, the guardrail checks the input, the model answers, and the guardrail checks and masks the reply before the application gets it. There is no extra call and no extra code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.3: "Create privacy-focused AI systems to protect user privacy while maintaining FM utility and effectiveness"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails"

Sources:

  • Detect prompt attacks with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters
  • How Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works

INCORRECT: In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in inputs and outputs, and call InvokeModel with the guardrail and input tags around the user's message.
Masking PII in inputs and outputs fits a chatbot that never needs the values that users type, for example one that answers general questions about plans. The single InvokeModel call is right. Here users type card numbers so the chatbot can find charges. With masking on inputs, the model gets only the type in place of each card number, so it cannot find the charge that the user asks about.

INCORRECT: In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in outputs only, and check the user's message and the model's reply in separate ApplyGuardrail calls.
The ApplyGuardrail API checks any text against a guardrail without calling a model. It fits a model that runs outside Amazon Bedrock, or a check at another point in the application, and the mask on outputs only is right. Here the requirements ask for the least latency and the least custom code. This design adds two API calls to every request and needs code that calls the model between them, while one InvokeModel call with the guardrail does the same work.

INCORRECT: In a guardrail with the prompt attack filter, set the sensitive information filter to mask the PII types in inputs and outputs, and check the user's message and the model's reply in separate ApplyGuardrail calls.
Separate ApplyGuardrail calls that mask PII in both directions fit a model outside Amazon Bedrock that must never see personal data. This design fails twice here. The mask on inputs hides the card numbers that the chatbot needs to find charges, and the two extra calls add latency and custom code to every request.

The agent performs research tasks that can take up to six hours. Between tool calls, the agent keeps contextual state, such as intermediate findings and tool outputs, in memory. Many users run the agent at the same time.
The solution must meet these requirements:
Deploy the agent as a container that is fully compatible with the AgentCore Runtime hosting environment.
Reclaim idle sessions after 30 minutes of inactivity, but let active sessions run for up to six hours.
Keep contextual state across tool calls within a session without an external database.
Which configuration meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A developer is deploying a multi-turn conversational AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The runtime runs each session in its own microVM. The agent performs research tasks that can take up to six hours. Between tool calls, the agent keeps contextual state, such as intermediate findings and tool outputs, in memory. Many users run the agent at the same time.
The solution must meet these requirements:
Deploy the agent as a container that is fully compatible with the AgentCore Runtime hosting environment.
Reclaim idle sessions after 30 minutes of inactivity, but let active sessions run for up to six hours.
Keep contextual state across tool calls within a session without an external database.
Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Build an x86_64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 21600 seconds.
Build an ARM64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 21600 seconds.
Build an ARM64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 1800 seconds.
Build an x86_64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 1800 seconds.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build an ARM64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 21600 seconds.
AgentCore Runtime runs an HTTP agent from a container that listens on port 8080. The container answers POST requests on /invocations, which carry the work for the agent, and GET requests on /ping, which AgentCore uses for health checks. On microVMs, AgentCore requires agents that are built for ARM64, so this image fits the hosting environment. The two lifecycle settings meet the time needs. The setting idleRuntimeSessionTimeout at 1800 seconds ends a session after 30 minutes with no activity. The setting maxLifetime at 21600 seconds lets the microVM of an active session run for six hours, so a long research task can finish. During the session, AgentCore keeps the context between invocations to the same session, so the findings stay in the agent's memory with no external database.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.1: "Develop intelligent autonomous systems with appropriate memory and state management capabilities"

Sources:

  • Configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore lifecycle settings
  • Get started without the AgentCore CLI
  • Use isolated sessions for agents

INCORRECT: Build an x86_64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 21600 seconds.
The lifecycle settings are right, and the port and the two paths follow the AgentCore contract for HTTP agents. An x86_64 image fits container hosts with x86 processors, which many build machines and container platforms use. This agent runs on AgentCore Runtime microVMs, and AgentCore requires agents there to be built for ARM64, with the linux/arm64 platform. So this image is not compatible with the hosting environment.

INCORRECT: Build an ARM64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 1800 seconds.
The container is right, and so is the idle setting. A maxLifetime of 1800 seconds fits short tasks, where a team wants the compute of each session to stop after 30 minutes. Here a research task can run for six hours. When maxLifetime is reached, AgentCore ends the microVM of the session even while the agent is still working, and the findings that the agent keeps in memory are lost when that microVM ends.

INCORRECT: Build an x86_64 container image that serves POST /invocations and GET /ping on port 8080, and set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout to 1800 seconds and maxLifetime to 1800 seconds.
This setup has two problems. The x86_64 image does not match the ARM64 build that AgentCore requires for agents on microVMs. A maxLifetime of 1800 seconds also ends the microVM of each session after 30 minutes, so a six-hour task loses the findings that it keeps in memory.

The agent must remember a user's product preferences across multiple sessions and provide accurate session-level conversation summaries for quality review. questions.promptText:
A developer is building a support agent using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory. The agent must remember a user's product preferences across multiple sessions and provide accurate session-level conversation summaries for quality review. During active conversations, the agent must also maintain the raw turn-by-turn interaction history within the current session.
Which memory configuration satisfies all three requirements?

options.text: Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a semantic strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using the user's ID as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a summary strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using a new ID for each conversation as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a summary strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using the user's ID as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a semantic strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using a new ID for each conversation as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a summary strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using the user's ID as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
The user preference strategy extracts preferences, choices and styles from the conversation and stores them under the actorId. Because the user's ID is the actorId on every event, the preferences from all of that user's sessions build one profile, and the agent finds them in the next session. The summary strategy writes summaries for each session and stores them under that session's ID, so the quality review can read the summary of any conversation. CreateEvent stores each raw turn as short-term memory, and the agent reads the history of the current session with ListEvents. AgentCore Memory builds the long-term records in the background, and the agent reads them with RetrieveMemoryRecords on the namespace of each strategy.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.1: "Develop intelligent autonomous systems with appropriate memory and state management capabilities"

Sources:

  • User preference memory strategy
  • Summary strategy
  • Memory scoping with namespaces

INCORRECT: Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a semantic strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using the user's ID as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
The semantic strategy extracts facts and knowledge from conversations, such as an order number or the version of a product that the user runs. It fits an agent that must recall those details later. With the user preference strategy and the user's ID as actorId, this setup does keep preferences across sessions. But it has no summary strategy, so AgentCore Memory writes no session summaries, and the quality review needs one for each conversation.

INCORRECT: Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a summary strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using a new ID for each conversation as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
A new actorId for each conversation fits an assistant for guest users, where nothing may link one visit to the next. The summary strategy would still write a summary for each session. But AgentCore Memory keeps user preferences under the actorId, so every conversation starts a new, empty profile. The agent must remember a user's product preferences across sessions, and this setup never brings back the preferences of an earlier session.

INCORRECT: Create a memory with a user preference strategy and a semantic strategy. Write each turn with CreateEvent, using a new ID for each conversation as actorId and the conversation's ID as sessionId.
This setup misses two needs. With a new actorId for each conversation, the preferences that AgentCore Memory extracts stay with that one conversation. The semantic strategy extracts facts, not summaries, so the quality review gets no summary of each session.

A developer is configuring an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to expose two enterprise tools to an AI agent. The agent sends each user's JWT, issued by the company's OAuth identity provider, with its requests to the gateway. The first tool is an internal REST API, documented with an OpenAPI specification, that accepts only a fixed secret string in a request header. The second tool is an AWS Lambda function that accesses internal resources inside a VPC.
Which gateway configuration correctly satisfies the authentication and target requirements for both tools?

options.text: Create one gateway with a JWT inbound authorizer for the company's identity provider. Add an OpenAPI target with an API key credential provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
Create one gateway with IAM inbound authorization for the agent's IAM role. Add an OpenAPI target with an OAuth client credentials provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
Create one gateway with IAM inbound authorization for the agent's IAM role. Add an OpenAPI target with an API key credential provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.

Create one gateway with a JWT inbound authorizer for the company's identity provider. Add an OpenAPI target with an OAuth client credentials provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create one gateway with a JWT inbound authorizer for the company's identity provider. Add an OpenAPI target with an API key credential provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
Inbound authorization is set once for the whole gateway. A JWT inbound authorizer checks the token that each caller sends, and here the agent sends each user's JWT from the company's identity provider. Outbound authorization is set for each target. A fixed secret string that an API checks in a request header is an API key. An OpenAPI target can take its API key from an API key credential provider in AgentCore Identity, and the gateway sends that key with each call. A Lambda target supports only the gateway service role, and that role needs permission for lambda:InvokeFunction on the function. Both targets sit on one gateway, so the agent sees the tools of both in one tools/list response.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.7: "Develop model extension frameworks to enhance FM capabilities"

Sources:

  • Set up outbound authorization for your gateway

INCORRECT: Create one gateway with IAM inbound authorization for the agent's IAM role. Add an OpenAPI target with an OAuth client credentials provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
IAM inbound authorization checks the AWS credentials that sign each request to the gateway. An OAuth credential provider with client credentials gets an access token from an authorization server for the target. Together they fit an AWS service that calls the gateway with its own IAM role, and a REST API that accepts OAuth access tokens. The Lambda target is right here. But this agent sends a JWT from the company's identity provider, not a signed AWS request, so the gateway would refuse every call. The REST API also accepts only a fixed secret string, and an access token changes when the old one expires.

INCORRECT: Create one gateway with IAM inbound authorization for the agent's IAM role. Add an OpenAPI target with an API key credential provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
IAM inbound authorization checks the AWS credentials that sign each request to the gateway. It fits callers that are AWS identities, such as a service that runs with its own IAM role. The two targets are right here: the API key credential provider suits the REST API, and the Lambda target uses the gateway service role. But this agent sends a JWT from the company's identity provider, not a signed AWS request, so the gateway would refuse every call before it reaches a target.

INCORRECT: Create one gateway with a JWT inbound authorizer for the company's identity provider. Add an OpenAPI target with an OAuth client credentials provider, and a Lambda target that uses the gateway service role.
An OAuth credential provider with client credentials gets an access token from an authorization server, and the gateway sends that token to the target. OpenAPI targets support it, and it fits a REST API that accepts OAuth access tokens. The inbound authorizer and the Lambda target are right here. An access token is not a fixed string: the authorization server issues a new one when the old one expires. This REST API accepts only a fixed secret string in a request header, so it would refuse the OAuth token.

The agent is invoked by an authenticated user whose identity is validated via an inbound JWT authorizer. questions.promptText:
A developer is building an agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime that accesses a user's Google Drive on their behalf. The agent is invoked by an authenticated user whose identity is validated via an inbound JWT authorizer. During tool invocation, the agent must obtain a scoped OAuth token to call the Google Drive API for that specific user. The developer wants the agent to make as few identity calls as possible.
Which sequence of API calls correctly implements this flow?

options.text: The agent reads the workload access token from the WorkloadAccessToken header. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the M2M flow and the Google Drive scopes, and calls Google Drive with the returned token.

The agent calls GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT with the user's JWT for a workload access token. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the USER_FEDERATION flow and the Google Drive scopes, and sends any returned authorization URL to the user.

The agent calls GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT with the user's JWT for a workload access token. It calls GetResourceApiKey with the Google Drive credential provider, and sends the returned API key with each Google Drive call.

The agent reads the workload access token from the WorkloadAccessToken header. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the USER_FEDERATION flow and the Google Drive scopes, and sends any returned authorization URL to the user.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The agent reads the workload access token from the WorkloadAccessToken header. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the USER_FEDERATION flow and the Google Drive scopes, and sends any returned authorization URL to the user.
When an agent runs on AgentCore Runtime with an inbound JWT authorizer, the runtime exchanges the user's JWT for a workload access token. It passes that token to the agent code in the WorkloadAccessToken header, so the agent makes no identity call to get it. GetResourceOauth2Token with the USER_FEDERATION flow uses the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, which gives user-delegated access. If the token vault holds no Google Drive token for this user yet, the call returns an authorization URL. The agent sends the URL to the user, the user grants consent, and AgentCore Identity keeps the token for later calls until it expires.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.3: "Create secure access frameworks to ensure appropriate security controls"
Example: "identity federation between FM services and enterprise systems"

Sources:

  • Authenticate and authorize with Inbound Auth and Outbound Auth

  • GetResourceOauth2Token

  • Get workload access token

INCORRECT: The agent reads the workload access token from the WorkloadAccessToken header. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the M2M flow and the Google Drive scopes, and calls Google Drive with the returned token.
The M2M flow gets a token for machine-to-machine calls, where the agent calls a service for itself and no person takes part. It fits a tool that reads a resource that belongs to the company, not to one user. The first step is right. Here the agent must read each user's own Google Drive on that user's behalf. A token from the M2M flow carries the identity of the agent, not of the user. The USER_FEDERATION flow asks the user for consent and gets a token that acts for that user.

INCORRECT: The agent calls GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT with the user's JWT for a workload access token. It calls GetResourceOauth2Token with the USER_FEDERATION flow and the Google Drive scopes, and sends any returned authorization URL to the user.
GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT exchanges the JWT of an end user for a workload access token. An agent calls it itself when no service delivers the token, for example when the agent is not invoked through AgentCore Runtime or Gateway with inbound authentication. The second step is right. But here the runtime already makes this exchange and passes the token in the WorkloadAccessToken header. The extra call is one more identity call, and the developer wants as few as possible.

INCORRECT: The agent calls GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT with the user's JWT for a workload access token. It calls GetResourceApiKey with the Google Drive credential provider, and sends the returned API key with each Google Drive call.
GetResourceApiKey returns the API key that an API key credential provider holds. It fits a tool that accepts one API key from every caller. This agent must get a scoped OAuth token for each user to call the Google Drive API, and an API key is not that token. The option also repeats the token exchange that the runtime already makes.

Some users now paste whole books into the chat to raise the company's model costs. Each of them sends only a few requests, at the same pace as other users. Normal prompts are short. The security team wants these prompts blocked before the Lambda function runs.
Which control meets this need?

A company offers a public chat assistant on its website. The web client sends each prompt in a JSON POST request to an Amazon API Gateway REST API and puts the user's session ID in a request header. An AWS Lambda function then calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API.
Some users now paste whole books into the chat to raise the company's model costs. Each of them sends only a few requests, at the same pace as other users. Normal prompts are short. The security team wants these prompts blocked before the Lambda function runs.
Which control meets this need?

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a rate-based rule that blocks each client IP address that sends requests faster than the normal pace.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a size constraint rule that blocks each request whose body is larger than the longest normal prompt.
In the Lambda function, set maxTokens in the inference configuration of each Converse call to the length of the longest answer that the assistant needs.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a rate-based rule that blocks each session ID header value that sends requests faster than the normal pace.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a size constraint rule that blocks each request whose body is larger than the longest normal prompt.
A size constraint rule compares the number of bytes in one part of a web request with a number that the team sets. It checks only the size of that part, not its content. On the request body, with Block as the action, the rule stops every request that carries a prompt longer than a normal one. API Gateway runs the rules of the web ACL before its other access checks and before it calls the Lambda function, so these prompts never reach the function or the model. AWS WAF inspects the body only up to a set size. When the oversize handling of the rule is set to Match, a body larger than that size counts as a match, so the longest prompts are blocked too. The rule does not depend on how fast a user sends requests.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "real-time validation mechanisms"

Sources:

  • Size constraint rule statement

  • Oversize web request components in AWS WAF

  • Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF

INCORRECT: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a rate-based rule that blocks each client IP address that sends requests faster than the normal pace.
A rate-based rule counts the requests from each IP address over a time window, and it blocks an address that goes over the limit. It fits a very large number of requests from a small number of sources. These users send only a few requests, at the same pace as everyone else. Their counts stay under any limit that lets normal users through, so the rule never blocks the long prompts.

INCORRECT: In the Lambda function, set maxTokens in the inference configuration of each Converse call to the length of the longest answer that the assistant needs.
The maxTokens setting caps the number of tokens that the model can generate in its response. It fits an application where long answers cause most of the cost. It does not limit the prompt. The long prompts still reach the Lambda function and the model, and the company still pays for their input tokens. The security team wants them blocked before the function runs.

INCORRECT: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API stage, and add a rate-based rule that blocks each session ID header value that sends requests faster than the normal pace.
A rate-based rule can also count requests for each value of a header, such as a session ID. This catches one user who sends a very large number of requests from many IP addresses. Here each user who pastes a book sends only a few requests at the normal pace. The count for each session stays normal, so the rule lets every long prompt through.

The data center already has a private network connection to a VPC in the AWS Region, and its servers resolve names through the bank's own DNS servers. Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A bank runs loan applications on servers in its own data center. The applications call models in Amazon Bedrock through the AWS SDK, which uses the default Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint name. The bank cannot change the endpoint settings of each application. The data center already has a private network connection to a VPC in the AWS Region, and its servers resolve names through the bank's own DNS servers. Security rules say that Bedrock traffic from the data center must go only to private IP addresses in the VPC, never to a public Amazon Bedrock address.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned on, and a Route 53 VPC Resolver outbound endpoint with a rule that forwards the bank's domain to the data center DNS servers.

Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime, and set the endpoint's own Regional DNS name, which resolves to its private IP addresses, as the Bedrock endpoint URL in each application's SDK settings.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned on, and a Route 53 VPC Resolver inbound endpoint to which the data center DNS servers forward the Bedrock runtime domain.

Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned off, and a private hosted zone for the Bedrock runtime domain with an alias record to the endpoint, associated with the VPC.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned on, and a Route 53 VPC Resolver inbound endpoint to which the data center DNS servers forward the Bedrock runtime domain.
An interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime gives Amazon Bedrock Runtime private IP addresses inside the VPC. With private DNS turned on, AWS creates a hidden private hosted zone that resolves the default Bedrock Runtime name to those addresses, so SDK calls that use the default name reach the endpoint with no change to the applications. That zone answers only inside the VPC, and servers outside the VPC cannot use Route 53 VPC Resolver directly. An inbound endpoint lets DNS servers outside the VPC send queries in. The data center DNS servers forward the Bedrock Runtime domain to it over the private connection and get the private addresses back. The applications then send their calls over the same private connection.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.4: "Develop cross-environment AI solutions to ensure data compliance across jurisdictions while enabling FM access"
Example: "secure routing between cloud and on-premises resources"

Sources:

  • Access AWS services through AWS PrivateLink

  • What is Route 53 VPC Resolver?

  • Working with private hosted zones

INCORRECT: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned on, and a Route 53 VPC Resolver outbound endpoint with a rule that forwards the bank's domain to the data center DNS servers.
An outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule sends DNS queries from the VPC to the data center. It fits workloads in the VPC that must resolve names that the bank's own DNS servers hold, such as the names of servers in the data center. Here the queries must go the other way: servers in the data center must resolve the Bedrock Runtime name. Without an inbound endpoint, the bank's DNS servers cannot get the private answer, so the applications still reach a public Bedrock address.

INCORRECT: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime, and set the endpoint's own Regional DNS name, which resolves to its private IP addresses, as the Bedrock endpoint URL in each application's SDK settings.
Each interface endpoint also gets its own Regional DNS name. These DNS records are public, and they resolve to the private IP addresses of the endpoint, so a server in the data center can use the name over the private connection. This design fits applications whose endpoint URL a team can set. Here the bank cannot change the endpoint settings of each application, and the applications keep using the default Bedrock Runtime name.

INCORRECT: Create an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with private DNS turned off, and a private hosted zone for the Bedrock runtime domain with an alias record to the endpoint, associated with the VPC.
Turning off private DNS and adding a private hosted zone with an alias record to the endpoint fits a shared endpoint, where several VPCs that are associated with the zone use one central endpoint. A private hosted zone answers only for EC2 instances in the associated VPCs, or for queries that arrive through an inbound endpoint. This design has no inbound endpoint, so the DNS servers in the data center cannot get an answer from the zone.

A software company offers a contract assistant to many business tenants. Each tenant has its own AWS Lambda function with its own IAM role, and every function calls the same model in Amazon Bedrock. Model invocation logging sends each call to one CloudWatch Logs log group.
Model costs rose sharply this month. Some tenants paste very long contracts and get short answers, while others ask many short questions. The operations team wants a graph that ranks the tenants by the size of what they send to the model, updated within minutes. Finance does not want a separate custom metric charge for each tenant.
Which monitoring setup meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A software company offers a contract assistant to many business tenants. Each tenant has its own AWS Lambda function with its own IAM role, and every function calls the same model in Amazon Bedrock. Model invocation logging sends each call to one CloudWatch Logs log group.
Model costs rose sharply this month. Some tenants paste very long contracts and get short answers, while others ask many short questions. The operations team wants a graph that ranks the tenants by the size of what they send to the model, updated within minutes. Finance does not want a separate custom metric charge for each tenant.
Which monitoring setup meets these needs?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch Contributor Insights rule on the log group with $.identity.arn as the key, Sum as the aggregation and $.input.inputTokenCount as the value.
Create a CloudWatch Contributor Insights rule on the log group with $.identity.arn as the key, Sum as the aggregation and $.output.outputTokenCount as the value.
Create a metric filter on the log group that publishes $.input.inputTokenCount as the metric value, with $.identity.arn as a dimension, and graph that metric.
Create a CloudWatch dashboard that graphs the OutputTokenCount metric that Amazon Bedrock publishes for the model ID, and compare it across the busy hours.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a CloudWatch Contributor Insights rule on the log group with $.identity.arn as the key, Sum as the aggregation and $.input.inputTokenCount as the value.
Contributor Insights reads log events as they arrive and ranks the contributors that a rule defines. Each invocation log entry holds the ARN of the caller, and that ARN includes the name of the role that made the call. Every tenant has its own function and its own role, so this key gives one row for each tenant. Sum adds up the field named as the value, and inputTokenCount counts the tokens in each request. A tenant that pastes a long contract adds a large number even when the answer is short, so the graph ranks tenants by what they send. Contributor Insights charges for each log event that matches the rule, not for each tenant, so finance gets no custom metric for each tenant.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.3: "Develop integrated observability solutions to provide actionable insights for FM applications"

Sources:

  • Contributor Insights rule syntax in CloudWatch

  • Use Contributor Insights to analyze high-cardinality data

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch Contributor Insights rule on the log group with $.identity.arn as the key, Sum as the aggregation and $.output.outputTokenCount as the value.
This rule has the same key and the same Sum, but it adds up outputTokenCount, the tokens in the answers that the model writes. That is the right field when a team wants to find the tenants that cause the longest answers. Here the tenants with long contracts get short answers, so a ranking by answer size puts them near the bottom, even though they send the most to the model.

INCORRECT: Create a metric filter on the log group that publishes $.input.inputTokenCount as the metric value, with $.identity.arn as a dimension, and graph that metric.
A metric filter can publish a number from a JSON log field as a metric and use another field as a dimension. This works well when a dimension has a few values, such as a few environments. Every different value of a dimension becomes its own metric and is charged as its own custom metric. With the role ARN as the dimension, every tenant adds one more custom metric, which finance does not want.

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch dashboard that graphs the OutputTokenCount metric that Amazon Bedrock publishes for the model ID, and compare it across the busy hours.
Amazon Bedrock publishes OutputTokenCount in CloudWatch for each model. A graph of this metric shows how the length of the answers from one model changes over time. Here every tenant calls the same model, so the graph shows one line for all tenants together. It cannot show which tenant sends the most, and it counts the answers, not what the tenants send.

An insurance company receives claim emails from brokers. An AWS Lambda function sends each PDF attachment to a model in Amazon Bedrock, which writes a summary of the policy terms. The summary depends only on the attachment, not on the email.
Brokers often send the same policy PDF in many emails. Each broker writes a different note, and many notes look alike, such as "Please review the attached policy", while the attachments differ. A policy that changes in one clause must get its own summary. Most of the cost and wait come from the long summary that the model writes.
Which design avoids the repeated summaries?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company receives claim emails from brokers. An AWS Lambda function sends each PDF attachment to a model in Amazon Bedrock, which writes a summary of the policy terms. The summary depends only on the attachment, not on the email.
Brokers often send the same policy PDF in many emails. Each broker writes a different note, and many notes look alike, such as "Please review the attached policy", while the attachments differ. A policy that changes in one clause must get its own summary. Most of the cost and wait come from the long summary that the model writes.
Which design avoids the repeated summaries?

options.text: Hash the bytes of each attachment with SHA-256, look up the hash in a DynamoDB table, and call the model only when no summary is stored.
Embed the text of each attachment, and reuse a stored summary when ElastiCache holds an attachment vector above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
Embed the text of each broker note, and reuse a stored summary when ElastiCache holds a note vector above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
Put a cache checkpoint after the attachment in each request to the model, so that Amazon Bedrock reads the repeated attachment from its prompt cache.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Hash the bytes of each attachment with SHA-256, look up the hash in a DynamoDB table, and call the model only when no summary is stored.
This design stores each result under a fingerprint of the one input that decides it. The hash of the file is the same every time the same PDF arrives, whatever its file name and whatever note the broker wrote. The function reads the table first and calls the model only for a file that it has not seen, so the long summary is written once and then reused. A policy that changes in one clause is a different file with a different hash, so it gets its own summary.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.4: "Create intelligent caching systems to reduce costs and improve response times by avoiding unnecessary FM invocations"
Example: "result fingerprinting"

Sources:

  • Optimize LLM response costs and latency with effective caching
  • Idempotency (Powertools for AWS Lambda)
  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Embed the text of each attachment, and reuse a stored summary when ElastiCache holds an attachment vector above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
Semantic caching reuses an answer for a request whose meaning is close to an earlier one, which suits questions that users word in different ways. Two versions of a policy that differ in one clause have almost the same text, so their vectors are very close. A similarity match would return the summary of the old version for the new one, and the scenario says that a changed clause must get its own summary.

INCORRECT: Embed the text of each broker note, and reuse a stored summary when ElastiCache holds a note vector above the similarity threshold that the team sets.
Semantic caching on the text of a request works when that text alone decides the answer. In this scenario the attachment decides the summary, not the note. Many notes look alike while their attachments differ, so a match on the note would return the summary of a different policy.

INCORRECT: Put a cache checkpoint after the attachment in each request to the model, so that Amazon Bedrock reads the repeated attachment from its prompt cache.
Prompt caching keeps a repeated start of the prompt, so the model reads that input faster and at a lower input token cost. It helps most when a long, fixed part of the prompt repeats and most of the cost is in the input. Here most of the cost and the wait come from the summary that the model writes. With prompt caching, the model still writes a new summary for every email.

questions.promptText:
A developer is deploying a multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime where a coordinator agent needs to discover and communicate with a specialized sub-agent. The sub-agent must be deployed using the A2A protocol so that the coordinator can discover its capabilities programmatically.
Which container configuration correctly implements the A2A protocol requirements for the sub-agent?

options.text: Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:9000 at the root path /. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP as the communication transport.

Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:8080 at the /invocations path. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP as the communication transport.

Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:9000 at the root path /. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use streamable HTTP with stateless_http=True as the communication transport.

Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:8000 at the /mcp path. Expose the agent's capabilities as MCP tool definitions via tools/list. Use streamable HTTP as the communication transport and rely on the Mcp-Session-Id header for session isolation.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:9000 at the root path /. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP as the communication transport.
This container meets each part of the A2A contract on AgentCore Runtime. An A2A server listens on port 9000 at the root path /, while the HTTP protocol uses port 8080 at /invocations and MCP uses port 8000 at /mcp. The Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json describes the sub-agent and what it can do, so the coordinator can read the card and discover its capabilities programmatically. A2A messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP, and AgentCore Runtime passes them from the InvokeAgentRuntime API to the container without changing them. All four options use an ARM64 container, so the port, the path, the discovery method and the transport decide the answer.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.1: "Develop intelligent autonomous systems with appropriate memory and state management capabilities"

Sources:

  • A2A protocol contract
  • Understand the AgentCore Runtime service contract

INCORRECT: Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:8080 at the /invocations path. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP as the communication transport.
This option correctly uses ARM64 and correctly includes the Agent Card for capability discovery, but configures the container to listen on port 8080 at /invocations. Port 8080 and the /invocations path are the correct configuration for the HTTP protocol in AgentCore Runtime, not the A2A protocol. Each protocol supported by AgentCore Runtime has distinct port and path requirements: HTTP uses 8080 at /invocations, MCP uses 8000 at /mcp, and A2A uses 9000 at /. Deploying an A2A server on port 8080 means AgentCore Runtime will not route A2A JSON-RPC messages correctly to the container.

INCORRECT: Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:9000 at the root path /. Expose an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json for capability discovery. Use streamable HTTP with stateless_http=True as the communication transport.
This container has the right port, the right root path and the Agent Card, so only the transport is wrong. Streamable HTTP with stateless_http=True is the recommended default for MCP servers on AgentCore Runtime, and MCP servers listen on port 8000 at /mcp. An A2A server uses JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP instead. AgentCore Runtime passes the A2A messages from the coordinator to the container without changing them, so the container must run an A2A server that reads JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, not an MCP server.

INCORRECT: Package the sub-agent as an ARM64 container. Configure it to listen on 0.0.0.0:8000 at the /mcp path. Expose the agent's capabilities as MCP tool definitions via tools/list. Use streamable HTTP as the communication transport and rely on the Mcp-Session-Id header for session isolation.
This option correctly uses ARM64 but configures the container entirely for MCP rather than A2A. Port 8000 at /mcp, tools/list for capability exposure, streamable HTTP transport, and Mcp-Session-Id session management are all MCP-specific requirements. While MCP is a valid and supported protocol for hosting tools on AgentCore Runtime, it does not provide the standardized agent discovery mechanism that A2A requires. The coordinator agent needs to discover the sub-agent's capabilities via an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, which is an A2A-specific construct with no equivalent in MCP. MCP exposes tools, not agent identity and capability metadata for peer discovery.

An AWS Lambda function in an HR policy assistant sends each employee question to an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain as a hybrid query with a match subquery and a neural subquery. A search pipeline normalizes the scores with min_max and gives both parts the same share of the final score.
Employees ask long questions in everyday words, and policies that repeat common words such as "leave" often rank above the policy that answers the question. In tests, the semantic part alone ranks the right policy first more often, but only the keyword part finds some short policy titles. The team wants no merge code in the function.
Which change improves the ranking?

options.text: Keep both subqueries, and set the combination weights in the normalization processor so the neural subquery gets a larger weight than the match subquery.
Remove the match subquery, and send the neural subquery alone through the same search pipeline, so that only semantic scores rank the policies.
Remove the neural subquery, and send the match subquery alone through the same search pipeline, so that only keyword scores rank the policies.
Send the match subquery and the neural subquery as two separate searches from the function, and add their scores in code with more weight on semantic scores.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Keep both subqueries, and set the combination weights in the normalization processor so the neural subquery gets a larger weight than the match subquery.
The normalization processor first puts the keyword scores and the semantic scores on one scale, and then combines them. The combination step takes a weight for each subquery, and the weights add up to 1. Today both parts get the same share. A larger weight on the neural subquery lets the semantic score decide more of the final rank, which the tests favor, while the match subquery still adds the short policy titles. The change is a setting in the search pipeline, so the function needs no merge code.

Skill 4.2.2: "Enhance retrieval performance to improve the relevance and speed of retrieved information for FM context augmentation"
Example: "hybrid search implementation with custom scoring"

Sources:

  • Hybrid Search with Amazon OpenSearch Service

  • Combine keyword and semantic search for text and images using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service

  • Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports hybrid query score normalization

INCORRECT: Remove the match subquery, and send the neural subquery alone through the same search pipeline, so that only semantic scores rank the policies.
A neural query alone suits a search where every question comes in natural language and exact words do not matter. The tests show that the semantic part ranks the right policy first more often. But only the keyword part finds some short policy titles, so removing it loses those results.

INCORRECT: Remove the neural subquery, and send the match subquery alone through the same search pipeline, so that only keyword scores rank the policies.
A keyword query alone suits searches where users type the exact words of a document, such as a title. Here employees ask long questions in everyday words, and common words already move the wrong policies up. A keyword query alone makes that problem worse, and it drops the semantic part that ranks the right policy first more often.

INCORRECT: Send the match subquery and the neural subquery as two separate searches from the function, and add their scores in code with more weight on semantic scores.
Two searches merged in the application is how teams built hybrid search before OpenSearch could combine the scores itself, and it still works when a team needs scoring logic that the engine does not offer. Keyword scores and semantic scores use different scales, so the code must also scale them before it adds them. The team wants no merge code in the function, and the search pipeline already combines the scores with weights.

questions.promptText:
A developer is building a generative AI workflow using Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows. The workflow receives an array of support tickets and must process each ticket individually through a prompt node that generates a resolution summary. The final output must be a single consolidated array of all resolution summaries returned in one response. The team does not want to write or maintain any code for this workflow.
Which node configuration correctly implements this workflow?

options.text: Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to the prompt node, the prompt node to a collector node, and the collector node to the output node.
Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to the prompt node, and the prompt node straight to the output node, with no collector node.
Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to a Lambda function node that calls the model, that node to a collector node, and the collector node to the output node.
Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to a Lambda function node that calls the model, and that node straight to the output node, with no collector node.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to the prompt node, the prompt node to a collector node, and the collector node to the output node.
An iterator node takes the array of tickets and sends its items to the next node one at a time. The prompt node then writes a resolution summary for each ticket. A collector node takes each summary, together with the size of the array, and puts the summaries back into one array. The output node then returns that array in one response, and the flow needs no code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.6: "Design complex prompt systems to handle sophisticated tasks with FMs"

Sources:

  • Node types for your flow

INCORRECT: Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to the prompt node, and the prompt node straight to the output node, with no collector node.
This flow splits the array and writes a summary for each ticket, but nothing gathers the summaries. When an iterator runs with no collector, the output node returns the result for each item in a separate response. That suits a caller that wants one response for each ticket. Here the caller needs all summaries in one array, in one response.

INCORRECT: Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to a Lambda function node that calls the model, that node to a collector node, and the collector node to the output node.
A Lambda function node runs the team's own code, and it can sit between an iterator node and a collector node. This design suits a flow that needs custom logic for each item, such as a call to another system before the summary. It returns one array, as the scenario needs. But the team does not want to write or maintain any code, and a prompt node writes each summary with no code.

INCORRECT: Connect the input node to an iterator node, the iterator node to a Lambda function node that calls the model, and that node straight to the output node, with no collector node.
This flow sends each ticket to a Lambda function that calls the model, and it returns each result in its own response. That suits a caller that wants one response for each ticket and needs custom code for each one. Here the team wants no code, and the caller needs all summaries in one array, in one response, which needs a collector node.

An engineer edits the working draft, and each release becomes a prompt version that the application calls. Last month a release broke two cases: emails with two order numbers and emails with no order number. Users got wrong replies for a week.
The team stores 150 edge case emails in Amazon S3, each with the rules that its reply must follow. Code can check every rule. The draft does not change while a check runs. One broken rule in any case must stop the release before a version exists, and no person should read the replies.
Which TWO parts should the release process include?

questions.promptText:
A retailer keeps the prompt of its order support assistant in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. An engineer edits the working draft, and each release becomes a prompt version that the application calls. Last month a release broke two cases: emails with two order numbers and emails with no order number. Users got wrong replies for a week.
The team stores 150 edge case emails in Amazon S3, each with the rules that its reply must follow. Code can check every rule. The draft does not change while a check runs. One broken rule in any case must stop the release before a version exists, and no person should read the replies.
Which TWO parts should the release process include?
Select TWO.

options.text: An AWS Step Functions workflow whose Map state sends each stored email to the model with the draft prompt, and whose last state then creates the prompt version.
An AWS Lambda function that checks each reply against the rules of its case, and raises an error when the reply breaks any one of those rules.
An AWS Lambda function that asks a judge model to score each reply against the rules of its case, and raises an error below a set score.
An Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model that scores the draft's replies to the stored emails, and allows the release when the average passes a bar.
A CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric that counts production replies that break a rule, which notifies the team to move the application back to the previous version.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An AWS Step Functions workflow whose Map state sends each stored email to the model with the draft prompt, and whose last state then creates the prompt version.
A Map state runs the same steps for each item in a list, so each stored email goes through the prompt and gets its own reply. A Lambda function in each iteration reads the prompt with GetPrompt and no version, which returns the working draft, and sends the email to the model with it, so the test uses the text that the engineer is about to release. The last state creates the version only after the Map state succeeds, so a version exists only for a draft that passed every case.

CORRECT: An AWS Lambda function that checks each reply against the rules of its case, and raises an error when the reply breaks any one of those rules.
Each case comes with rules that code can check, such as which order number the reply must name. The function runs in each iteration of the Map state and tests these rules the same way on every run. When it raises an error, its iteration fails, and the failure of any iteration makes the Map state fail and stops the other iterations. The workflow then never reaches the state that creates the version, so one broken rule stops the release.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.4: "Develop quality assurance systems to ensure prompt effectiveness and reliability for FMs"
Example: "Step Functions to test edge cases"

Sources:

  • Using Map state in Inline mode in Step Functions workflows

  • GetPrompt

  • Deploy a prompt to your application using versions in Prompt management

INCORRECT: An AWS Lambda function that asks a judge model to score each reply against the rules of its case, and raises an error below a set score.
A judge model helps when a rule needs judgment, such as whether a reply sounds polite. Here code can check every rule. A judge is itself a model, and a model can give a slightly different output for the same input, so the same reply could pass on one run and fail on the next. A code check gives the same result every time.

INCORRECT: An Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model that scores the draft's replies to the stored emails, and allows the release when the average passes a bar.
An evaluation job with a judge model scores each reply in a dataset and reports the scores for the whole set. It suits a comparison of overall quality, for example between two prompts. A pass mark on the average lets a release go ahead even when one case breaks a rule, because the other cases raise the average. Here one broken rule in any case must stop the release.

INCORRECT: A CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric that counts production replies that break a rule, which notifies the team to move the application back to the previous version.
An alarm on production replies finds problems after users see them. It is useful as a second check for problems that the tests do not cover. Here the release must stop before a version exists. This alarm can fire only after the new version runs and users get wrong replies, which is what happened last month.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs an HR assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The knowledge base stores its vectors in an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection that the team created. For each chat message, the app calls Retrieve with the message text and then calls Converse with the returned chunks.
First questions get good answers, even long questions with several parts. Follow-up questions such as "And for part-time staff?" get answers about other policies. The team does not want to add another model call to each chat turn, and it does not want to keep the chat history in its own database.
Which change fixes the answers to follow-up questions?
questions.promptText:
A company runs an HR assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The knowledge base stores its vectors in an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection that the team created. For each chat message, the app calls Retrieve with the message text and then calls Converse with the returned chunks.
First questions get good answers, even long questions with several parts. Follow-up questions such as "And for part-time staff?" get answers about other policies. The team does not want to add another model call to each chat turn, and it does not want to keep the chat history in its own database.
Which change fixes the answers to follow-up questions?

options.text: Call RetrieveAndGenerate in place of Retrieve and Converse, and send with each later message of a chat the sessionId that the first response of that chat returned.
Call RetrieveAndGenerate in place of Retrieve and Converse, set QUERY_DECOMPOSITION in its orchestration configuration, and send each message of a chat with no sessionId.
Keep Retrieve and Converse, and add a step where a model rewrites each follow-up message into a full question from the earlier turns before the Retrieve call.
Keep Retrieve and Converse, save each turn in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and send the last three messages together as the query text of each Retrieve call.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call RetrieveAndGenerate in place of Retrieve and Converse, and send with each later message of a chat the sessionId that the first response of that chat returned.
RetrieveAndGenerate retrieves the chunks and writes the answer in one call to Amazon Bedrock. On the first request of a chat, Amazon Bedrock creates a session ID and returns it in the response. When the app sends that same sessionId with each later message, Amazon Bedrock keeps the context of the earlier turns of that chat for the model. So a short follow-up such as "And for part-time staff?" is handled as part of the policy question that the user asked before. One RetrieveAndGenerate call replaces the Retrieve call and the Converse call, so the change adds no model call. Amazon Bedrock keeps the session, so the team stores no chat history in a database of its own.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.5: "Develop sophisticated query handling systems to improve the retrieval effectiveness and result quality for FM augmentation"

Sources:

  • RetrieveAndGenerate

  • Query a knowledge base and generate responses based off the retrieved data

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation

INCORRECT: Call RetrieveAndGenerate in place of Retrieve and Converse, set QUERY_DECOMPOSITION in its orchestration configuration, and send each message of a chat with no sessionId.
Query decomposition breaks a complex question into smaller sub-queries and searches for each one. It helps when one question has several parts, for example a question that compares two policies. The question says that long questions with several parts already get good answers. The failing messages are short follow-ups that do not name their subject, and splitting "And for part-time staff?" into parts cannot bring that subject back. With no sessionId, each message also starts a new session, so Amazon Bedrock has no earlier turn to work with.

INCORRECT: Keep Retrieve and Converse, and add a step where a model rewrites each follow-up message into a full question from the earlier turns before the Retrieve call.
A rewrite step is a common way to handle follow-ups in a custom RAG app. The model turns "And for part-time staff?" into a full question, such as a question about the leave policy for part-time staff, and that question finds the right chunks. Here the team does not want to add another model call to each chat turn. This design adds a rewrite call to every message, in addition to the Converse call.

INCORRECT: Keep Retrieve and Converse, save each turn in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and send the last three messages together as the query text of each Retrieve call.
Sending the last few messages as the search text gives a short follow-up the words it lacks, and a DynamoDB table is a common place to keep chat history. Here the team does not want to keep the chat history in its own database. This design stores every turn in a DynamoDB table that the team owns and runs.

A company runs a custom RAG search on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. Its k-NN index uses the HNSW method. Users say that answers often miss facts that the documents hold.
The team takes 200 test questions and compares the top 10 results of each search with a full scan that scores every stored vector against the same query vector. The full scan often ranks chunks in its top 10 that the normal search never returns. Search latency is far below the team's target. CPU use is low on every data node, and the memory that the vector graphs use stays far below its limit.
Which change should the team make first?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a custom RAG search on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. Its k-NN index uses the HNSW method. Users say that answers often miss facts that the documents hold.
The team takes 200 test questions and compares the top 10 results of each search with a full scan that scores every stored vector against the same query vector. The full scan often ranks chunks in its top 10 that the normal search never returns. Search latency is far below the team's target. CPU use is low on every data node, and the memory that the vector graphs use stays far below its limit.
Which change should the team make first?

options.text: Raise the ef_search value of the k-NN index, so each search keeps a longer list of candidate vectors to visit before it returns its top results.
Fine-tune the embedding model on the company's documents, embed every chunk again with the new model, and load the new vectors into a new k-NN index.
Raise number_of_replicas on the k-NN index, so more copies of its shards spread across the data nodes and more of the nodes can answer each search.
Add data nodes to the domain, so the shards of the k-NN index spread across more data nodes and more memory can hold its vector graphs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Raise the ef_search value of the k-NN index, so each search keeps a longer list of candidate vectors to visit before it returns its top results.
ef_search sets the size of the list of candidate nodes that an HNSW search visits as it moves through the graph. A larger value adds search latency, but the search gets closer to the true nearest neighbors, so recall rises. The test shows a recall problem in the search itself: with the same query vectors, the full scan finds close chunks that the HNSW search misses. Latency is far below the target, so the team can accept some extra latency to raise recall. This setting is the first change to try, before any work on the index or on the embedding model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.4: "Troubleshoot retrieval system issues to identify and resolve problems that affect information retrieval effectiveness for FM augmentation"
Example: "vector search performance optimization"

Sources:

  • Choose the k-NN algorithm for your billion-scale use case with OpenSearch
  • AOSREL04-BP03 Enable index replication for your critical indices
  • k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) search in Amazon OpenSearch Service

INCORRECT: Fine-tune the embedding model on the company's documents, embed every chunk again with the new model, and load the new vectors into a new k-NN index.
Fine-tuning an embedding model helps when the vectors do not place related text close together, for example when the documents use special terms that the base model does not know. In that case even a full scan ranks the wrong chunks first. Here the full scan uses the same vectors and finds the missing chunks in its top 10. So the current vectors already place the right chunks near each question. The loss happens in the approximate search, and new vectors do not change how that search chooses its candidates.

INCORRECT: Raise number_of_replicas on the k-NN index, so more copies of its shards spread across the data nodes and more of the nodes can answer each search.
Replica shards spread read requests across the domain, which raises search throughput, and they keep the data available when a primary shard fails. More replicas help a domain where many searches at the same time raise latency. Here CPU use is low and latency is far below the target, so the domain has no throughput problem. More copies change how many searches the domain can serve at once, not how many candidates each HNSW search visits.

INCORRECT: Add data nodes to the domain, so the shards of the k-NN index spread across more data nodes and more memory can hold its vector graphs.
More data nodes give the index more memory and compute. They help when the vector graphs need more memory than the k-NN limit on each node allows, because performance suffers when graph memory use goes past that limit. Here the memory that the vector graphs use stays far below its limit, and CPU use is low. More nodes do not change how many candidates each search visits, so the same chunks stay missing.
