A bank uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy a GenAI loan approval application that includes an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. Before any Knowledge Base configuration change is promoted to Production, it must pass an automated golden set evaluation where the F1 score must be at least 0.85. If the score falls below this threshold, the pipeline must automatically roll back.
Which solution correctly implements this requirement?

options.text: Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and exit with code 1 if the score is below 0.85. Enable automatic rollback on the deployment stage so a CodeBuild failure triggers rollback to the last successful execution.

Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and exit with code 1 if the score is below 0.85. The non-zero exit code will automatically roll back the deployment stage.

Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric. Configure a CloudWatch Alarm to notify the team when the score drops below 0.85.

Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base RetrieveAndGenerate API against golden questions and use the generated text responses to calculate the F1 score against reference answers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and exit with code 1 if the score is below 0.85. Enable automatic rollback on the deployment stage so a CodeBuild failure triggers rollback to the last successful execution.
The CodeBuild test action runs in the deployment stage, after the action that applies the knowledge base change. The buildspec scores the golden questions and exits with code 1 when the F1 score is below 0.85. A command that exits with a code other than zero fails the build, so the test action fails and the whole stage fails. Automatic rollback is a stage setting of a V2 type pipeline. When the stage fails, CodePipeline rolls the stage back to its most recent successful execution. This works only after the stage has had one successful execution, so the first change must pass before rollback can protect the later ones. The test gives the score gate, and the rollback setting gives the automatic return to the last version that passed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.4: "Create systematic quality assurance processes to maintain consistent performance standards for FMs"
Example: "automated quality gates for deployments"

Sources:

  • Configure a stage for automatic rollback
  • What type of pipeline is right for me?
  • Configure conditions for a stage

INCORRECT: Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and exit with code 1 if the score is below 0.85. The non-zero exit code will automatically roll back the deployment stage.
The score gate here is the same as in the correct option: a low score makes the build exit with code 1, and the test action fails. A failed action fails the stage and stops the pipeline. It does not undo the deploy action that already ran earlier in that stage. A stage rolls back only when automatic rollback is set on it for a failure. This option sets no rollback, so the new knowledge base configuration stays in place after the failed test.

INCORRECT: Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base Retrieve API against golden questions, calculate the F1 score, and publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric. Configure a CloudWatch Alarm to notify the team when the score drops below 0.85.
In a V2 type pipeline, a CloudWatch alarm can be part of a gate: a stage condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule can fail a stage or roll it back. This option uses the alarm in no stage condition. The alarm only sends a notice to the team, and the build does not fail when the score is low. So the pipeline moves on with the new configuration, and people learn about the low score only after the change is in place.

INCORRECT: Add a CodeBuild test action to the pipeline stage. In the buildspec, invoke the Knowledge Base RetrieveAndGenerate API against golden questions and use the generated text responses to calculate the F1 score against reference answers.
This option has no gate and no rollback. The buildspec calculates a score, but nothing fails the build when the score is below 0.85, and the option sets no rollback on the stage. The score is also measured on generated answers, which depend on the model's wording as well as on the retrieved chunks. So the score does not show the effect of the knowledge base change alone.

A compliance officer tests each version and sets its status in Model Registry. Today an engineer checks the registry and deploys approved versions to the production endpoint by hand. Last quarter, an engineer deployed a version that was still pending.

Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company fine-tunes a claims summary model on Amazon SageMaker AI each month. A pipeline registers each new version in SageMaker Model Registry with the status PendingManualApproval. A compliance officer tests each version and sets its status in Model Registry. Today an engineer checks the registry and deploys approved versions to the production endpoint by hand. Last quarter, an engineer deployed a version that was still pending.
Each version must start its deployment within minutes after the officer approves it, with no person in the deployment. No version that waits for approval may reach production. The officer will not use any tool other than Model Registry.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus Approved, and that starts the deployment pipeline in AWS CodePipeline.

Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus PendingManualApproval, and that starts the deployment pipeline in AWS CodePipeline.

Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus PendingManualApproval, and that starts the deployment pipeline, which waits at a manual approval action.

Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus Approved, and that sends an email through Amazon SNS to the deployment engineer.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus Approved, and that starts the deployment pipeline in AWS CodePipeline.
SageMaker AI sends a "SageMaker Model Package State Change" event to the account's default event bus when a model version changes, and the event holds the ModelApprovalStatus field. A rule that matches this event with the value Approved fires when the compliance officer approves a version in Model Registry. The rule starts the CodePipeline pipeline that deploys that version, so the deployment starts within minutes and no engineer takes part. A version that still waits keeps the status PendingManualApproval, so the rule never starts a deployment for it. The SageMaker AI project templates use the same idea: setting a version to Approved starts the CI/CD deployment.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"
Example: "automated deployment pipelines to update models"

Sources:

  • Events that Amazon SageMaker AI sends to Amazon EventBridge

  • Update the Approval Status of a Model

  • Use SageMaker AI-Provided Project Templates

INCORRECT: Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus PendingManualApproval, and that starts the deployment pipeline in AWS CodePipeline.
This rule uses the same event, but it matches the status PendingManualApproval. A version gets that status when the pipeline registers it, so the rule starts the deployment pipeline for each new version before the officer looks at it. A rule on new versions fits a team that first deploys each version to a test endpoint. Here the pipeline deploys to production, and no version that waits for approval may reach production.

INCORRECT: Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus PendingManualApproval, and that starts the deployment pipeline, which waits at a manual approval action.
A manual approval action stops a CodePipeline pipeline until a person with the right IAM permissions approves or rejects it. A pipeline that starts for each new version and waits at this action fits a team whose approver works in CodePipeline. Here the compliance officer will not use any tool other than Model Registry, so no one approves the action. The status that the officer sets in Model Registry also does not move the pipeline on.

INCORRECT: Create a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge that matches the model package state change event with ModelApprovalStatus Approved, and that sends an email through Amazon SNS to the deployment engineer.
This rule matches the right event and the right status, so it fires when the officer approves a version. An email to an engineer fits a team that wants a person to choose when each approved version reaches production. Here each deployment must run with no person in it. After the email, an engineer still deploys by hand, which is how a pending version reached production last quarter.

No tickets arrive at night. Each morning, the first calls fail with ModelNotReadyException, and the same tickets succeed when the function sends them again a few minutes later. The function's timeout allows a wait of several minutes. The team does not want to pay for a running model copy at night.
Which change stops the morning failures?
questions.promptText:
A support team imported its own fine-tuned model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import. A Lambda function drafts a reply for each new ticket by calling the model with InvokeModel through the AWS SDK. When a call fails, the function marks the ticket for staff to answer by hand.
No tickets arrive at night. Each morning, the first calls fail with ModelNotReadyException, and the same tickets succeed when the function sends them again a few minutes later. The function's timeout allows a wait of several minutes. The team does not want to pay for a running model copy at night.
Which change stops the morning failures?

options.text: Raise the maximum number of attempts in the retry settings of the SDK client, so the client tries each call again with exponential backoff while the model loads.
Create an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that calls the model every few minutes through the night, so a copy of the model stays loaded for the first morning ticket.
Deploy the fine-tuned model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a minimum of one instance, so a copy of the model stays loaded for the first morning ticket.
Change the function to call the model with the Converse API instead of InvokeModel, so each request uses one message format that many models share.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Raise the maximum number of attempts in the retry settings of the SDK client, so the client tries each call again with exponential backoff while the model loads.
Custom Model Import removes models that are not active, to make good use of the hardware. The first call after the quiet night reaches a removed model and gets ModelNotReadyException, and that call starts to restore the model. The SDK retries this error with exponential backoff, and the team can raise the maximum number of attempts in the retry settings of the client. With more attempts, the client keeps trying while the model is restored, and the call succeeds once the model is ready. The function's timeout allows that wait, and no model copy runs during the night.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.2: "Diagnose and resolve FM integration issues to identify and fix API integration problems specific to GenAI services"

Sources:

  • Invoke your imported model

  • Calculate the cost of running a custom model

  • Config Reference (Botocore)

INCORRECT: Create an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that calls the model every few minutes through the night, so a copy of the model stays loaded for the first morning ticket.
A call every few minutes keeps the model active, so it is not removed, and the first morning call works at once. That fits a team that needs a fast first answer and accepts the cost. Amazon Bedrock bills an imported model by the model copies that run and the time they run. The night calls keep a copy running and billed all night, and the team does not want to pay for that.

INCORRECT: Deploy the fine-tuned model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a minimum of one instance, so a copy of the model stays loaded for the first morning ticket.
A real-time endpoint keeps its instances running, so the model answers the first call of the day at once. That fits steady traffic or a strict latency target. An endpoint charges for as long as it runs, and with a minimum of one instance it runs all night. The team does not want to pay for a running model copy at night, and this design also moves the model off Amazon Bedrock.

INCORRECT: Change the function to call the model with the Converse API instead of InvokeModel, so each request uses one message format that many models share.
The Converse API gives one message format for many models. It helps a team that switches between models or sends request bodies in the wrong format. Here the same tickets succeed when the function sends them again a few minutes later, so the request bodies are fine. The error comes from the state of the model after the quiet night, and a change of API does not load the model.

questions.promptHtml:
A developer is building a cost-optimized pipeline to analyze thousands of research papers overnight. Each paper must be processed by a foundation model to extract structured metadata. Results must be stored in Amazon DynamoDB. The pipeline must handle the asynchronous nature of Bedrock batch inference, resume automatically when the batch job completes, and minimize inference costs. Job run times change a lot from night to night. Each night must show as one workflow execution, from the job start to the stored results.
Which architecture correctly implements this pipeline?
questions.promptText:
A developer is building a cost-optimized pipeline to analyze thousands of research papers overnight. Each paper must be processed by a foundation model to extract structured metadata. Results must be stored in Amazon DynamoDB. The pipeline must handle the asynchronous nature of Bedrock batch inference, resume automatically when the batch job completes, and minimize inference costs. Job run times change a lot from night to night. Each night must show as one workflow execution, from the job start to the stored results.
Which architecture correctly implements this pipeline?

options.text: A Standard workflow's Lambda task with .waitForTaskToken starts the job and saves the token in DynamoDB, and a default event bus rule on the job's state change runs a function that calls SendTaskSuccess.
A Standard workflow starts the batch job with an AWS SDK task, waits in a Wait state for a fixed number of hours, then reads the job output and writes the results to DynamoDB.
A Standard workflow starts the batch job with an AWS SDK task and ends, then a default event bus rule starts a second workflow that reads the job output and writes the results to DynamoDB.
A Standard workflow runs a Map state that calls InvokeModel on demand for each paper, retries throttling errors with backoff, and writes each result to DynamoDB as it arrives.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A Standard workflow's Lambda task with .waitForTaskToken starts the job and saves the token in DynamoDB, and a default event bus rule on the job's state change runs a function that calls SendTaskSuccess.
This is the callback pattern. A Lambda task with .waitForTaskToken gives the function a task token and pauses the workflow until a SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure call returns that token.

The function starts the batch inference job and saves the token in DynamoDB with the job ARN. When the job changes state, Amazon Bedrock sends a Batch Inference Job State Change event to the default event bus. The rule passes the event to a function that checks for the Completed status, reads the token for that job ARN and calls SendTaskSuccess.

The same execution then resumes and writes the results to DynamoDB, however long the job ran. Only Standard workflows support the callback pattern, and batch inference keeps the inference cost low.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.3: "Implement FM throughput optimization to address the specific throughput challenges of GenAI workloads"
Example: "batch inference strategies"

Sources:

  • How EventBridge for Amazon Bedrock works

  • Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions

  • Process multiple prompts with batch inference

INCORRECT: A Standard workflow starts the batch job with an AWS SDK task, waits in a Wait state for a fixed number of hours, then reads the job output and writes the results to DynamoDB.
A Wait state with a fixed time fits a job that always ends within a known time, such as a small job that runs the same way every night. Here job run times change a lot from night to night. When the job runs longer than the wait, the workflow reads output that is not complete yet. When the job ends sooner, the results wait for no reason.

INCORRECT: A Standard workflow starts the batch job with an AWS SDK task and ends, then a default event bus rule starts a second workflow that reads the job output and writes the results to DynamoDB.
Starting a second workflow from the job's state change event is a simple way to chain two workflows that can each run on their own. The rule on the default event bus does receive the event, and the second workflow can write the results. Here each night must show as one workflow execution, from the job start to the stored results. This design splits each night into two executions, and the first one ends without waiting for the job.

INCORRECT: A Standard workflow runs a Map state that calls InvokeModel on demand for each paper, retries throttling errors with backoff, and writes each result to DynamoDB as it arrives.
On-demand calls in a Map state fit a small set of papers, or results that people need at once. Amazon Bedrock prices batch inference lower than on-demand inference for the models that offer it. The pipeline must use Bedrock batch inference and keep inference costs low. On-demand calls for thousands of papers cost more and do not use batch inference at all.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A developer is choosing the vector store for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The workload is an internal HR policy chatbot. Employees query it a few times an hour during business hours, and it sits idle overnight and on weekends. The corpus is small and changes a few times a year.
The team already runs an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Two requirements drive the decision. Idle infrastructure cost must be as close to zero as possible. The first query after a long idle period must still return in under a second, because staff abandon the tool when it hangs. Filtering by department and policy year is also required.
Which vector store setup meets all three needs?
questions.promptText:
A developer is choosing the vector store for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The workload is an internal HR policy chatbot. Employees query it a few times an hour during business hours, and it sits idle overnight and on weekends. The corpus is small and changes a few times a year.
The team already runs an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Two requirements drive the decision. Idle infrastructure cost must be as close to zero as possible. The first query after a long idle period must still return in under a second, because staff abandon the tool when it hangs. Filtering by department and policy year is also required.
Which vector store setup meets all three needs?

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 Vectors vector bucket and index as the knowledge base vector store, and attach department and policy year to each vector as filterable metadata keys.
Use an index in an Amazon S3 Vectors bucket for the knowledge base, and list department and policy year as non-filterable metadata keys when the team creates the index.
Create an Aurora Serverless cluster with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store, and set its minimum capacity to 0 ACUs so that it pauses when idle.
Create an Aurora Serverless cluster with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store, and set its minimum capacity above 0 ACUs so that it never pauses.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon S3 Vectors vector bucket and index as the knowledge base vector store, and attach department and policy year to each vector as filterable metadata keys.
S3 Vectors keeps the embeddings in a vector bucket, with no servers and no capacity for the team to run. The team pays for the vectors it stores and the queries it sends, so a chatbot that sits idle at night and on weekends costs very little. A query to an index that nobody used for hours still returns in under one second, so the first question of the morning gets a fast answer. Metadata on each vector is filterable unless the index says otherwise, so the knowledge base can filter by department and policy year.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.1: "Create advanced vector database architectures specifically for FM augmentation to enable efficient semantic retrieval beyond traditional search capabilities"

Sources:

  • Using S3 Vectors with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • Metadata filtering (Amazon S3 User Guide)
  • Scaling to Zero ACUs with automatic pause and resume for Aurora serverless

INCORRECT: Use an index in an Amazon S3 Vectors bucket for the knowledge base, and list department and policy year as non-filterable metadata keys when the team creates the index.
Non-filterable metadata is a real setting of S3 Vectors. The team declares these keys when it creates the index, and they can hold larger values, such as text that the application only shows next to each result. A query cannot use them in a filter. The chatbot must filter by department and policy year, so these two keys must stay filterable.

INCORRECT: Create an Aurora Serverless cluster with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store, and set its minimum capacity to 0 ACUs so that it pauses when idle.
A minimum of 0 ACUs lets Aurora pause the instance after a time with no connections, and the instance charge then drops to zero. This saves money for a database that can wait. When the first query of the morning arrives, Aurora must resume the instance first, and this takes many seconds, longer still after a long pause. Staff stop using the tool when it hangs, so this fails the need for a fast first answer.

INCORRECT: Create an Aurora Serverless cluster with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store, and set its minimum capacity above 0 ACUs so that it never pauses.
With a minimum above 0 ACUs, the instance never pauses, so the first query of the morning gets a fast answer. This is a good choice when steady speed matters more than cost. The instance runs and bills at its minimum capacity every hour, also at night and on weekends. The team wants idle cost as close to zero as possible, so this fails the cost need.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A home goods retailer stores short product demonstration videos in Amazon S3. Each video shows a person using one product, with background music and no speech. When a new video arrives in the bucket, an AWS Lambda function must write a short text summary of what the video shows for the product page.
The team uses an Amazon Nova Lite model in Amazon Bedrock, which accepts video input, and Amazon Bedrock has permission to read the bucket. The videos are large, and a security rule says that the function must not download or hold the video files.
How should the function send each video to the model?
questions.promptText:
A home goods retailer stores short product demonstration videos in Amazon S3. Each video shows a person using one product, with background music and no speech. When a new video arrives in the bucket, an AWS Lambda function must write a short text summary of what the video shows for the product page.
The team uses an Amazon Nova Lite model in Amazon Bedrock, which accepts video input, and Amazon Bedrock has permission to read the bucket. The videos are large, and a security rule says that the function must not download or hold the video files.
How should the function send each video to the model?

options.text: Call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and a video block whose source is the location of the video in Amazon S3.
Read the video from Amazon S3, call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and a video block with the file bytes.
Read the video from Amazon S3, call the InvokeModel API with the Nova Lite model, and send the summary request with the video as a Base64 string in the request body.
Start an Amazon Transcribe job on the audio of the video, call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and the finished transcript.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and a video block whose source is the location of the video in Amazon S3.
A video block in a Converse request can point to an object in Amazon S3 instead of carrying the file. Amazon Bedrock then reads the video from the bucket itself, so the function never downloads it. This is also the way to send larger video files. Nova Lite understands a video from its frames, so it can describe what the person does with the product. One request carries one video, so the function sends one request for each new file.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock multimodal models"

Sources:

  • Multimodal understanding (Amazon Nova 2 User Guide)

  • VideoSource

  • Video understanding (Amazon Nova User Guide)

INCORRECT: Read the video from Amazon S3, call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and a video block with the file bytes.
Sending the file bytes in the video block works well for a small video. To do it, the function must first download the whole file from Amazon S3 and hold it in memory. The security rule says that the function must not download or hold the videos.

INCORRECT: Read the video from Amazon S3, call the InvokeModel API with the Nova Lite model, and send the summary request with the video as a Base64 string in the request body.
InvokeModel also works with Nova models, and teams that already use it can put the video in the request body as a Base64 string. The function must still download and encode the whole file, which the security rule does not allow.

INCORRECT: Start an Amazon Transcribe job on the audio of the video, call the Converse API with the Nova Lite model, and send a text block with the summary request and the finished transcript.
A transcript is a good input when people explain a product in the video. These videos have only background music and no speech, so the transcript holds nothing about the product. The summary must describe what the video shows, and only the frames hold that.

A company's support assistant uses its own retrieval code. For each question, the code rewrites the question, searches an Amazon OpenSearch Service index, and sends the top passages with the question to a model in Amazon Bedrock. The code logs each question, the passages it retrieved and the final answer.
The team wants Amazon Bedrock built-in scores for the answers that users get today, judged against the passages that the code retrieved. The documents must stay in the current index.
Which evaluation setup gives the team these scores?
questions.promptText:
A company's support assistant uses its own retrieval code. For each question, the code rewrites the question, searches an Amazon OpenSearch Service index, and sends the top passages with the question to a model in Amazon Bedrock. The code logs each question, the passages it retrieved and the final answer.
The team wants Amazon Bedrock built-in scores for the answers that users get today, judged against the passages that the code retrieved. The documents must stay in the current index.
Which evaluation setup gives the team these scores?

options.text: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the team's own inference responses, where each record holds the question, the logged passages and the logged answer to it.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the team's own inference responses, where each record holds the question and the passages that the code logged for it.
Create a knowledge base on a copy of the documents in Amazon S3, and run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job that sends each logged question to it.
Create a knowledge base on a copy of the documents in Amazon S3, and run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job that sends each logged question to it.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the team's own inference responses, where each record holds the question, the logged passages and the logged answer to it.
A RAG evaluation job can score a pipeline that is not a knowledge base. The team brings its own inference responses: each record holds the question, the passages its code retrieved, the answer, and a name for the RAG source. Amazon Bedrock skips the knowledge base call and scores the records as they are, so the scores describe the system that users get today. A retrieve-and-generate job scores the answers, and its built-in metrics include checks of each answer against the retrieved passages. The documents stay in their index.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.5: "Develop comprehensive assessment systems to ensure thorough evaluation from multiple perspectives for FM outputs"
Example: "RAG evaluation"

Sources:

  • Creating a prompt dataset for retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation jobs
  • Amazon Bedrock now supports RAG Evaluation (generally available)
  • Create a prompt dataset for retrieve-only RAG evaluation jobs

INCORRECT: Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the team's own inference responses, where each record holds the question and the passages that the code logged for it.
A retrieve-only job with the team's own responses is right when only the search step needs scores. Its records hold the question and the retrieved passages, with no answer, and its metrics rate the passages only. The team needs scores for the answers, so this job leaves out the part that the team cares about.

INCORRECT: Create a knowledge base on a copy of the documents in Amazon S3, and run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job that sends each logged question to it.
Evaluating a knowledge base is the right choice for an assistant that uses one. Here, the knowledge base would split, search and answer in its own way, so its scores would describe a different system, not the code that rewrites and searches for users today. The team needs scores for the answers that users already got, judged against the passages that the code retrieved for them.

INCORRECT: Create a knowledge base on a copy of the documents in Amazon S3, and run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job that sends each logged question to it.
A retrieve-only evaluation of a knowledge base is the right check when an assistant uses a knowledge base and only its search step needs scores. Here, the knowledge base would split and search the documents in its own way, so its scores would describe a different system, not the code that rewrites and searches for users today. A retrieve-only job also gives no scores for the answers, which the team needs.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's assistant answers staff questions through an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. The team has set its own goal: at least 95 percent of all answers in any 28 days must arrive within 8 seconds. Short slow periods are acceptable while the goal holds.
Today, an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the p95 Duration of the function fires on every short slow period, so the on-call team ignores it. Answer times have also grown slowly for months as the documents grow. The team wants an alert only when slow answers use up the goal's allowance quickly, and a view of how close it is to the goal.
Which monitoring setup meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A company's assistant answers staff questions through an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. The team has set its own goal: at least 95 percent of all answers in any 28 days must arrive within 8 seconds. Short slow periods are acceptable while the goal holds.
Today, an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the p95 Duration of the function fires on every short slow period, so the on-call team ignores it. Answer times have also grown slowly for months as the documents grow. The team wants an alert only when slow answers use up the goal's allowance quickly, and a view of how close it is to the goal.
Which monitoring setup meets these needs?

options.text: Turn on Application Signals for the function, create a request-based SLO on the latency of the function with the team's goal, and add a burn rate alarm to the SLO.
Turn on Application Signals for the function, create a period-based SLO on the latency of the function with the team's goal in one-minute periods, and add a burn rate alarm.
Keep the Duration metric of the function, and change the alarm so that it fires only when p95 stays above 8 seconds in 3 out of 5 evaluation periods.
Keep the Duration metric of the function, and replace the alarm with an anomaly detection alarm on p95 that fires when the value leaves its expected band.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on Application Signals for the function, create a request-based SLO on the latency of the function with the team's goal, and add a burn rate alarm to the SLO.
Application Signals instruments the Lambda function and collects its latency and availability. A service level objective (SLO) tracks that latency against the goal that the team sets. A request-based SLO counts good requests out of all requests in the interval, which matches a goal stated as a share of answers over a rolling 28 days. The burn rate shows how fast slow answers use up the allowed share of the goal. A burn rate alarm fires only when this rate passes a threshold that the team chooses, so a short slow period does not trigger it. The SLO also shows how close the team is to its goal.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.2: "Implement comprehensive GenAI monitoring systems to proactively identify issues and evaluate key performance indicators specific to FM implementations"

Sources:

  • Service level objectives (SLOs)
  • Monitor application performance with Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals
  • Application Signals now supports burn rate for application performance goals

INCORRECT: Turn on Application Signals for the function, create a period-based SLO on the latency of the function with the team's goal in one-minute periods, and add a burn rate alarm.
A period-based SLO splits the interval into periods and marks each period as good or bad. This fits a goal stated in time, such as the share of minutes with good service. The team's goal counts answers. A quiet night minute with one slow answer would weigh as much as a busy minute with many, so this SLO would not measure the goal that the team set.

INCORRECT: Keep the Duration metric of the function, and change the alarm so that it fires only when p95 stays above 8 seconds in 3 out of 5 evaluation periods.
Asking for several breaching periods before an alarm fires is a common way to make a noisy alarm fire less often. This alarm still looks only at the last few periods. It knows nothing about the allowance over 28 days, so it can stay silent while the goal is at risk, and it can fire when the goal is safe. It also gives no view of how close the team is to the goal.

INCORRECT: Keep the Duration metric of the function, and replace the alarm with an anomaly detection alarm on p95 that fires when the value leaves its expected band.
Anomaly detection is useful when no fixed goal exists, because it learns the normal pattern and trend of a metric and keeps adjusting to them. Answer times have grown slowly for months, so the band grows with them, and the alarm no longer follows the team's fixed goal. It also shows nothing about how close the team is to the goal.

An insurance company hosts a fine-tuned open-weight model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Its claims system calls the endpoint to extract fields from claim letters. The team has built a new version of the model with a different serving container.
Last time, a new version passed every test with saved requests but was slow on long letters in production. The team must now compare the latency and errors of the new version with the current version on live requests. Until the comparison ends, the claims system must get every result from the current version.
How should the team test the new version?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company hosts a fine-tuned open-weight model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Its claims system calls the endpoint to extract fields from claim letters. The team has built a new version of the model with a different serving container.
Last time, a new version passed every test with saved requests but was slow on long letters in production. The team must now compare the latency and errors of the new version with the current version on live requests. Until the comparison ends, the claims system must get every result from the current version.
How should the team test the new version?

options.text: Start a shadow test on the endpoint with the new version as the shadow variant, and compare the latency and error metrics of the two variants on the test dashboard.
Update the endpoint so that the new version gets 10 percent of the live requests through two weighted production variants, and add alarms on the latency and error metrics of the new version.
Update the endpoint so that the new version gets 10 percent of the live requests through a blue/green canary traffic shift, and add alarms on the latency and error metrics to its auto-rollback setup.
Deploy the new version to a second endpoint, send it a large set of saved claim requests, and compare its latency and error metrics with those of the current endpoint.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Start a shadow test on the endpoint with the new version as the shadow variant, and compare the latency and error metrics of the two variants on the test dashboard.
A shadow test sends a copy of each live request to the shadow variant on the same real-time endpoint. Only the production variant's responses go back to the caller, so the claims system keeps getting every result from the current version. The test dashboard compares metrics such as ModelLatency and the error counts of the two variants on the same live traffic. If the new version does well, the team can then promote it to production.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.9: "Create deployment validation systems to maintain reliability during FM updates"

Sources:

  • Shadow tests

  • Monitor a shadow test

INCORRECT: Update the endpoint so that the new version gets 10 percent of the live requests through two weighted production variants, and add alarms on the latency and error metrics of the new version.
Two production variants with weights split the live traffic, and each request goes to one of them. This is right when users should see the new version's results, for example to measure real reactions. Here, about one request in ten would get its result from the new version, and the claims system must get every result from the current version.

INCORRECT: Update the endpoint so that the new version gets 10 percent of the live requests through a blue/green canary traffic shift, and add alarms on the latency and error metrics to its auto-rollback setup.
A blue/green deployment with canary traffic shifting and auto-rollback alarms is a safe way to release a version that the team already trusts. During the canary step, part of the live traffic gets its results from the new version. The claims system must get every result from the current version until the comparison ends.

INCORRECT: Deploy the new version to a second endpoint, send it a large set of saved claim requests, and compare its latency and error metrics with those of the current endpoint.
A load test with saved requests on a separate endpoint finds many problems and touches no live traffic. The last version passed tests like this and was still slow on long letters in production, because the saved requests did not match the live mix. The team must compare the versions on live requests.

A bank will host a vendor's proprietary model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The vendor delivers a container image, which the bank pushes to Amazon ECR, and model artifacts, which the bank stores in Amazon S3. The bank cannot review the vendor's code.
The bank's VPC has a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 and databases that other applications use. The security team's rule: the vendor's code must not send any data out of its container, whether to the internet, to an AWS service or to any system in the VPC. SageMaker AI must still load the model artifacts.
Which setting meets the security team's rule?
questions.promptText:
A bank will host a vendor's proprietary model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The vendor delivers a container image, which the bank pushes to Amazon ECR, and model artifacts, which the bank stores in Amazon S3. The bank cannot review the vendor's code.
The bank's VPC has a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 and databases that other applications use. The security team's rule: the vendor's code must not send any data out of its container, whether to the internet, to an AWS service or to any system in the VPC. SageMaker AI must still load the model artifacts.
Which setting meets the security team's rule?

options.text: Create the SageMaker AI model with network isolation turned on in its settings, and give the model a VPC configuration that uses the bank's existing subnets.
Create the SageMaker AI model with a VPC configuration that uses private subnets with no route to the internet, and no NAT gateway or internet gateway in the VPC.
Create the SageMaker AI model with a VPC configuration that uses private subnets with no route to the internet, and an S3 endpoint policy that allows only reads of the artifacts.
Create the SageMaker AI model in subnets that route through a NAT gateway, and give its execution role permission to read only the vendor's model files.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create the SageMaker AI model with network isolation turned on in its settings, and give the model a VPC configuration that uses the bank's existing subnets.
Network isolation is a setting of the SageMaker AI model that removes all network access from the container. With network isolation on (the EnableNetworkIsolation setting of the model), the container cannot make any outbound call to any service, not even to Amazon S3, and it gets no AWS credentials. SageMaker AI still downloads the model artifacts with its execution role, outside the container, and with a VPC configuration the download goes through the bank's subnets. The container cannot reach any resource in the VPC or on the internet, which is what the security team asks for.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"

Sources:

  • Run Training and Inference Containers in Internet-Free Mode
  • Give SageMaker AI Hosted Endpoints Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC

INCORRECT: Create the SageMaker AI model with a VPC configuration that uses private subnets with no route to the internet, and no NAT gateway or internet gateway in the VPC.
Private subnets with no NAT gateway or internet gateway stop traffic to the internet, which is enough for many workloads. The container still has a network connection inside the VPC. It can reach the S3 gateway endpoint and the databases there, so the vendor's code could still send data out of the container.

INCORRECT: Create the SageMaker AI model with a VPC configuration that uses private subnets with no route to the internet, and an S3 endpoint policy that allows only reads of the artifacts.
An endpoint policy that allows only reads of one bucket is a good control when a container must read Amazon S3 and write nothing there. The container still has a network connection inside the VPC, so it can still reach the databases that other applications use. The rule says that the vendor's code must send no data to any system in the VPC.

INCORRECT: Create the SageMaker AI model in subnets that route through a NAT gateway, and give its execution role permission to read only the vendor's model files.
A NAT gateway is the right choice when a model must call a service on the internet, and a narrow execution role limits what the role's credentials can do in AWS. The NAT gateway still gives the container a path to the internet, and the role does not stop calls that need no AWS credentials. The vendor's code could send data to the internet.

Before it releases a new version of the stricter prompt, the team wants a score that shows how often each prompt turns away valid questions. It has 300 valid staff questions and no reference answers. The assistant uses no guardrail, and no staff may test the new prompt.
How should the team measure this problem before the next release?
questions.promptText:
A company's HR assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with a system prompt. After the team added stricter rules to the system prompt, staff said that the assistant declined many normal questions, such as how to request leave. The team went back to the old prompt.
Before it releases a new version of the stricter prompt, the team wants a score that shows how often each prompt turns away valid questions. It has 300 valid staff questions and no reference answers. The assistant uses no guardrail, and no staff may test the new prompt.
How should the team measure this problem before the next release?

options.text: Answer the 300 questions with each prompt, run an Amazon Bedrock judge evaluation job on each set of answers with the built-in Refusal metric, and compare the two scores.
Answer the 300 questions with each prompt, run an Amazon Bedrock judge evaluation job on each set of answers with the built-in Harmfulness metric, and compare the two scores.
Release each prompt to a small group of staff for a week, add a rating button to the assistant, and compare the share of low ratings that each prompt receives.
Add an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the assistant, answer the 300 questions with each prompt, and compare the InvocationsIntervened metric of the guardrail for each prompt.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Answer the 300 questions with each prompt, run an Amazon Bedrock judge evaluation job on each set of answers with the built-in Refusal metric, and compare the two scores.
The Refusal metric checks whether a response declines to answer the prompt or rejects the request. The team answers the valid questions with the old prompt and with the stricter prompt, and brings each set of answers to a judge evaluation job as its own inference responses. All responses in one job must carry the same model identifier, so each prompt gets its own job. The two Refusal scores then show how often each prompt turns valid questions away. The Refusal metric needs no reference answers, and no staff take part.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.1: "Develop comprehensive assessment frameworks to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of FM outputs beyond traditional ML evaluation approaches"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand model performance

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

  • Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation LLM-as-a-judge is now generally available

INCORRECT: Answer the 300 questions with each prompt, run an Amazon Bedrock judge evaluation job on each set of answers with the built-in Harmfulness metric, and compare the two scores.
Harmfulness is the right metric when the team worries about harmful content in the answers. A polite answer that declines a leave question contains nothing harmful, so both prompts could score well. The problem here is answers that turn valid questions away, which this metric does not measure.

INCORRECT: Release each prompt to a small group of staff for a week, add a rating button to the assistant, and compare the share of low ratings that each prompt receives.
Ratings from real users are a good way to learn how people feel about the answers after a release. Here, no staff may test the new prompt, and the team wants the score before the release.

INCORRECT: Add an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the assistant, answer the 300 questions with each prompt, and compare the InvocationsIntervened metric of the guardrail for each prompt.
InvocationsIntervened counts the calls in which a guardrail intervened, for example to block or mask content. It is a useful metric when a guardrail blocks content. The assistant uses no guardrail, and the declines come from the model, which follows the rules in the system prompt. A new guardrail would count only its own interventions, not the model's declines.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A developer is configuring an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a global e-commerce platform. The knowledge base contains product descriptions in English, German, French, and Japanese. Many products have a description in only one of these languages. Users submit queries in their native language and expect to retrieve relevant products regardless of the document language. Storage cost is a secondary concern, but the team wants to minimize it where possible without sacrificing retrieval accuracy.
Which embedding model configuration correctly addresses both requirements?
questions.promptText:
A developer is configuring an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a global e-commerce platform. The knowledge base contains product descriptions in English, German, French, and Japanese. Many products have a description in only one of these languages. Users submit queries in their native language and expect to retrieve relevant products regardless of the document language. Storage cost is a secondary concern, but the team wants to minimize it where possible without sacrificing retrieval accuracy.
Which embedding model configuration correctly addresses both requirements?

options.text: Create one knowledge base for all four languages with Cohere Embed Multilingual, so that a query in one language can find a product described in another language.
Create one knowledge base for all four languages with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 256 dimensions, so that each vector takes less storage than at 1,024.
Create one knowledge base for each language with Cohere Embed Multilingual, have a Lambda function detect the language of each query, and send the query only to that knowledge base.
Create one knowledge base for each language with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, have a Lambda function detect the language of each query, and send the query only to that knowledge base.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create one knowledge base for all four languages with Cohere Embed Multilingual, so that a query in one language can find a product described in another language.
Cohere Embed Multilingual is an embedding model in Amazon Bedrock that is built for cross-lingual search, so a query in German can find a Japanese description of the same product. Here many products have a description in only one language, and users search in their own language. One knowledge base with this model lets every user find every product. In Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, this model has only one number of dimensions, so the team cannot choose shorter vectors, as it can with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2. The question puts retrieval accuracy first and storage cost second, so this trade is the right one.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.2: "Select and configure optimal embedding solutions to create efficient vector representations for semantic search"
Example: "by evaluating performance characteristics of Amazon Bedrock embedding models"

Sources:

  • Embed Multilingual
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models
  • Supported models and Regions for Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Create one knowledge base for all four languages with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 256 dimensions, so that each vector takes less storage than at 1,024.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 lets the team choose a smaller vector size, and the model keeps most of its retrieval accuracy at 256 dimensions. Smaller vectors cut the storage cost. This is a good choice for a knowledge base where the queries and the documents are in the same language. But the model is optimized for English, and a query in one language against documents in another language gives weak results with it. Here a user who writes in French must find products that have only a Japanese description. The storage saving would cost retrieval accuracy, and the team does not accept that.

INCORRECT: Create one knowledge base for each language with Cohere Embed Multilingual, have a Lambda function detect the language of each query, and send the query only to that knowledge base.
One knowledge base for each language is a real design. It fits a company whose users need content only in their own language, for example separate regional stores. In this design, each query searches only the knowledge base of the user's language. A user who writes in German never searches the Japanese knowledge base, so a product with only a Japanese description never appears. The multilingual model cannot help when the query never reaches the right documents.

INCORRECT: Create one knowledge base for each language with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, have a Lambda function detect the language of each query, and send the query only to that knowledge base.
With one knowledge base for each language, every search stays inside one language. This avoids the weak cross-language results of Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, and it works when every product has a description in every language. Here many products have a description in only one language. A user who writes in English cannot find a product that has only a French description, because the query goes only to the English knowledge base.

questions.promptHtml:
A retailer's support line takes voice messages in US English after hours. Each morning, an AWS Lambda function starts an Amazon Transcribe batch job for each recorded message. A model in Amazon Bedrock then reads each transcript and drafts a reply for an agent. Some callers leave threats or insults for the staff. When the trust team read the transcripts of known abusive messages, the words often looked polite. The threat was in how the caller spoke. Each abusive message must go to a supervisor, and the model must not read any part of it.
Which design meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A retailer's support line takes voice messages in US English after hours. Each morning, an AWS Lambda function starts an Amazon Transcribe batch job for each recorded message. A model in Amazon Bedrock then reads each transcript and drafts a reply for an agent. Some callers leave threats or insults for the staff. When the trust team read the transcripts of known abusive messages, the words often looked polite. The threat was in how the caller spoke. Each abusive message must go to a supervisor, and the model must not read any part of it.
Which design meets these needs?

options.text: Turn on toxicity detection in each Transcribe job, and send each message with a high threat or insult score to a supervisor before the model step.
Turn on toxicity detection in each Transcribe job, and remove each segment with a high threat or insult score from the text before the model step.
Send each transcript to Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection, and send each message with a high threat or insult score to a supervisor before the model step.
Check each segment of the transcript with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail through the ApplyGuardrail API, and remove each segment that its violence or insults filter blocks before the model step.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on toxicity detection in each Transcribe job, and send each message with a high threat or insult score to a supervisor before the model step.
Amazon Transcribe can detect toxic speech in a batch transcription job. It uses the words and also speech cues, such as tone and pitch. It gives each speech segment a confidence score for each category, such as violence or threat and insults. Here the trust team found that abusive messages often used polite words, and the threat was in the caller's voice. A check that hears the audio can catch these messages. The workflow reads the scores in the job output and sends each flagged message to a supervisor before the model step, so the model never reads it. The feature works for batch jobs in US English, which matches these recorded messages.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.5: "Implement advanced threat detection to protect against adversarial inputs and security vulnerabilities"
Example: "safety classifiers"

Sources:

  • Detecting toxic speech

  • Using toxic speech detection

  • Trust and safety

INCORRECT: Turn on toxicity detection in each Transcribe job, and remove each segment with a high threat or insult score from the text before the model step.
Removing the flagged segments is a way to clean the input when the model may still answer the rest of a message. Toxicity detection scores each segment, so a function can drop the worst parts and keep the others. Here the rules say that each abusive message goes to a supervisor and that the model reads no part of it. This design still sends the rest of the message to the model, and no supervisor sees it.

INCORRECT: Send each transcript to Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection, and send each message with a high threat or insult score to a supervisor before the model step.
Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection scores text for categories such as insult and violence or threat. It fits text channels, such as chat messages, where the abuse is in the words. It reads only the text that the application sends. Here the words of many abusive messages looked polite, and the threat was in how the caller spoke. A text check cannot hear tone or pitch, so it misses these messages.

INCORRECT: Check each segment of the transcript with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail through the ApplyGuardrail API, and remove each segment that its violence or insults filter blocks before the model step.
The ApplyGuardrail API checks text against an Amazon Bedrock guardrail without a model call, so an application can check each part of a text and drop each part that a content filter blocks. Content filters for violence and insults are a good check for written prompts and answers. But the guardrail reads only the transcript text. The threats in these messages were in the caller's voice, not in the words, so the filter finds nothing to remove. This design also sends the rest of each message to the model, and no supervisor sees it.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs live online training sessions, each with several hundred participants. During a session, the trainer types a question, and a model in Amazon Bedrock answers it. Every participant's browser must show the answer word by word while the model writes it. The team does not want to keep a list of browser connections or write code that sends each piece of the answer to each browser.
How should the team deliver each answer to the participants?
questions.promptText:
A company runs live online training sessions, each with several hundred participants. During a session, the trainer types a question, and a model in Amazon Bedrock answers it. Every participant's browser must show the answer word by word while the model writes it. The team does not want to keep a list of browser connections or write code that sends each piece of the answer to each browser.
How should the team deliver each answer to the participants?

options.text: A Lambda function calls ConverseStream once and publishes each chunk of the answer to the session's channel in an AWS AppSync Events API, which every browser subscribes to.
A Lambda function calls ConverseStream once and posts each chunk of the answer to every browser's connection on an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API, using IDs stored in DynamoDB.
A Lambda function calls Converse once and publishes the complete answer to the session's channel in an AWS AppSync Events API, which every browser subscribes to.
A Lambda function calls Converse once and posts the complete answer to every browser's connection on an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API, using IDs stored in DynamoDB.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A Lambda function calls ConverseStream once and publishes each chunk of the answer to the session's channel in an AWS AppSync Events API, which every browser subscribes to.
AWS AppSync Events gives the team a serverless WebSocket API that broadcasts events to every subscriber of a channel, and AppSync manages the connections. Each browser subscribes to the session's channel over WebSocket. The Lambda function calls ConverseStream once, so the model writes one answer. As each chunk arrives, the function publishes it to the channel with an HTTP request, and AppSync sends it to every subscribed browser. All participants see the same words while the model writes them, and the team keeps no list of connections.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.2: "Develop real-time AI interaction systems to provide immediate feedback from FM"
Example: "WebSockets or server-sent events to generate text in real time"

Sources:

  • What is AWS AppSync Events?

  • Publish events via HTTP

  • AWS AppSync Events and API Gateway

INCORRECT: A Lambda function calls ConverseStream once and posts each chunk of the answer to every browser's connection on an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API, using IDs stored in DynamoDB.
An Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API also keeps an open connection to each browser, and a backend sends data to one connection at a time by its connection ID. This fits a chat where each user gets an answer of their own. To reach several hundred participants, the application must store every connection ID, for example in DynamoDB, and post each chunk to each connection. The team does not want to keep a list of connections or write that sending code.

INCORRECT: A Lambda function calls Converse once and publishes the complete answer to the session's channel in an AWS AppSync Events API, which every browser subscribes to.
Publishing to an AppSync Events channel reaches every participant with no list of connections, and one Converse call gives one answer. This design fits a short answer that can appear all at once. But Converse returns the answer only when the model has finished it. The participants see nothing while the model writes, and then the whole text appears at once. The session needs the answer word by word.

INCORRECT: A Lambda function calls Converse once and posts the complete answer to every browser's connection on an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API, using IDs stored in DynamoDB.
An Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API keeps an open connection to each browser, and a backend sends data to one connection at a time by its connection ID. Sending one finished answer to every connection fits a short notice that all users must get at the same moment. But Converse returns the answer only when the model has finished it, so the participants see nothing while the model writes. The design also makes the team store every connection ID and send the answer to each connection, which the team does not want.

questions.promptHtml:
A telecom company's billing system sends an event each time an account changes, such as a new plan, a payment or a support call. A Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock to update a short summary of each account, which support agents read. The events of one account must change its summary in the order they happened. The fraud team's application must also read every event, at its own pace. Recently, a prompt error made the function write poor summaries for two days, with no failed calls. After a fix, the team wants to process those events again without asking the billing system to send them again.
Which design should the team build?
questions.promptText:
A telecom company's billing system sends an event each time an account changes, such as a new plan, a payment or a support call. A Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock to update a short summary of each account, which support agents read. The events of one account must change its summary in the order they happened. The fraud team's application must also read every event, at its own pace. Recently, a prompt error made the function write poor summaries for two days, with no failed calls. After a fix, the team wants to process those events again without asking the billing system to send them again.
Which design should the team build?

options.text: Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream with the account ID as partition key and extended retention, and after a fix, replace the event source mapping with one starting at a past timestamp.
Use an Amazon SNS FIFO topic with the account ID as the message group ID and two subscribed SQS FIFO queues, and after a fix, redrive the messages from their dead-letter queues.
Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID and a dead-letter queue, and after a fix, redrive the messages from the dead-letter queue.
Use a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge with an archive of all events, and after a fix, replay the archived events of the affected days to the bus.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream with the account ID as partition key and extended retention, and after a fix, replace the event source mapping with one starting at a past timestamp.
A partition key groups the records of a Kinesis data stream by shard, and Lambda processes the records of each partition key in order. With the account ID as the partition key, the events of one account update its summary in the order they happened.

Many applications can read one stream on their own and at the same time, so the fraud team's application reads the same events at its own pace. The stream keeps each record for its retention period, and extended retention keeps it longer than the default period, so the events of the past days are still there.

After a fix, the team replaces the function's event source mapping with a new one that uses the AT_TIMESTAMP starting position, and Lambda reads the events of the affected days again. The billing system sends nothing twice.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"
Example: "event-driven architectures to implement loose coupling"

Sources:

  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Terminology and concepts

  • CreateEventSourceMapping

  • Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, or Amazon EventBridge?

INCORRECT: Use an Amazon SNS FIFO topic with the account ID as the message group ID and two subscribed SQS FIFO queues, and after a fix, redrive the messages from their dead-letter queues.
An SNS FIFO topic delivers each message to every subscribed SQS FIFO queue, and the account ID as the message group ID keeps the events of one account in order. One queue feeds the function, and the other lets the fraud team's application read every event at its own pace. Each queue has a dead-letter queue that holds the messages that a consumer did not process successfully, and a redrive moves them back for another try. This design fits ordered fan-out where the main risk is a failed call. Here the function made no failed calls, so no message went to a dead-letter queue. SQS deleted each message after the function processed it, so nothing is left to process again.

INCORRECT: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID and a dead-letter queue, and after a fix, redrive the messages from the dead-letter queue.
An SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID processes the messages of each account one at a time, in order. A dead-letter queue holds messages that the function did not process successfully, and a redrive moves them back for another try. This design fits ordered work where the main risk is a failed call. Here the function made no failed calls, so no message went to the dead-letter queue. SQS deletes each message after the function processes it, so nothing is left to process again, and the fraud team's application cannot read the events later at its own pace.

INCORRECT: Use a rule on the default event bus in Amazon EventBridge with an archive of all events, and after a fix, replay the archived events of the affected days to the bus.
An EventBridge rule on the default event bus can send each event to the function, a second rule can send it to the fraud team's application, and an archive can resend past events after a fix. This fits events that do not depend on each other. But EventBridge delivers events to targets in no fixed order, and a replay also does not keep the order in which the events arrived. The summary of one account could take in a payment before the plan change that came first.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's contact center agents use an assistant on Amazon Bedrock that suggests answers while a caller waits on the line. The same model also writes report summaries for managers during the day, and those reports have no deadline. Both workloads call Converse on demand. At peak hours, the assistant's answers arrive too slowly for the agents, but no request fails. The model that the team uses offers the Priority service tier. The assistant is idle at night and on weekends, so the company will not pay a fixed hourly or monthly charge for capacity.
Which change keeps the assistant fast at peak hours?
questions.promptText:
A company's contact center agents use an assistant on Amazon Bedrock that suggests answers while a caller waits on the line. The same model also writes report summaries for managers during the day, and those reports have no deadline. Both workloads call Converse on demand. At peak hours, the assistant's answers arrive too slowly for the agents, but no request fails. The model that the team uses offers the Priority service tier. The assistant is idle at night and on weekends, so the company will not pay a fixed hourly or monthly charge for capacity.
Which change keeps the assistant fast at peak hours?

options.text: Set the service tier of the assistant's requests to priority, and keep sending the report requests with no service tier, as today.
Reserve tokens-per-minute capacity for the model with the Reserved service tier, and send the assistant's requests to that reserved capacity during peak hours.
Create Provisioned Throughput for the model, send the assistant's requests to that capacity, and keep the report requests on demand, as today.
Request a higher tokens-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, so that more of the assistant's requests can run at the same time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the service tier of the assistant's requests to priority, and keep sending the report requests with no service tier, as today.
Amazon Bedrock service tiers let each request choose how it is served, with one optional setting on the request. The Priority tier gives the fastest response times, and Priority requests are served before Standard and Flex requests. It costs more than the Standard tier, but it needs no reservation, so the company still pays only for the requests that it sends. The assistant's answers get faster at peak hours. A request that names no tier goes to the Standard tier, so the report requests, which have no deadline, keep their normal price.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.1: "Create responsive AI systems to address latency-cost tradeoffs and improve the user experience with FMs"

Sources:

  • Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost

  • Amazon Bedrock introduces Priority and Flex inference service tiers

  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Reserve tokens-per-minute capacity for the model with the Reserved service tier, and send the assistant's requests to that reserved capacity during peak hours.
The Reserved tier sets aside tokens-per-minute capacity with priority for a workload. It fits a mission-critical workload that runs all day, every day, and needs capacity that is always ready. The company reserves the capacity for a fixed term and pays a fixed price each month, whether it sends requests or not. Here the assistant is idle at night and on weekends, and the company will not pay a fixed monthly charge.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the model, send the assistant's requests to that capacity, and keep the report requests on demand, as today.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model a fixed level of throughput, measured in model units. It fits a steady, high-volume workload that keeps that capacity busy. AWS bills it by the hour until the team deletes it, even with no commitment term. The assistant is idle at night and on weekends, so the company would pay for hours with no use, which it will not do. Also, Amazon Bedrock offers Provisioned Throughput for base models only for some older models.

INCORRECT: Request a higher tokens-per-minute quota for the model through Service Quotas, so that more of the assistant's requests can run at the same time.
A quota sets how many tokens or requests an account can use in a minute. When calls pass it, Amazon Bedrock rejects them with a ThrottlingException, and a higher quota fixes that. Here no request fails. The answers arrive, but slowly, so the calls are not passing the quota. A higher quota does not make each answer arrive sooner.
