questions.promptHtml:
A bank has eight product teams that build generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock. The bank's architecture team wrote its own rules for these workloads: which foundation models are approved, which data classes may appear in prompts, and how a team tests its prompts before a release. These rules are the bank's own and appear in no AWS guidance. The architecture team wants each product team to review its own workload against the rules in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and to see each missing practice as a risk with a plan to fix it.
What should the architecture team do?
questions.promptText:
A bank has eight product teams that build generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock. The bank's architecture team wrote its own rules for these workloads: which foundation models are approved, which data classes may appear in prompts, and how a team tests its prompts before a release. These rules are the bank's own and appear in no AWS guidance. The architecture team wants each product team to review its own workload against the rules in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, and to see each missing practice as a risk with a plan to fix it.
What should the architecture team do?

options.text: Create a custom lens with the bank's questions, best practices and risk rules, share it with the product teams' accounts, and have each team apply it to its workload.
Apply the Generative AI Lens from the lens catalog to each workload, and have each product team answer its questions and fix the high and medium risks it shows.
Create a review template with the architecture team's answers to the Well-Architected Framework questions, share it with the teams' accounts, and have each team define its workload from it.
Write IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks for the approved models, run them in each team's AWS CodeBuild project, and have each build fail when a policy breaks a rule.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a custom lens with the bank's questions, best practices and risk rules, share it with the product teams' accounts, and have each team apply it to its workload.
A custom lens lets a company write its own pillars, questions and best practices in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, with an improvement plan for each best practice. Its risk rules decide which answers count as high risk, medium risk or no risk. The architecture team writes the bank's rules on approved models, data classes in prompts and prompt tests as questions and best practices, and shares the lens with the product teams' accounts. Each team applies the lens to its workload the same way it applies an AWS lens and answers the questions for its own design. Each missing practice then shows as a risk with a plan to fix it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.3: "Create standardized technical components to ensure consistent implementation across multiple deployment scenarios"

Sources:

  • Custom lenses for workloads in AWS WA Tool
  • Lens format specification in AWS WA Tool
  • Sharing a custom lens in AWS WA Tool

INCORRECT: Apply the Generative AI Lens from the lens catalog to each workload, and have each product team answer its questions and fix the high and medium risks it shows.
The Generative AI Lens is an official lens in the lens catalog, and AWS creates and maintains it. It holds best practices for generative AI workloads, and a review with it shows high and medium risks. It fits a company that wants AWS guidance that AWS keeps current. Here the rules are the bank's own, such as its list of approved models and its data classes. An AWS lens cannot ask about rules that only the bank wrote.

INCORRECT: Create a review template with the architecture team's answers to the Well-Architected Framework questions, share it with the teams' accounts, and have each team define its workload from it.
A review template holds answers that one team fills in once, so new workloads start their review with those answers in place. It fits questions that have the same answer for every workload, for example the design of a shared platform. Here the Well-Architected Framework questions do not cover the bank's own rules, and the architecture team wants each product team to review its own workload. Answers that the architecture team writes do not show what each product team built.

INCORRECT: Write IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks for the approved models, run them in each team's AWS CodeBuild project, and have each build fail when a policy breaks a rule.
IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks test an IAM policy against a rule, for example that the policy does not grant access to a model that is not on the approved list. In a build, they stop a policy that breaks the rule before it is deployed. This fits a rule that a policy can show. Most of the bank's rules, such as the data classes in prompts and the prompt tests before a release, are not in any IAM policy. The checks also give no review in the AWS Well-Architected Tool and no list of risks with a plan to fix them.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs twelve AWS Lambda functions. Each function sends its own prompt text to the same model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. The model ID is written in each function's code, and the team moves to a newer model a few times each year.
Each move must be one change in one place, with no code change and no new deployment of any function. Calls that still use the old model for a few minutes after a move are acceptable.
Where should the functions get the model ID?
questions.promptText:
A company runs twelve AWS Lambda functions. Each function sends its own prompt text to the same model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. The model ID is written in each function's code, and the team moves to a newer model a few times each year.
Each move must be one change in one place, with no code change and no new deployment of any function. Calls that still use the old model for a few minutes after a move are acceptable.
Where should the functions get the model ID?

options.text: Store the model ID in one AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter, and have each function get it through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension on each request.
Set an environment variable with the model ID on each of the twelve functions, and have each function read the variable from its environment on each request.
Set an environment variable on each of the twelve functions from one Parameter Store parameter with a CloudFormation dynamic reference, and have each function read the variable on each request.
Create one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management that names the model, and have each function call Converse with the ARN of that prompt's version.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Store the model ID in one AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter, and have each function get it through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension on each request.
Parameter Store keeps the model ID as one value that all twelve functions read. The AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension is added to each function as a Lambda layer. The function asks the extension for the parameter on a local port, and the extension keeps the value in a cache, so the functions do not call Parameter Store on every request. After a one-time code change to read the parameter, each move to a newer model is one change to that parameter. No function code changes, and no function is deployed again. The cache does not see the change at once: a function keeps the old value until its cached copy expires, after a time that the team can set. The question accepts a few minutes on the old model, so this short delay is fine.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.2: "Create flexible architecture patterns to enable dynamic model selection and provider switching without requiring code modifications"

Sources:

  • Using Parameter Store parameters in AWS Lambda functions

  • Get a plaintext value from Systems Manager Parameter Store

  • Converse

INCORRECT: Set an environment variable with the model ID on each of the twelve functions, and have each function read the variable from its environment on each request.
An environment variable gives one function a setting without a code change. It works well when only one or two functions use the value. Here twelve functions hold the model ID, so each move means twelve configuration updates, one on each function. The question asks for one change in one place.

INCORRECT: Set an environment variable on each of the twelve functions from one Parameter Store parameter with a CloudFormation dynamic reference, and have each function read the variable on each request.
A CloudFormation dynamic reference copies a Parameter Store value into a template property, such as an environment variable, when CloudFormation runs a stack operation. This keeps one source for a value that changes rarely. CloudFormation does not watch the parameter for changes. A new model ID reaches the functions only after a stack update, and that update deploys the functions again, which the question does not allow.

INCORRECT: Create one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management that names the model, and have each function call Converse with the ARN of that prompt's version.
Prompt Management stores a prompt together with its model and inference settings, so it suits many functions that share one prompt. These functions each send their own prompt text. When Converse uses a managed prompt, the request names the ARN of a prompt version, and it cannot add its own system prompt or inference settings. A model move then needs a new prompt version, and every function must change to the new version ARN.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
Each morning, a model in Amazon Bedrock creates the delivery schedules for a logistics company's drivers. A developer wrote the prompt, which lists 15 business rules, such as "Driver A must not work after 5 PM" and "Zone B is closed on Tuesdays." Each order in the prompt shows its delivery date and its day of the week. At the end, the prompt asks: "Given these rules and this list of orders, create a schedule for Driver A."

The schedules have the right format, but many of them break one or two rules, for example a delivery to Zone B on a Tuesday.

Which prompt engineering technique should the developer use to help the model follow every rule?
questions.promptText:
Each morning, a model in Amazon Bedrock creates the delivery schedules for a logistics company's drivers. A developer wrote the prompt, which lists 15 business rules, such as "Driver A must not work after 5 PM" and "Zone B is closed on Tuesdays." Each order in the prompt shows its delivery date and its day of the week. At the end, the prompt asks: "Given these rules and this list of orders, create a schedule for Driver A."
The schedules have the right format, but many of them break one or two rules, for example a delivery to Zone B on a Tuesday.
Which prompt engineering technique should the developer use to help the model follow every rule?

options.text: Use a chain-of-thought (CoT) instruction: tell the model to list the rules that apply, check each order against them, build the schedule, and check the schedule again.
Use a ReAct (reasoning and acting) pattern: give the model a tool that calls a calendar API for the current date before the model builds the schedule.
Use few-shot prompting: add 3 to 5 examples to the prompt, each with a list of orders and a correct schedule that follows all 15 rules.
Use structured output: ask the model to return the schedule as JSON, with one entry for each order and fields for the time, the zone, and the driver.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a chain-of-thought (CoT) instruction: tell the model to list the rules that apply, check each order against them, build the schedule, and check the schedule again.
A chain-of-thought instruction asks the model to solve a task in steps before it gives the final answer. The technique breaks a complex question into smaller, logical parts, and it can improve results on tasks that need reasoning. Here the prompt already contains all 15 rules and the date and day of every order, but the model skips one or two rules. When the instruction tells the model to list the rules that apply, check each order, build the schedule, and check the schedule again, each rule has its own step. A missed rule becomes less likely.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.5: "Enhance FM performance to refine prompts iteratively and improve response quality beyond basic prompting techniques"
Example: "chain-of-thought instruction patterns"

Sources:

  • Optimizing generative AI prompts

  • Design a prompt

  • AGENTPERF02-BP01 Design efficient reasoning pipelines

INCORRECT: Use a ReAct (reasoning and acting) pattern: give the model a tool that calls a calendar API for the current date before the model builds the schedule.
In a ReAct loop, the model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result, and then decides its next step. This fits open-ended tasks where the next step depends on what a tool returns. The model does not lack information. Each order in the prompt already shows its delivery date and its day of the week, and the 15 rules are in the prompt too. A calendar tool adds a call but no new fact, and it does not make the model check the Zone B rule against each order.

INCORRECT: Use few-shot prompting: add 3 to 5 examples to the prompt, each with a list of orders and a correct schedule that follows all 15 rules.
Few-shot prompting puts example inputs and their correct outputs into the prompt. It is a strong way to show the model a format, a tone, or the shape of a task. Each example here shows only a finished schedule, not the rule checks that led to it. The model learns what a good schedule looks like, but not how to test each order against each rule. So the examples help less with rules that are easy to miss on new orders.

INCORRECT: Use structured output: ask the model to return the schedule as JSON, with one entry for each order and fields for the time, the zone, and the driver.
Asking for JSON with named fields controls the shape of the answer, which helps when code must read the schedule. Here the schedules already have the right format. The problem is that some entries break a rule. A field layout does not check what an entry says, so the model can still write a Tuesday delivery to Zone B into a well-formed entry.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's agents reach 30 tools through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Most tools are AWS Lambda function targets, and five are OpenAPI targets that call partners' REST APIs. The team has set up AgentCore observability for the gateway.
Over the past month, agent answers became slower, and the team cannot tell which tool causes it. The team wants a graph of each tool's response time over the past weeks, and an alarm when any single tool becomes slow.
What should the team graph and alarm on?
questions.promptText:
A company's agents reach 30 tools through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Most tools are AWS Lambda function targets, and five are OpenAPI targets that call partners' REST APIs. The team has set up AgentCore observability for the gateway.
Over the past month, agent answers became slower, and the team cannot tell which tool causes it. The team wants a graph of each tool's response time over the past weeks, and an alarm when any single tool becomes slow.
What should the team graph and alarm on?

options.text: Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Name dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Method dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Resource dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
Graph the Duration and Errors metrics of each Lambda function behind the tools in CloudWatch, and create an alarm on the Duration line of each function.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Name dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
The gateway publishes its own metrics to CloudWatch, and its Name dimension holds the name of the tool. Latency is the time until the gateway starts to send its response. TargetExecutionTime is the time that the target, such as a Lambda function or a partner's REST API behind an OpenAPI target, takes to run. When the team splits these metrics by Name, each of the 30 tools gets its own line, whatever kind of target runs it. The team sees which tool slowed down over the weeks, and an alarm on each line warns when one tool becomes slow.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.4: "Create tool performance frameworks to ensure optimal tool operation and utilization for FMs"
Example: "performance metric collection"

Sources:

  • AgentCore generated gateway observability data
  • Core concepts for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
  • Types of metrics for Lambda functions

INCORRECT: Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Method dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
The Method dimension holds the MCP operation, such as tools/list or tools/call. It helps when the team must know whether listing the tools or calling them is slow. Every call to any of the 30 tools is the same tools/call operation, so all tools share one line, and the team still cannot see which tool causes the delay.

INCORRECT: Graph the gateway's Latency and TargetExecutionTime metrics in CloudWatch split by the Resource dimension, and create an alarm on each line of the graph.
The Resource dimension holds the gateway's ARN. A company with several gateways uses it to compare them. This company has one gateway, so the split gives one line for all the tools, and no alarm can point to a single tool.

INCORRECT: Graph the Duration and Errors metrics of each Lambda function behind the tools in CloudWatch, and create an alarm on the Duration line of each function.
Lambda publishes Duration and Errors for each function, and Duration shows well how long a Lambda tool runs. Five tools, however, are OpenAPI targets that call partners' REST APIs, and no Lambda function runs behind them. A slow partner API never shows up in these graphs, so the team can miss the tool that causes the delay.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a chat service and a nightly batch job on the same Amazon EKS nodes. The chat service calls a model in Amazon Bedrock, and the batch job must have no way to gain Amazon Bedrock permissions. Today pods can reach the instance metadata service (IMDS) on the nodes, so every pod can use the node IAM role, which allows bedrock:InvokeModel.

Both workloads run in three clusters and must keep sharing the same nodes. The security team wants one IAM role for the chat service in all three clusters, and does not want to create an identity provider for each cluster.

How should the security team give only the chat service access to the model?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a chat service and a nightly batch job on the same Amazon EKS nodes. The chat service calls a model in Amazon Bedrock, and the batch job must have no way to gain Amazon Bedrock permissions. Today pods can reach the instance metadata service (IMDS) on the nodes, so every pod can use the node IAM role, which allows bedrock:InvokeModel.
Both workloads run in three clusters and must keep sharing the same nodes. The security team wants one IAM role for the chat service in all three clusters, and does not want to create an identity provider for each cluster.
How should the security team give only the chat service access to the model?

options.text: Associate a role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with the service account of the chat service through EKS Pod Identity, install the EKS Pod Identity Agent add-on, remove that permission from the node role, and block pod access to IMDS.

Associate a role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with the service account of the chat service through IAM roles for service accounts, annotate the service account with the role ARN, remove that permission from the node role, and block pod access to IMDS.
Run the chat service and the batch job in two separate managed node groups with their own node roles, and allow bedrock:InvokeModel only on the node role of the group that runs the chat service.

Replace the Amazon Bedrock permission of the node role with sts:AssumeRole on a second role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel, and have the chat service assume the second role before each call to the model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Associate a role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with the service account of the chat service through EKS Pod Identity, install the EKS Pod Identity Agent add-on, remove that permission from the node role, and block pod access to IMDS.
An EKS Pod Identity association maps an IAM role to one service account in one namespace of a cluster. The role trusts the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service principal, not an identity provider of one cluster, so the team creates the same association in each of the three clusters and needs no OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider. EKS Pod Identity needs the EKS Pod Identity Agent, which runs on each node and gives pods the credentials of their associations, so each cluster needs the agent add-on. Removing bedrock:InvokeModel from the node role removes the access that every pod has today. With IMDS blocked, a pod receives only the credentials of the role that is linked to its own service account, and the batch job has no such role.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "IAM policies to enforce secure data access patterns"

Sources:

  • Learn how EKS Pod Identity grants pods access to AWS services

  • IAM roles for service accounts

  • create-nodegroup

INCORRECT: Associate a role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with the service account of the chat service through IAM roles for service accounts, annotate the service account with the role ARN, remove that permission from the node role, and block pod access to IMDS.
IAM roles for service accounts also give one service account its own role, and many existing clusters use this method. The annotation on the service account names the role, and blocking pod access to IMDS is a good step with this method too. But this method needs an IAM OIDC identity provider for each cluster, and the trust policy of the role names that provider. The security team does not want to create an identity provider for each cluster, so this method breaks that requirement.

INCORRECT: Run the chat service and the batch job in two separate managed node groups with their own node roles, and allow bedrock:InvokeModel only on the node role of the group that runs the chat service.
Each managed node group has its own node IAM role, so separate node groups keep workloads apart at the node level. This is a good design when the workloads may run on different nodes. Here both workloads must keep sharing the same nodes.

INCORRECT: Replace the Amazon Bedrock permission of the node role with sts:AssumeRole on a second role that allows bedrock:InvokeModel, and have the chat service assume the second role before each call to the model.
One role that assumes another is a common pattern, for example to reach a role in another account. The problem is the node role. Pods can reach IMDS today, so every pod on the nodes can use the node role. The batch job could also call sts:AssumeRole, receive the second role, and call the model. The batch job must have no way to gain Amazon Bedrock permissions.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A safety team stores recordings from factory cameras in Amazon S3. The cameras have no microphones, and most recordings run close to an hour. Staff will type searches such as "a forklift backs into a loading bay" and open each result at the right moment in the recording.
Queries and recordings must share one vector space from one model in Amazon Bedrock. The team will not host or scale any model endpoint.
How should the team build the search index?
questions.promptText:
A safety team stores recordings from factory cameras in Amazon S3. The cameras have no microphones, and most recordings run close to an hour. Staff will type searches such as "a forklift backs into a loading bay" and open each result at the right moment in the recording.
Queries and recordings must share one vector space from one model in Amazon Bedrock. The team will not host or scale any model endpoint.
How should the team build the search index?

options.text: On each upload, call StartAsyncInvoke for Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings with an S3 output location, check the job with GetAsyncInvoke, and index each segment vector with its start time.
On each upload, call StartTranscriptionJob in Amazon Transcribe, split the transcript into timed sections, and index an Amazon Bedrock text embedding of each section with its start time.
On each upload, call StartLabelDetection in Amazon Rekognition Video for the S3 object, and index each detected label with its timestamp in an OpenSearch Service index for keyword search.
On each upload, have a Lambda function call InvokeEndpointAsync on a SageMaker AI asynchronous endpoint that hosts an open-weight video embedding model, and index each vector from S3.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: On each upload, call StartAsyncInvoke for Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings with an S3 output location, check the job with GetAsyncInvoke, and index each segment vector with its start time.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings is one model that turns text, images, video and audio into vectors in one shared space, so a typed search and a camera recording can be compared directly. For long video, the model works through StartAsyncInvoke. The call returns at once with an invocation ARN, and the model splits the video into short segments. It writes one embedding for each segment, with the segment's start and end seconds, to the S3 location in the request. GetAsyncInvoke shows when the job is complete. The team indexes each segment vector with its start time, so a match opens the recording at that moment. Amazon Bedrock runs the model, so the team hosts no endpoint.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.1: "Create flexible model interaction systems"

Sources:

  • Using Nova Embeddings
  • Complete embeddings request and response schema
  • GetAsyncInvoke

INCORRECT: On each upload, call StartTranscriptionJob in Amazon Transcribe, split the transcript into timed sections, and index an Amazon Bedrock text embedding of each section with its start time.
Amazon Transcribe turns the speech in a media file into text, and timed transcript sections are a good way to search what people say in a video. These cameras have no microphones, so the recordings hold no speech. The transcripts would be empty, and nothing would describe what the cameras show.

INCORRECT: On each upload, call StartLabelDetection in Amazon Rekognition Video for the S3 object, and index each detected label with its timestamp in an OpenSearch Service index for keyword search.
Rekognition Video label detection finds objects and concepts in a stored video, with the time of each one. Labels with times work well for keyword search on known objects. The team wants queries and recordings in one vector space from one model in Amazon Bedrock. A keyword index of labels holds no vectors, and Rekognition is not a model in Amazon Bedrock.

INCORRECT: On each upload, have a Lambda function call InvokeEndpointAsync on a SageMaker AI asynchronous endpoint that hosts an open-weight video embedding model, and index each vector from S3.
A SageMaker AI asynchronous endpoint queues requests with large inputs or long processing times and writes each result to S3. It suits a team that wants to run its own open-weight model. This team will not host or scale any model endpoint, and an asynchronous endpoint is an endpoint that the team hosts and scales. The model also runs outside Amazon Bedrock.

questions.promptHtml:
A company offers a public chat API from two stacks, one in an EU Region and one in a US Region. Each stack calls Amazon Bedrock only in its own Region. The API's domain name is in a public hosted zone in Amazon Route 53.
Rules say that requests from users anywhere in Europe, including countries outside the European Union, must reach only the EU stack. Users in every other place must reach the US stack, and so must users whose location cannot be found from their IP address.
Which records should the team create in the hosted zone?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company offers a public chat API from two stacks, one in an EU Region and one in a US Region. Each stack calls Amazon Bedrock only in its own Region. The API's domain name is in a public hosted zone in Amazon Route 53.
Rules say that requests from users anywhere in Europe, including countries outside the European Union, must reach only the EU stack. Users in every other place must reach the US stack, and so must users whose location cannot be found from their IP address.
Which records should the team create in the hosted zone?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create a geolocation record with the location set to the continent Europe, and point it to the endpoint of the EU stack.
Create a geolocation record with the location set to Default, and point it to the endpoint of the US stack.
Create a geolocation record for each continent other than Europe, and point each one to the endpoint of the US stack.
Create a geolocation record for each European Union member country, and point each one to the endpoint of the EU stack.
Create a latency record for the AWS Region of each stack, and point each one to the endpoint of the stack in that Region.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a geolocation record with the location set to the continent Europe, and point it to the endpoint of the EU stack.
Geolocation routing answers each DNS query by the place the query comes from, which Route 53 finds by mapping IP addresses to locations. One common use is to limit content to the places where a company may serve it. A record for the continent Europe matches users in European countries, whether or not the country is in the European Union, so all of those users reach the EU stack.

CORRECT: Create a geolocation record with the location set to Default, and point it to the endpoint of the US stack.
The Default record answers two kinds of queries: queries from places that have no geolocation record of their own, and queries from IP addresses that Route 53 cannot map to any place. With the Europe record in place, every other user, and every user with an unknown location, reaches the US stack. No user is left without an answer.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.4: "Develop cross-environment AI solutions to ensure data compliance across jurisdictions while enabling FM access"

Sources:

  • Geolocation routing

  • Latency-based routing

INCORRECT: Create a geolocation record for each continent other than Europe, and point each one to the endpoint of the US stack.
A record for each continent is a correct way to send each part of the world to its own stack. It does not cover IP addresses that Route 53 cannot map to a place. With no Default record, Route 53 returns "no answer" for those queries, so those users never reach the US stack.

INCORRECT: Create a geolocation record for each European Union member country, and point each one to the endpoint of the EU stack.
Country records fit a rule that covers only European Union members. These rules cover all of Europe, including countries outside the European Union. Users in those countries match none of these records, so the Default record or another record sends them to the US stack, which breaks the rule.

INCORRECT: Create a latency record for the AWS Region of each stack, and point each one to the endpoint of the stack in that Region.
Latency routing sends each user to the Region with the lowest latency, which improves speed for a service in several Regions. It follows network latency, not the user's location, and latency changes over time, so a user's requests can move from one Region to another. A user in Africa or Asia could also reach the EU stack. The rules are about where users are, so latency routing cannot keep them.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's agent reaches hundreds of tools from many teams through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. When each session starts, the agent gets the full tool list from the gateway and sends every tool definition to the model. The model often picks the wrong tool, and each request uses many input tokens.
The platform team is about to create a new gateway for the agent. The team will keep one agent, and it will not keep a second copy of the tool definitions.
Which design fixes both problems?
questions.promptText:
A company's agent reaches hundreds of tools from many teams through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. When each session starts, the agent gets the full tool list from the gateway and sends every tool definition to the model. The model often picks the wrong tool, and each request uses many input tokens.
The platform team is about to create a new gateway for the agent. The team will keep one agent, and it will not keep a second copy of the tool definitions.
Which design fixes both problems?

options.text: Store a description of every gateway tool in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, retrieve the closest tools for each request, and send the model only those tools.
Keep sending every tool definition to the model, and add a cache checkpoint after the tool definitions in each model request, so repeated tool lists come from the cache.
Create the new gateway with semantic search turned on, and have the agent call its search tool for each request and send the model only the tools it returns.
Split the tools among several specialist agents that each have a small tool set, and add an orchestrator agent that passes each request to one specialist.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create the new gateway with semantic search turned on, and have the agent call its search tool for each request and send the model only the tools it returns.
Semantic search is a gateway setting that adds a built-in search tool to the gateway. The agent sends the request in plain words to this tool, and the gateway returns the tools that are relevant to it. The model then sees a short list of tools that fit the request instead of the whole catalog, so it chooses among far fewer tools and reads far fewer tool definitions on each call. A team can turn on semantic search only when it creates a gateway, and this team is about to create one. The tools stay in the gateway, so there is no second copy to keep current, and the company keeps its one agent.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.7: "Develop model extension frameworks to enhance FM capabilities"

Sources:

  • Search for tools in your AgentCore gateway with a natural language query

  • Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway

  • AGENTPERF06-BP01 Design optimized tool integration strategies

INCORRECT: Store a description of every gateway tool in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, retrieve the closest tools for each request, and send the model only those tools.
A knowledge base of tool descriptions is one way to build a pre-filter: each request retrieves the closest tools, and only those reach the model. It fits a team that has no built-in tool search and accepts the work of keeping that index current. Here the team will not keep a second copy of the tool definitions, and the knowledge base would be exactly that copy. It would need a change every time a team adds or edits a tool.

INCORRECT: Keep sending every tool definition to the model, and add a cache checkpoint after the tool definitions in each model request, so repeated tool lists come from the cache.
A cache checkpoint after the tool definitions lets Amazon Bedrock read that part of the prompt from the cache on later requests. This lowers the cost and the response time of input that repeats, so it fits an agent that sends the same fixed tool list on every call. Here the model still receives every tool definition on each call. It still chooses among hundreds of tools, so it still picks the wrong tool.

INCORRECT: Split the tools among several specialist agents that each have a small tool set, and add an orchestrator agent that passes each request to one specialist.
Specialist agents with small tool sets, called by an orchestrator agent, are a common multi-agent pattern. Each specialist sees only its own tools, so it chooses among a few. This fits a team that is ready to build and run several agents. This team will keep one agent, and the design adds one new agent for each specialist and one more for the orchestrator.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company will launch a feature that sorts support tickets by topic. The feature uses the company's own fine-tuned small text classification model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and it has no users yet.
Before launch, finance must approve one instance type and a fixed number of instances. The team must show that this setup keeps 95 percent of predictions under 100 milliseconds at the expected peak. The test must use real ticket text and the expected traffic shape: users arrive in steps each morning until the peak. The team wants the cheapest setup that passes.
Which approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A company will launch a feature that sorts support tickets by topic. The feature uses the company's own fine-tuned small text classification model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and it has no users yet.
Before launch, finance must approve one instance type and a fixed number of instances. The team must show that this setup keeps 95 percent of predictions under 100 milliseconds at the expected peak. The test must use real ticket text and the expected traffic shape: users arrive in steps each morning until the peak. The team wants the cheapest setup that passes.
Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Deploy each candidate instance type as a shadow variant beside the production variant, and compare the latency and cost of each variant during the morning peak.
Run a SageMaker Inference Recommender default job on the registered model package, and pick the candidate instance type that it lists with the lowest cost per inference.
Deploy the model on the cheapest candidate instance type, and add a target tracking policy on invocations per instance so the endpoint adds instances as traffic grows.
Run a SageMaker Inference Recommender advanced job on the candidate instance types, with sample payloads, a stairs traffic pattern to the peak, and a P95 latency limit.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run a SageMaker Inference Recommender advanced job on the candidate instance types, with sample payloads, a stairs traffic pattern to the peak, and a P95 latency limit.
An Inference Recommender advanced job is a custom load test. The team selects the instance types to test, gives sample payloads, sets a traffic pattern, and sets its latency requirement. A stairs traffic pattern adds users in steps over the test, which matches the morning traffic, and the P95 latency threshold sets the 100 millisecond goal as a stopping condition. For each instance type, the results show the cost per inference, the cost per hour, the model latency and the instance count it recommends. So the team can pick the cheapest setup that meets the goal and give finance one type and one count before launch.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.3: "Develop high-performance FM systems to maximize resource utilization and throughput for GenAI workloads"
Example: "capacity planning"

Sources:

  • Run a custom load test
  • Recommendation jobs with Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender
  • Shadow tests

INCORRECT: Deploy each candidate instance type as a shadow variant beside the production variant, and compare the latency and cost of each variant during the morning peak.
A shadow test deploys a new variant beside the production variant and sends it a copy of the live inference requests. Teams use it to compare latency and errors before they move a model to a new instance type. It needs an endpoint that already serves real users. This feature has no users yet, so there is no production variant and no live traffic to copy.

INCORRECT: Run a SageMaker Inference Recommender default job on the registered model package, and pick the candidate instance type that it lists with the lowest cost per inference.
A default job runs a set of load tests on instance types that Inference Recommender recommends, and it needs only the model package. It is a fast way to see which instance types suit a model. It takes no custom traffic pattern and no latency requirement, so it cannot show that the setup meets the 100 millisecond goal when users arrive in steps up to the peak.

INCORRECT: Deploy the model on the cheapest candidate instance type, and add a target tracking policy on invocations per instance so the endpoint adds instances as traffic grows.
A target tracking policy on invocations per instance adds and removes instances as traffic changes, which fits an endpoint whose instance count may change after launch. Here finance must approve one instance type and a fixed number of instances before launch. The policy does not show that the cheapest type meets the latency goal, and it does not choose a fixed count. It only reacts to traffic after launch.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A financial services firm is building a document intelligence application on Amazon Bedrock. It must process complete regulatory filings that average 180 pages (about 120,000 tokens). The model must cross-reference clauses across the entire filing in a single pass. Processing runs overnight in batch, so latency is not a constraint, but accuracy is critical. The firm has no labeled examples of past filings.
Which two criteria should the developer use to choose the model?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A financial services firm is building a document intelligence application on Amazon Bedrock. It must process complete regulatory filings that average 180 pages (about 120,000 tokens). The model must cross-reference clauses across the entire filing in a single pass. Processing runs overnight in batch, so latency is not a constraint, but accuracy is critical. The firm has no labeled examples of past filings.
Which two criteria should the developer use to choose the model?
Select TWO.

options.text: Choose the model with the lowest price per input token, so that each overnight run over many long filings costs as little as possible.
Choose a model whose context window holds the longest filing with room for the answer, so each filing fits in one call with no chunking.
Choose a model that supports response streaming, so the application can store parts of each answer before the model has written all of it.
Choose a model that supports reasoning, so it can break each complex task into smaller steps and work through them before it writes each answer.
Choose a model that Amazon Bedrock can fine-tune, so the team can train it on labeled past filings to raise the accuracy of each answer.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Choose a model whose context window holds the longest filing with room for the answer, so each filing fits in one call with no chunking.
The context window limits how much text a model can work with in one call, and each model card lists it beside the maximum output size. The filings average about 120,000 tokens, so some filings are longer than that. The model must cross-reference clauses across the entire filing in a single pass, so the window must hold the longest filing and still leave room for the answer. A smaller window would force the team to split filings into parts, and the model could then miss links between clauses that sit in different parts.

CORRECT: Choose a model that supports reasoning, so it can break each complex task into smaller steps and work through them before it writes each answer.
A model that supports reasoning breaks a large task into smaller steps before it answers. This helps most with multi-step analysis, such as tracing how one clause changes another, and it often improves accuracy. The cost is more latency and more output tokens. Here accuracy is critical and the job runs overnight, so the extra time and tokens do not matter.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.1: "Assess and choose FMs to ensure optimal alignment with specific business use cases and technical requirements"
Example: "capability analysis"

Sources:

  • Amazon Nova Pro
  • Enhance model responses with model reasoning
  • Customize your model to improve its performance for your use case

INCORRECT: Choose the model with the lowest price per input token, so that each overnight run over many long filings costs as little as possible.
The lowest price per input token is a fair rule for simple bulk work, such as short summaries, where many models give good enough results. Here accuracy is critical, and each answer depends on links across a long filing. Price can help choose between models that meet both needs, but it should not be the main rule for this job.

INCORRECT: Choose a model that supports response streaming, so the application can store parts of each answer before the model has written all of it.
Response streaming sends the answer in parts while the model writes it. It fits a chat app, where a user waits and wants to see the first words soon. This job runs overnight in batch and latency is not a constraint, so nobody waits for the first words.

INCORRECT: Choose a model that Amazon Bedrock can fine-tune, so the team can train it on labeled past filings to raise the accuracy of each answer.
Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on labeled examples, which are pairs of inputs and the outputs that the team wants. It can improve a model on a specific task, and it fits a team that already holds such examples. This firm has no labeled examples of past filings, so it cannot train the model in the way that this option describes.

The team's automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock showed no problems in its built-in metrics. However, during the campaign launch, the marketing director rejected 80% of the captions for being "boring and off-brand."
Before the next release, the developer needs an evaluation that shows how close each caption comes to the brand voice, not only whether it passes.

A creative advertising agency uses Amazon Bedrock to generate witty social media captions for a beverage brand. The brand has a very specific, quirky "voice" that is difficult to quantify. Captions that follow the brand's written style guide are still off-brand.
The team's automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock showed no problems in its built-in metrics. However, during the campaign launch, the marketing director rejected 80% of the captions for being "boring and off-brand."
Before the next release, the developer needs an evaluation that shows how close each caption comes to the brand voice, not only whether it passes.
Which evaluation method should the developer choose?

options.text: Create a judge model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the brand style guide in a custom brand voice metric, and a rating scale from 1 for poor to 5 for excellent.
Create a human evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the agency's senior copywriters as the work team, and a custom brand voice metric that they rate on a Likert scale.
Create a judge model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the brand style guide in a custom brand voice metric, and a rating scale of pass or fail for each caption.
Create a human evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the agency's senior copywriters as the work team, and a custom brand voice metric that they rate thumbs up or down.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a human evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the agency's senior copywriters as the work team, and a custom brand voice metric that they rate on a Likert scale.
A human evaluation job sends the captions to a work team that the agency chooses, here its senior copywriters, who know the brand voice from their own work. A custom metric takes a name, a description and a rating method. With the Likert scale for a single response, each copywriter shows on a five-point scale how strongly a caption fits the voice. So the team sees how close each caption comes to the voice, and it can separate a caption that is almost right from a caption that misses the voice completely. A subjective quality such as alignment to a brand voice is the kind of metric that human evaluation is built for.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.3: "Develop user-centered evaluation mechanisms to continuously improve FM performance based on user experience"
Example: "rating systems for model outputs"

Sources:

  • Review a human-based model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock (console)
  • Model evaluation on Amazon Bedrock is now Generally Available
  • Manage a work team for human evaluations of models in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Create a judge model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the brand style guide in a custom brand voice metric, and a rating scale from 1 for poor to 5 for excellent.
A judge model evaluation job with a custom metric scores each caption against the instructions in the metric's prompt, here the style guide, on a scale that the team defines. It fits a quality that a written rubric describes well, and it scores many captions quickly. Here captions that follow the style guide are still off-brand, so a judge that scores against that guide would rate off-brand captions well.

INCORRECT: Create a judge model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the brand style guide in a custom brand voice metric, and a rating scale of pass or fail for each caption.
A custom metric for a judge model can also use text values such as pass and fail. That fits a clear rule that a written guide states, for example a required hashtag in every caption. This option fails twice: the judge scores against a style guide that does not capture the voice, and a pass or fail result does not show how close each caption comes.

INCORRECT: Create a human evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with the agency's senior copywriters as the work team, and a custom brand voice metric that they rate thumbs up or down.
The right people rate the captions here, but thumbs up or down only marks each caption as acceptable or not acceptable. That fits a quick yes or no check on each output. The developer needs to see how close each caption comes to the voice, and a two-value rating gives the same result to a caption that is almost right and to a caption that misses the voice completely.

questions.promptHtml:
A company serves its own model through an API on Amazon ECS. Application Load Balancers front the API in two AWS Regions, and Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks send traffic to the second Region when the first fails.
In a failover test, the company's apps kept working, but every partner call failed. Partner firewalls allow traffic only to IP addresses listed in advance, and partners will not change those lists during an outage. Failover must stay automatic.
Which change keeps partner calls working during a failover?
questions.promptText:
A company serves its own model through an API on Amazon ECS. Application Load Balancers front the API in two AWS Regions, and Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks send traffic to the second Region when the first fails.
In a failover test, the company's apps kept working, but every partner call failed. Partner firewalls allow traffic only to IP addresses listed in advance, and partners will not change those lists during an outage. Failover must stay automatic.
Which change keeps partner calls working during a failover?

options.text: Keep the failover records, and shorten the health check request interval and the failure threshold, so Route 53 marks the first Region unhealthy sooner.
Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one endpoint group for the first Region, have partners allow its static IP addresses, and add the second Region in an outage.
Replace the failover records with Route 53 latency records that have health checks, so each partner reaches the closest healthy Region by the same name.
Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with an endpoint group for each Region's load balancer, and have partners allow its static IP addresses.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with an endpoint group for each Region's load balancer, and have partners allow its static IP addresses.
Global Accelerator gives each accelerator static IP addresses that stay with it for as long as it exists. An endpoint group holds endpoints in one Region, so the team adds one group for each Region's load balancer. Global Accelerator watches the health of the endpoints, and when the first Region fails, it sends new connections to the healthy endpoint in the other Region with no manual step. Partners add the static addresses to their allow lists once, and the same addresses keep working wherever the traffic goes.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.3: "Design resilient AI systems to ensure continuous operation during service disruptions"
Example: "cross-Region model deployment"

Sources:

  • Understanding AWS Global Accelerator use cases

  • How AWS Global Accelerator works

  • How Elastic Load Balancing works

INCORRECT: Keep the failover records, and shorten the health check request interval and the failure threshold, so Route 53 marks the first Region unhealthy sooner.
A shorter request interval and a lower failure threshold make Route 53 notice an unhealthy endpoint sooner. That fits a failover that works but starts too late. In the test, the company's apps kept working, so the failover itself worked. Partner calls failed because the second Region answers on addresses that the partner firewalls do not list, and faster health checks do not change those addresses.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one endpoint group for the first Region, have partners allow its static IP addresses, and add the second Region in an outage.
One endpoint group gives partners fixed addresses for an API in a single Region, which fits an API that runs in one place. Here a person must add the second Region during the outage, and the failover must stay automatic. Until someone adds it, the accelerator has no healthy endpoint to send partner calls to.

INCORRECT: Replace the failover records with Route 53 latency records that have health checks, so each partner reaches the closest healthy Region by the same name.
Latency records send each caller to the Region with the lowest latency, and with health checks Route 53 stops answering with a Region that is unhealthy. They fit an API in several Regions whose clients call it by name. The name still leads to the IP addresses of the load balancers, which Elastic Load Balancing can change as it scales them. Partner firewalls allow only addresses listed in advance, so calls to other addresses still fail.

questions.promptHtml:
A travel company's support assistant on Amazon Bedrock uses a guardrail on the Classic tier, with content filters for hate and insults and a denied topic for legal advice. At the current filter strength, the guardrail blocks hateful and insulting user messages in English and Spanish.
After the company launched the assistant in Brazil and Japan, many hateful and insulting messages in Portuguese and Japanese reached the model. These messages use many different words, so no fixed word list can cover them.
Which change makes the guardrail catch these messages?
questions.promptText:
A travel company's support assistant on Amazon Bedrock uses a guardrail on the Classic tier, with content filters for hate and insults and a denied topic for legal advice. At the current filter strength, the guardrail blocks hateful and insulting user messages in English and Spanish.
After the company launched the assistant in Brazil and Japan, many hateful and insulting messages in Portuguese and Japanese reached the model. These messages use many different words, so no fixed word list can cover them.
Which change makes the guardrail catch these messages?

options.text: Keep the content filters on the Classic tier, and raise the strength of the hate and insults filters to HIGH for the user messages that the guardrail checks.
Turn on the Standard tier for the legal advice denied topic, select a guardrail profile for cross-Region inference, and leave the hate and insults filters as they are.
Move the content filters to the Standard tier, and choose a guardrail profile when the team modifies the guardrail, so it can use cross-Region inference.
Keep the content filters on the Classic tier, and add a word filter that lists Portuguese and Japanese words for hate and insults in the messages that the guardrail checks.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Move the content filters to the Standard tier, and choose a guardrail profile when the team modifies the guardrail, so it can use cross-Region inference.
The Classic tier supports content filters only in English, French and Spanish, and guardrails are not effective in a language that is not supported. That is why the filters block these messages in English and Spanish but miss them in Portuguese and Japanese. The Standard tier gives content filters wide language support, and both Portuguese and Japanese are on its list. A guardrail on the Standard tier must use cross-Region inference, which the team turns on by choosing a guardrail profile when it modifies the guardrail. The requests then stay within Regions of the same geography. Each policy has its own tier setting, and the denied topic for legal advice is not part of the problem, so it needs no change.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content"

Sources:

  • Safeguard tiers for guardrails policies
  • Languages supported by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • Distribute guardrail inference across AWS Regions

INCORRECT: Keep the content filters on the Classic tier, and raise the strength of the hate and insults filters to HIGH for the user messages that the guardrail checks.
A higher filter strength makes the guardrail more likely to block content. It fits a case where harmful messages in a supported language still reach the model at the current strength. Here the guardrail already blocks these messages in English and Spanish at the current strength. The misses are in languages that the Classic tier does not support, and a higher strength does not add a language.

INCORRECT: Turn on the Standard tier for the legal advice denied topic, select a guardrail profile for cross-Region inference, and leave the hate and insults filters as they are.
Denied topics also have a Standard tier, and turning it on gives the legal advice topic wider language support. That fits a team whose denied topic misses questions in other languages. The messages that get through here are hate and insults, which the content filters handle. Those filters stay as they are, on the Classic tier, so they still miss messages in Portuguese and Japanese.

INCORRECT: Keep the content filters on the Classic tier, and add a word filter that lists Portuguese and Japanese words for hate and insults in the messages that the guardrail checks.
A word filter blocks exact words and phrases from a custom list. It fits a known, fixed set of terms, such as the names of competitors. These messages use many different words, so a list cannot cover them, and the content filters would still miss every message that the list does not hold.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A legal technology company is building a contract review application. When a user uploads a contract, the application uses Amazon Bedrock to perform three distinct, independent analyses: identifying high-risk clauses, checking for GDPR compliance, and summarizing termination conditions.
Currently, the application code executes these three model invocations sequentially (one after the other). Users report that the application feels sluggish, taking nearly 20 seconds to return the final consolidated report. The developer needs to minimize the total wall-clock time required to generate the report without sacrificing the quality of the analysis.
Which implementation strategy should the developer choose?
questions.promptText:
A legal technology company is building a contract review application. When a user uploads a contract, the application uses Amazon Bedrock to perform three distinct, independent analyses: identifying high-risk clauses, checking for GDPR compliance, and summarizing termination conditions.
Currently, the application code executes these three model invocations sequentially (one after the other). Users report that the application feels sluggish, taking nearly 20 seconds to return the final consolidated report. The developer needs to minimize the total wall-clock time required to generate the report without sacrificing the quality of the analysis.
Which implementation strategy should the developer choose?

options.text: Refactor the application to dispatch the three InvokeModel API requests concurrently using asynchronous programming (for example, asyncio or threads) or an AWS Step Functions Parallel state. Aggregate the results once all three requests complete.

Update the application to use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API for each of the three requests. Display the text of the first analysis to the user while the second and third analyses are still processing in the background.

Enable Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching for the system instructions shared across the three prompts. This will reduce the processing time for the input tokens, thereby lowering the total latency of the sequential sequence.

Refactor the application to use AWS Step Functions Express Workflow with three sequential Task states, each invoking Amazon Bedrock via the optimized arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel service integration, replacing raw SDK calls with managed orchestration to reduce per-invocation overhead.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Refactor the application to dispatch the three InvokeModel API requests concurrently using asynchronous programming (for example, asyncio or threads) or an AWS Step Functions Parallel state. Aggregate the results once all three requests complete.
The three analyses do not depend on each other, so no analysis has to wait for another one to finish. Today the application sends each request only after the previous one returns, so the report takes the time of all three calls added together. When the application sends the three InvokeModel requests at the same time, the report takes about as long as the slowest single call. Asynchronous code in the application can do this. A Step Functions Parallel state can do it too: it runs its branches as concurrently as possible, waits until every branch finishes, and passes on an array with the result of each branch. The application then joins the three results into one report. Each analysis keeps its own prompt and model, so the quality of the analysis does not change.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.1: "Create responsive AI systems to address latency-cost tradeoffs and improve the user experience with FMs"
Example: "parallel requests for complex workflows"

Sources:

  • Parallel workflow state

  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions

  • Prompt caching for faster model inference

INCORRECT: Update the application to use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API for each of the three requests. Display the text of the first analysis to the user while the second and third analyses are still processing in the background.
InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the model's response in a stream, so text can appear on the screen while the model is still writing it. Streaming fits a chat window, where users want to see the first words quickly. Here the developer must cut the time until the final consolidated report is ready. The second and third analyses still start only after the first one, so the report is complete no sooner than before. The user sees the first analysis earlier, but waits just as long for the whole report.

INCORRECT: Enable Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching for the system instructions shared across the three prompts. This will reduce the processing time for the input tokens, thereby lowering the total latency of the sequential sequence.
Prompt caching stores a repeated part of a prompt, such as long shared instructions, so that later requests do not process those input tokens again. It reduces response latency and input token costs for supported models, and it fits workloads that send the same long context many times. Here it does not change the order of the work. The three calls still run one after another, and the report still waits for the sum of the three call times. Running the calls at the same time removes that wait, which is what the developer must minimize.

INCORRECT: Refactor the application to use AWS Step Functions Express Workflow with three sequential Task states, each invoking Amazon Bedrock via the optimized arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel service integration, replacing raw SDK calls with managed orchestration to reduce per-invocation overhead.
An Express workflow can call InvokeModel through the optimized Amazon Bedrock integration of Step Functions, because that integration supports the Request Response pattern that Express workflows use. The integration replaces the team's own SDK code with a managed call. Here the three Task states run one after another, and each one starts only when the state before it ends. The report still takes the time of all three calls. A change in who makes the calls does not change their order. A Parallel state with one branch for each analysis would remove the wait.

questions.promptHtml:
A company summarizes support tickets with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Last month, the team moved the prompt to a model from another provider, and the company must stay on that model. Since the move, many summaries no longer follow the required three-part layout. Last week, the prompt writers added three examples of the layout to the prompt, and the results did not change. Each summary may use only one model call.
How should the team fix the prompt?
questions.promptText:
A company summarizes support tickets with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Last month, the team moved the prompt to a model from another provider, and the company must stay on that model. Since the move, many summaries no longer follow the required three-part layout. Last week, the prompt writers added three examples of the layout to the prompt, and the results did not change. Each summary may use only one model call.
How should the team fix the prompt?

options.text: Select the new model for the prompt in Prompt Management, choose Optimize, run the optimized variant and the original on sample tickets, and save the better one as a new version.
Add more examples of the layout to the prompt in Prompt Management, compare the changed prompt with the current version on sample tickets, and create a new version if it is better.
Set the prompt in Prompt Management back to the previous model, compare the changed prompt with the current version on sample tickets, and create a new version if it is better.
Split the prompt in Prompt Management into one prompt for the summary and one for the layout, and run them as two prompt nodes in a flow.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Select the new model for the prompt in Prompt Management, choose Optimize, run the optimized variant and the original on sample tickets, and save the better one as a new version.
Prompt optimization in Amazon Bedrock rewrites a prompt for one model. In Prompt Management, the team selects a model and chooses Optimize, and Amazon Bedrock optimizes the prompt for the model that the team chose. The optimized prompt appears as a variant beside the original, so the team can run both on the same sample tickets and compare their layouts. If the optimized variant follows the layout, the team replaces the original with it and chooses Create version, which takes a snapshot of the draft. This is a change beyond adding examples, which the writers already tried. The company stays on the new model, and each summary still uses one model call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.3: "Troubleshoot prompt engineering problems to improve FM response quality and consistency beyond basic prompt adjustments"

Sources:

  • Optimize a prompt
  • Prompt Optimization in Amazon Bedrock now generally available
  • Node types for your flow

INCORRECT: Add more examples of the layout to the prompt in Prompt Management, compare the changed prompt with the current version on sample tickets, and create a new version if it is better.
Examples of the expected output are a common first step when a model does not follow a format. Here the prompt writers already added three examples of the layout last week, and the results did not change. More examples of the same kind repeat a change that the new model has already shown it does not follow. The team needs a different kind of change to the prompt for this model.

INCORRECT: Set the prompt in Prompt Management back to the previous model, compare the changed prompt with the current version on sample tickets, and create a new version if it is better.
Moving a prompt back to the model that it was written for is a quick way to undo a model change that failed. It fits a company that is free to choose its model. Here the company must stay on the new model. The old model would bring the layout back, but it would break that rule.

INCORRECT: Split the prompt in Prompt Management into one prompt for the summary and one for the layout, and run them as two prompt nodes in a flow.
A chain of prompt nodes in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows splits a hard task into steps. Each prompt node sends its prompt to a model and passes on the generated response, so a second node can put the first node's text into a layout. This fits a task that can pay for several model calls. Here each summary may use only one model call. Two prompt nodes make two model calls for every summary.
