A daily Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the bucket already finds every file that holds card numbers. The data owners read the findings once a week, and twice a flagged file reached a fine-tuning job first. The privacy team approved Macie as the only tool that decides which files hold sensitive data. Now each flagged file must leave the training prefix within minutes of its finding, with no person's action, and its data owner must get an alert.
Which setup meets these needs?
questions.promptText:
A company fine-tunes a model in Amazon Bedrock each week on chat files that teams upload to an Amazon S3 bucket. A daily Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the bucket already finds every file that holds card numbers. The data owners read the findings once a week, and twice a flagged file reached a fine-tuning job first. The privacy team approved Macie as the only tool that decides which files hold sensitive data. Now each flagged file must leave the training prefix within minutes of its finding, with no person's action, and its data owner must get an alert.
Which setup meets these needs?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for Macie sensitive data findings on the bucket, with a Lambda target that moves the file to a quarantine prefix and alerts its owner.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for Macie sensitive data findings on the bucket, with an Amazon SNS topic target that emails each new finding to the bucket's data owners.
Add an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function for each new training file, which checks it with Amazon Comprehend, moves files with PII to a quarantine prefix, and alerts their owners.
Add an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function for each new training file, which checks it with Amazon Comprehend and sends each PII finding to an Amazon SNS topic for the data owners.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for Macie sensitive data findings on the bucket, with a Lambda target that moves the file to a quarantine prefix and alerts its owner.
Macie publishes each new sensitive data finding to Amazon EventBridge immediately after it finishes processing the finding. Events from AWS services go to the account's default event bus, so a rule on that bus can match the Macie findings for the training bucket. The rule's target is an AWS Lambda function. The function moves the flagged file to a quarantine prefix that the fine-tuning job does not read, and it sends an alert to the file's data owner, for example through an Amazon SNS topic. The daily Macie job still decides which files hold card numbers, and no person has to act before the file leaves the training prefix.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "automated alerting and remediation workflows"

Sources:

  • Processing Macie findings with Amazon EventBridge

  • Configuring publication settings for Macie findings

  • Events from AWS services

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for Macie sensitive data findings on the bucket, with an Amazon SNS topic target that emails each new finding to the bucket's data owners.
An SNS topic target sends each Macie finding to the data owners soon after Macie publishes it. This fits a team that only needs to hear about findings quickly and then acts on each one by hand. Here each flagged file must leave the training prefix with no person's action. An email still waits for a data owner to move the file, and a fine-tuning job can start first.

INCORRECT: Add an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function for each new training file, which checks it with Amazon Comprehend, moves files with PII to a quarantine prefix, and alerts their owners.
An S3 event notification can invoke a Lambda function for each new object, and Amazon Comprehend can detect PII such as card numbers in text. This design checks each file as soon as it arrives, moves it, and alerts its owner, so it fits a team that has no Macie job. Here the privacy team approved Macie as the only tool that decides which files hold sensitive data. With this design, Comprehend would make that decision instead of Macie.

INCORRECT: Add an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function for each new training file, which checks it with Amazon Comprehend and sends each PII finding to an Amazon SNS topic for the data owners.
This design checks each new file with Amazon Comprehend and sends an alert through Amazon SNS. It fits a team without Macie that only needs to hear about PII and then decides by hand what to do. It fails two rules here. The privacy team approved Macie as the only tool that decides which files hold sensitive data, and an alert alone leaves the file in the training prefix until a person moves it.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs its AI applications in one AWS account that is not part of an organization in AWS Organizations. Developers create the IAM roles for their own AWS Lambda functions that call Amazon Bedrock, and they must keep doing so without waiting for another team. They also write the policies for these roles. The governance team maintains a managed policy, ApprovedModels, that allows the actions that the functions need, with bedrock:InvokeModel only on the approved models. No role that a developer creates may invoke any other model, and developers must not be able to remove this limit later.

What should the governance team configure?
questions.promptText:
A company runs its AI applications in one AWS account that is not part of an organization in AWS Organizations. Developers create the IAM roles for their own AWS Lambda functions that call Amazon Bedrock, and they must keep doing so without waiting for another team. They also write the policies for these roles. The governance team maintains a managed policy, ApprovedModels, that allows the actions that the functions need, with bedrock:InvokeModel only on the approved models. No role that a developer creates may invoke any other model, and developers must not be able to remove this limit later.
What should the governance team configure?

options.text: Allow developers iam:CreateRole only with an iam:PermissionsBoundary condition that names ApprovedModels, and deny them permission to remove or replace the boundary of a role and to change ApprovedModels.

Set ApprovedModels as the permissions boundary of the developers themselves, allow them iam:CreateRole with no condition, and deny them permission to remove or replace the boundary of a role and to change ApprovedModels.
Attach a service control policy to the account that denies bedrock:InvokeModel on every model except the approved models, and allow developers iam:CreateRole with no condition.
Remove iam:CreateRole from the developers, and have the governance team create each function role with ApprovedModels as the only policy of that role for Amazon Bedrock.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Allow developers iam:CreateRole only with an iam:PermissionsBoundary condition that names ApprovedModels, and deny them permission to remove or replace the boundary of a role and to change ApprovedModels.
A permissions boundary is a managed policy that sets the maximum permissions that identity-based policies can grant to a role. The role can perform only the actions that both its policies and its boundary allow. Here developers can call iam:CreateRole only when the request sets ApprovedModels as the boundary of the new role, which the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key checks. So every new role can invoke only the approved models. The deny statements keep this limit: developers cannot remove the boundary of a role, replace it with another policy, or change ApprovedModels. Developers still create their own roles without waiting for another team.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.3: "Create organizational governance systems to ensure consistent oversight of FM implementations"

Sources:

  • Permissions boundaries for IAM entities

  • Creating a permissions boundary

  • Service control policies (SCPs)

INCORRECT: Set ApprovedModels as the permissions boundary of the developers themselves, allow them iam:CreateRole with no condition, and deny them permission to remove or replace the boundary of a role and to change ApprovedModels.
A permissions boundary on the developers themselves limits only what the developers can do, and the deny keeps that boundary in place. This fits a team that wants to limit the access of its developers. Here it fails in two ways. ApprovedModels allows only the actions that the functions need, so as the boundary of the developers, it blocks iam:CreateRole. Also, a boundary on the developers does not pass to the roles that they create. A developer could create a role with no boundary, and that function role could invoke any model.

INCORRECT: Attach a service control policy to the account that denies bedrock:InvokeModel on every model except the approved models, and allow developers iam:CreateRole with no condition.
A service control policy (SCP) is a type of organization policy that manages permissions for the accounts in an organization. An SCP that denies other models is a strong control when many accounts belong to one organization. SCPs are available only in an organization that has all features enabled. This account is not part of an organization in AWS Organizations, so there is no SCP to attach to it.

INCORRECT: Remove iam:CreateRole from the developers, and have the governance team create each function role with ApprovedModels as the only policy of that role for Amazon Bedrock.
A central team that creates every role keeps full control of the policies of each role. This fits a company where developers may not change IAM at all. Here developers must keep creating their own roles without waiting for another team. With this design, every new function waits for the governance team.

questions.promptText:
A company's RAG assistant searches approximate k-NN vector indexes in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. A nightly job adds the vectors of new documents. Last week, OpenSearch rejected the new vectors one night, while other document writes succeeded and JVM memory pressure and free storage stayed normal. The team found out the next morning. The team adds data nodes when needed, and it wants a warning several days before new vectors are rejected again.
Which Amazon CloudWatch alarm gives this warning?

options.text: Create an alarm on KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to a percentage that the team picks below 100.
Create an alarm on JVMMemoryPressure with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to a percentage that the team picks below 100.
Create an alarm on KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to 1, the value that the metric reports once the breaker triggers.
Create an alarm on ClusterIndexWritesBlocked with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to 1, the value that the metric reports once writes are blocked.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an alarm on KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to a percentage that the team picks below 100.
KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage is a per-node metric for the share of native memory that k-NN graphs use, compared with the k-NN circuit breaker limit. When it reaches 100 percent, the circuit breaker triggers and OpenSearch rejects new knn_vector indexing. That is what happened on the night of the failure. Because the metric shows how close each node is to the limit, an alarm on its Maximum statistic at a percentage below 100 enters the ALARM state before the limit is reached. The team then has time to add data nodes. AWS gives no recommended threshold, so the team picks its own value.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.5: "Create vector store operational management systems to ensure optimal vector store operation and reliability for FM augmentation"
Example: "performance monitoring for vector databases"

Sources:

  • Monitoring OpenSearch cluster metrics with Amazon CloudWatch

INCORRECT: Create an alarm on JVMMemoryPressure with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to a percentage that the team picks below 100.
JVMMemoryPressure shows the highest share of the Java heap in use across the data nodes. An alarm on it fits a cluster where heap use slows searches or blocks writes. Here JVM memory pressure stayed normal on the night that OpenSearch rejected the new vectors. The limit that stopped the vectors is the k-NN circuit breaker limit for native memory, which a separate k-NN metric measures, so this alarm would stay in the OK state before the next failure.

INCORRECT: Create an alarm on KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to 1, the value that the metric reports once the breaker triggers.
KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered reports 1 when the k-NN circuit breaker has triggered in the cluster. An alarm on it fits a team that wants to know at once when vector indexing stops. Here the team wants a warning several days before new vectors are rejected. This metric changes to 1 only when the limit is already reached, so the alarm enters the ALARM state only at the moment of the failure, not before it.

INCORRECT: Create an alarm on ClusterIndexWritesBlocked with the Maximum statistic, and set its threshold to 1, the value that the metric reports once writes are blocked.
ClusterIndexWritesBlocked reports 1 when the cluster blocks incoming write requests. Common causes are free storage that is too low or JVM memory pressure that is too high. An alarm on it fits a cluster that fills its disks or its heap. Here other document writes still succeeded, and free storage and JVM memory pressure stayed normal, so the cluster did not block writes. Only the new vectors were rejected, and this alarm would stay in the OK state.

questions.promptHtml:
An online gaming platform is launching a GenAI-powered support assistant using multiple foundation models (FMs) from different providers in Amazon Bedrock. The security team has issued strict requirements for the assistant's input handling. Users must be prevented from submitting email addresses or phone numbers. Hate speech and insults must be blocked immediately. A specific list of known cheat codes and exploit keywords must be blocked from entering the model context. These rules must apply uniformly across all used FMs without rewriting application logic for each model.
Which solution should you implement to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An online gaming platform is launching a GenAI-powered support assistant using multiple foundation models (FMs) from different providers in Amazon Bedrock. The security team has issued strict requirements for the assistant's input handling. Users must be prevented from submitting email addresses or phone numbers. Hate speech and insults must be blocked immediately. A specific list of known cheat codes and exploit keywords must be blocked from entering the model context. These rules must apply uniformly across all used FMs without rewriting application logic for each model.
Which solution should you implement to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Apply one guardrail to every model call, with sensitive information filters that block email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
Apply one guardrail to every model call, with sensitive information filters that mask email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
Apply a separate guardrail to each model's calls, with sensitive information filters that block email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
Apply a separate guardrail to each model's calls, with sensitive information filters that mask email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Apply one guardrail to every model call, with sensitive information filters that block email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails work with a foundation model when each inference call names the guardrail ID and version, so one guardrail can serve every model that the assistant uses. Its sensitive information filters with the Block action stop a prompt that holds an email address or a phone number, and the guardrail returns the message that the team configures. Content filters for the Hate and Insults categories block hate speech and insults in prompts. A word filter blocks custom words and phrases by exact match, which fits a known list of cheat codes and exploit keywords. One guardrail keeps the rules the same for every model, and the team changes them in one place.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content"

Sources:

  • Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters
  • Block harmful words and conversations with content filters

INCORRECT: Apply one guardrail to every model call, with sensitive information filters that mask email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
The Mask action of a sensitive information filter replaces an email address or a phone number with its type, such as {EMAIL}, and lets the request go on. It fits an application that may receive personal data but must not pass it on, such as a tool that summarizes conversations between users and support agents. Here users must be prevented from submitting email addresses and phone numbers. With Mask, a prompt that holds them still goes through, so this rule is not met.

INCORRECT: Apply a separate guardrail to each model's calls, with sensitive information filters that block email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
A separate guardrail for each model fits a team whose models need different rules, such as a stricter filter strength for one model. Here the rules must be the same for every model. With one guardrail per model, the team keeps several guardrails with the same settings, changes each of them for every rule change, and tracks which guardrail goes with which model. One shared guardrail avoids that work, so this design does not have the LEAST operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Apply a separate guardrail to each model's calls, with sensitive information filters that mask email and phone, content filters for hate and insults, and a word filter for the cheat codes.
This design has two problems. A separate guardrail for each model adds guardrails that the team must keep the same, while the rules are the same for every model and the question asks for the LEAST operational overhead. The Mask action also lets a prompt with an email address or a phone number go through with the value replaced by its type, while users must be prevented from submitting these values.

questions.promptHtml:
A large financial services enterprise is building a centralized platform to allow internal development teams to consume foundation models (FMs) from Amazon Bedrock. For compliance and governance, the organization requires a GenAI gateway architecture with three requirements.
All internal applications must route requests through a single control point that logs every prompt and response for auditing. Whenever a prompt engineer updates a standard system prompt, it must be automatically evaluated for toxicity and accuracy before being made available to applications. PII must be automatically redacted from prompts before they are sent to the model provider.
Which combination of actions should you implement to achieve this?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A large financial services enterprise is building a centralized platform to allow internal development teams to consume foundation models (FMs) from Amazon Bedrock. For compliance and governance, the organization requires a GenAI gateway architecture with three requirements.
All internal applications must route requests through a single control point that logs every prompt and response for auditing. Whenever a prompt engineer updates a standard system prompt, it must be automatically evaluated for toxicity and accuracy before being made available to applications. PII must be automatically redacted from prompts before they are sent to the model provider.
Which combination of actions should you implement to achieve this?
Select TWO.

options.text: Build a REST API in Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda function that removes the PII that Amazon Comprehend finds, logs each prompt and response to CloudWatch Logs, and calls Amazon Bedrock.
Release each system prompt change through AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeBuild test stage that scores toxicity and accuracy, so a prompt that misses a threshold stops before deployment.
Grant each application role bedrock:InvokeModel, and turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to deliver the full prompt and response of every call to Amazon S3.
Create one Amazon Bedrock guardrail that masks PII and blocks toxic content, and require it in every model call with an IAM policy that uses the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.
Store the system prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and have an EventBridge rule on the default event bus invoke a Lambda function that scores each new version for toxicity and accuracy.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build a REST API in Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda function that removes the PII that Amazon Comprehend finds, logs each prompt and response to CloudWatch Logs, and calls Amazon Bedrock.
A GenAI gateway puts one API in front of the models. Amazon API Gateway gives every internal application the same REST API, and an AWS Lambda function behind it handles each request, so every request passes the same control point. The function calls Amazon Comprehend DetectPiiEntities, which returns each PII entity with its type and its position in the text, and the function replaces those parts of the prompt. It writes each prompt and response to CloudWatch Logs for audits, and only then calls Amazon Bedrock. The PII is gone before the request reaches the model provider.

CORRECT: Release each system prompt change through AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeBuild test stage that scores toxicity and accuracy, so a prompt that misses a threshold stops before deployment.
A CI/CD pipeline tests each change before it reaches applications. AWS CodePipeline starts a CodeBuild stage that runs test inputs through the updated system prompt and scores the outputs for toxicity and accuracy. When a score misses its threshold, the test stage fails. A failed action does not move the change to the next stage of the pipeline, so the deploy stage never makes the prompt available. Every update runs through the same tests, and no person has to start them.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.5: "Implement CI/CD pipelines and GenAI gateway architectures to implement secure and compliant consumption patterns in enterprise environments"
Example: "centralized abstraction layers"

Sources:

  • Create a Generative AI Gateway to allow secure and compliant consumption of foundation models
  • How pipeline executions work
  • Detecting PII entities

INCORRECT: Grant each application role bedrock:InvokeModel, and turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to deliver the full prompt and response of every call to Amazon S3.
Model invocation logging collects the full request data, response data and metadata of supported calls, and it delivers them to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs. It fits an audit need where applications call Amazon Bedrock directly. Here every application must route its requests through a single control point, and PII must be removed before a prompt reaches the model. Direct calls give no single control point, and the logs only record the PII that each prompt carried.

INCORRECT: Create one Amazon Bedrock guardrail that masks PII and blocks toxic content, and require it in every model call with an IAM policy that uses the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.
The bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key lets an IAM policy deny any inference request that does not include the named guardrail, and a guardrail can mask PII and filter harmful content. This fits a company that lets each application call Amazon Bedrock directly but wants the same safety settings on every call. Here all applications must route requests through a single control point that logs every prompt and response. Each application would still call Amazon Bedrock on its own, and a guardrail does not write the audit log of prompts and responses.

INCORRECT: Store the system prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and have an EventBridge rule on the default event bus invoke a Lambda function that scores each new version for toxicity and accuracy.
Prompt Management keeps numbered versions of each prompt, and each new version gets its own ID and ARN. CloudTrail records each CreatePromptVersion call. When a trail logs these calls, an EventBridge rule on the default event bus can match each one and invoke a Lambda function that scores the new version. This fits a team that wants a score for every version, for example for a weekly report. Here each updated prompt must be evaluated before it is made available to applications. The version already exists when the function scores it, and nothing in this design holds back a version that scores badly.
